div.p: CONFERENCE OF SCHOOL ATTEND- ANCE OFFICERS AT WARRINGTON. The Attendance Problem. The Warrington and District branch of the School Attendance Officers' National Association held their quarterly meeting in the old School Attendance Office, Sankey-street, on Saturday. Mr. T. Martindale, of Earlestown, presided, and there were present: Messrs. W. Bamber, W. Rutter, W. Farrar, and T. W. Holbrook (Warrington), T. Bromilow (St. Helens), 0. Davies (Widnes), W. Pasquill (Golborne), F. W. Barnes (Leigh), and T. Hipwell (Salford). THE LATE MR. JONES. Mr. Martindale was elected president pro tern. He referred to the death of Mr. William Jones, for many years chief School Attendance Officer at Warrington and said they had lost in him a valuable and esteemed friend. On the motion of Mr. RurrErt, seconded by Mr. BROMILOW, the following resolution was unanimously passed: "That this meeting of School Attendance Officers desires to place on record its regret at the loss sustained by the death of Mr. William Jones, who had been president of the branch since its formation in November, 1900, and to convey to Mrs. Jones and • her family their deep sympathy with them in their bereavement." THE SUPERANNUATION SCHEME. Mr. HIPWELL,in advocating a superannuation scheme, said it would be more profitable for the authorities in the long run as they would have greater efficiency. The proper scheme would be the passing of the Local Authorities Officers Superannuation Bill, which was on the lines of the Poor Law Officers Superannuation Act of 1896. Efficiency was lost thr9ugh the employment' of officers who were really too old for their work, but whom the committee could hardly discharge on account of their long service. The Post Office servants,teachers, and police had superannuation, and he thought school attendance officers were entitled to it also. The CHAIRMAN said he thought superannuation was farther off than ever under the County Councils. On the motion of Mr. BARNES, seconded by Mr. Buommow, Mr. Hipwell was cordially thanked for his °duress.
THE ATTENDANCE DIFFICULTY. TEE POVERTY AND IGNORANCE OF PARENTS.

Mr. Barnes, of Leigh, in a paper on theschool attend- ance problem, said the majority of those who discussed this question did not realise, because they did not live and move among the people, the extent of the moral depravity of a very large number of parents whom school attendance officers were constantly visiting, appealing to, and prosecuting in vain. Neither had they fathomed the depth of the poverty and ignorance in which man 7 of the lower classes were hopelessly submerged. English society was just waking up to see the results of generations of neglect cind injustice suffered by its poorer members. He thought it would take generations to repair the mischief of bygone cen- turies; to plant in the minds of these people a true appreciation of the value of education. It must be admitted also that the difficulties of many poor parents were overwhelmingly great. To feed and clothe half a dozen or more strong children with the paltry sum of twenty or twenty-five shillings per week, which the wages of hundreds of thousands of unskilled workers did not exceed, was a problem of which well-to-do classes had no conception. Indeed, it rarely had been solved. Food in many a home was often scarce and of the poorest kind; barefooted and half-clad children were common and unavoidable in such cases. The least derangement in the work of the bread winner, or in the health of the family, upset everything. How many hundreds of times had school attendance officers turned away from many a door baffled and saddened by the spectacle of wretchedness and misery. The effect of this state of things upon the health of the children and upon school attendance, bad never been calculated, not even by those omniscient talkers and writers on the subject. A thoroughly satis- factory attendance could never be obtained until the standard of the intelligence of the people was consider- ably raised, and their moral and material condition much improved. Notwithstanding these difficulties there was room for improvement in school attendance and as men experienced in all the obstacles with which the work was surrounded, they owed the nation a special obligation in this matter. The primary duty of a school authority was to provide proper accommoda- tion for every child in its district and to see that the name of every child was on the register of some school. Means must also be adopted to ensure that a child once in the fold should not again be lost, by its name being illegally removed from the registers. The most elementary duties were,he thought neglected by the majority of school authorities more than any other part of their work. They manifested much more anxiety about the ninety-nine within the fold than concerning the one lost sheep. School attendance officers had heard much within the last few years of the "derelict million "—a million children who were said to be not receiving education. The figures were themselves the wild product of some "derelict" imagination. He did not think that a sixth of the number stated could be properly termed "derelict.' The , large majority of absentees were children under five, and older scholars who habitually attended nine, eight or seven times per week, very large numbers of whom belonged to highly-respectable families. He agreed with the Board of education that there ought to be 20 per cent, of the total population on the school registers. The two chief reasons why this pro- portion vas not on the books of all districts were, first, the neglect of many local authorities to provide proper accommodation in time, instead of waiting until all the schools were overcrowded and the gutters filled with children; and secondly, the prevailing habit of taking the names of children off the books, who had not left the district or been admitted to another school. During nine years as an attendance officer, the conviction had been growing stronger and stronger in his mind that every year many thousands of the poorest, most neglected, and unfor- tunate children become derelict by this means. The annual census and the duplicate register were indispen- sable necessities to efficient work. An adequate number of intelligent officers should be employed in towns and all populous districts. There should be one officer to every 3,000 children, and before the duties could be satisfactorily carried out the officers must be in some measure connected with the State. Mr. BARNES was thanked for his paper, on the motion of Mr.RUTTER, seconded by Mr. DAVIES. It was decided that the next meeting should he held in November at Earlestown. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: YOUNGSTERS' FIRE.
div.p: THE YOUNGSTERS' FIRE.

The Cheshire Coroner has been notified of the death, at Runcorn Hospital, of Arthur Hewitt, aged three years, son of John Hewitt, Nelson-street. Two youths made a fire on the fair ground of rubbish from the shops of a draper and clothier. The child, playing there, set its clothing on fire, and was terribly burned.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Queen spent quite two hours at the sale and exhi- bition of the Home Arts and Industries Association at the Albert Ball, when. her Majesty visited all the stalls and made many purchases, especially of toys and models for her little grandchildren. The place oi honour was given to the stand belonging to the Sandringham School and next to this, was that of- the Irish branch -of the Association, but the Queen distributed her favors very equally, buying articles from nearly all the schools and centres represented. Her Majesty has from the first taken the greatest interest in the work of the Associa- tion which it has carried on for the past twenty years, and her patronage is a great encouragement to the movement. This is mainly to train poor people in their spare time in some useful art or craft, but many of the workers are cripples, or are unable for some or other reason to go out to work, and therefore these home industries which they are enabled to carry on, are in many instances their only source of livelihood. Cruelty and Fashion.—Professor Ray Lankester mani- fested a wise sense of the exigencies of the position when he sought to enlist the sympathy and co-opera- tion of the Princess of Wales for his crusade against the destruction of ospreys. Aigrettes which are ob- tained in such circumstances as to threaten the extinc- tion of the osprey, or white heron, appear to be worn as much as ever, but the representation is made that they are artificial. Professor Lankester who is Director of the natural history department of the British Museum, has had hundreds of these aigrettes submitted to him with a request that he would say whether or not they were artificial, and in every case he has found that they are not. The Press, and humane individuals have done their best to stay the slaughter of these beautiful birds. apparently without any success,and the only hope seems to be in the direction of a good example by the mem- bers of the Royal Family.. , Horsemanship Still Comes First.—Motoring and cycling have both taken a prominent place among the outdoor pleasures of women, but neither have diminished to any extent the display of fine horsemanship which is to be seen on any fine day in Hyde Park. There was some talk that women would be seen in the Row this season wearing the ride-astride skirt, but this style has not yet made its appearance in the park, nor is it likely to. There is no intention on the part of women riders to abandon the sidesaddle, either on the score of health or elegance. The old style is infinitely more graceful, and never does a girl—provided she knows how to ride —look more charming than on horseback. Fine Equipages.—Motor cars and electric broughams are increasing in London very rapidly, but in the parks there are still to be seen smartly turned out carriages with fine horses and splendid liveries. That belonging to the Duchess of Marlborough may be distinguished by its dark crimson lining, the servants being in black and silver liveries. The Duchess of Buccleuch may be seen almost any day in Hyde Park, and her landau is quite a feature of the throng of carriages, with the servants in wigs and powder, and knee breeches and silk stockings. The Countess Cadogan's carriages are always very attractive, as are also those of the Marchionness of Tweeddale. but the latter is often seen in a motor car. Other fashionable women who use the motor carriage are the Countess of Mar and Keine, Georgiana Countess of Dudley, Lady Wimborne, Lady Maud Warrender, the Countess of Aberdeen, Lady Wolverton, Lady Cynthia Graham and others too numerous to mention.

Are we a Musical People ?—As a nation we have always been supposed to be backward in the cultivation of music, but Dr. Cowen said the other day that "there is more good music performed throughout Great Britain in a day, than in many other countries in a week or a month.' Moreover he added that our orchestras are comix)sed chiefly of native instrumentalists. If that is the case it is very often concealei from 0- the public, as there was only recently an outcry amongst our musicians about the difficulty qf finding employment unless they disguised themselves as "Blue Hungarians " or some other non-English name. It is the same with bands. Many have vastly increased their popularity by changing an English title for a foreign one, though the instrumentalists have remained the same. It is interesting to note, whilst on this sub- ject that Mr. Andrew Carnegie was recently made an honorary member of the Guild of Musicians. Mr. Carnegie said on that occasion that music had always been one of his chief aspirations through life' and at Skibo Castle he is awakened every morning by the play- ing of the organ. The bagpipes are also a familiar feature in his Highland home, but Mr. Carnegie is very fond of the organ,and through his benefactions upwards .of five hundred organs have been installed in the Churches of Scotland.

The Second Court.—The second Court of the season was notable for the large number of perbonages in the Royal circle; the debut on her marriage of Princess Alexander of Teck ; and the first appearance at such a function of Princess Patricia of Connaught. Princess Alexander, looking very sweet and girlish, wore her soft white wedding dress, and carried a large posy of white flowers, and the young Princesses of Connaught were dressed alike, also in white satin, with trains of white gauze, lined with cloth of silver, and edged with frills of white chiffon. Taken altogether there was of course more colour than on the occasion of the first Court, but quite a number came in black, and white was greatly in evidence, both in the Royal circle and among the guests. Linen and Cloth Gowns.—The heat wav6 brought out muslin and linen gowns in vast numbers, and the idea of dressmakers to combine cloth with their linen crea- tions has proved a happy one. Linen when worn in May is apt to look previous, but the cloth trimmings give them just that touch of warmth necessary and when the cleaner has to be considered, it will be found that both fabrics respond equally well to the process. Irish linen of the coarser qualities is in great request just now, the fashionable colours being Eau de Nil, and a deep shade of emerald green, which are most effective when made up. The Arts of dyeing and Bleaching.—To have a white or light garment dyed some darker shade, is a process familiar to all of us but few know that it is now possible to have a coloured silk frock or wrap trans- formed into a white, or creamy white one.by the bleach- ing process. In the dyeing world, too,vast strides have been made of late and no one need have the least fear when submitting a handsome garment to this process. Dressmakers and tailors are great patrons of big dyeing firms, often sending fabrics, lace and trimmings of divers kinds to be dyed the exact shade required. The Green Veil.—Green or blue net, sprinkled thickly with bright red, blue or green chenille spots, I are the latest ideas in the veiling world, and they cannot be classed as fortunate ones. Few indeedare the women who can wear a drapery of green successfully, the average complexion being turned absolutely livid by such a veiling. If coloured veils are worn at all— always a risky procedure—certain shades in brown and pink are the wisest choice, but clear black, and ivory white veilings are the best from every point of view.
MADGE.

div.head: 1 FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: 1 FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

The fine weather we had recently brought out the foliage with a rush, and painted the public parks in all the colours of the rainbow, with many-hued fragrant blossoms., Sym- pathetic womankind at once responded to this aspect of Nature by appearing in dainty toilettes and gaily tinted floral hats which rivalled the hues of the trees and flower-beds. Easter is the acknowledged time for the debut of the latest creations of the millinery and modistic world; and, thanks to the delicious springlike weather of last month, there was no lack of pretty gowns and hats to be seen every- where. The fashions this year do not differ very greatly from those of last, and the lines of the newest skirts and bodices are quite as flowing and graceful as delighted our eyes last summer. I cannot but fancy that this lack of any great change results from the long- continued rain last season, when we had little or no opportnuity of displaying summer toilettes, but had to rest content with less diaphanous but more comfortable and warmer

div.head: rA USEFUL COSTUME.
div.p: rA USEFUL COSTUME.

garments suited to the dismal state of the atmosphere. Hence the fashions languished in unavoidable retirement, and there were consequently none, or, at least, very few, of the ordinary developments of the modes. This season we look for better things, and trust that the next few months will offer abundant op- portunity for the display of charming dresses of delicate shades of colour. Nevertheless, we cannot hope to get through the summer without the services of at least one useful cos- tume of cloth or serge. A pretty style is given in my first sketch of a smart yet simple coat and skirt which can stand any amount of hard wear, and yet is not at all dowdy- looking, It is made in. this instance of black cloth of a light make, with a dull surface free from the slightest suspicion of gloss. The front revers are of white satin spotted with tiny dull green dots of chenille, while the collar-band is of the satin plain stitched in rows. The coat is caught in at the waist by a band of soft green kid. The toilette is com- pleted by a green rustic straw hat trimmed with one or two large pink roses and a cream lace scarf, which forms a hanging veil at the back, With a pretty blouse worn underneath the little coat a costume like this would be found invaluable on many occasions, and could be worn on well into autumn, Brown cloth costumes are considered very modish

TOQUE. this season, but do not look so summer-like as navy blue, fawn, or black, for they seem to harmonise better with the tones of the falling Leaf than with the delicate verdant tints of the young leaves. Brown hats and toques, however, look very pretty with contrasting touches of pink introduced among the trim- ming; while one of the prettiest hats of cream lace and roses I have seen owed its cachet to brown velvet strings. The pretty toque depicted is made of brown drawn•tulle of a tint which verges on coffee in its dull, soft tint. It is trimmed with wreaths of pink and white flowers interspersed with tiny leaves, which after forming an edging to the brim, fall in heavy clusters on to the hair at the back. The shape is quite the latest, and the effect of the blending of the different delicate colours against the softly-tinted tulle is altogether charming. Crinoline, lace, and fine chip 'are among the most fashionable materials for the evolution of hats of the picturesque order, and some of the latest models display quite a high crown of the jam - pot order, very little trimming being used in these instances, the cunning skill of the milliner lying in the successful arrangement of the lace veil which drapes the crown and falls down the back, In contrast to this style of hat is the mushroom or bergere mode, which has been in vogue since

div.head: MORNING BLOUSE.
div.p: A MORNING BLOUSE.

Christmas, and which is eminently becoming to a Madonna style of face. The morning blouse shown in my last illus tration is of clear washing muslin, which has the deep yoke and sleeves lined in the latter being slightly tighter than the sleeve itself. The success of this blouse lies in its cut and fit, for the only trimming consists of groups of tiny ornamental buttons. For a summer morning, with or without a coat, a blouse of this style, whether expressed in muslin, silk, or cashmere, would be at once smart-looking and suitable to a time of day when one's dress should be as simple as possible to be in good taste. Muslin is a material eminently de- signed for the fashionable blouse of the moment, for it lends itself readily to gaugings and tuckings, and harmonises sweetly with insertions and railings of fine lace. It falls in soft folds should frills or pleats be neces- sary, and it clings when necessary to the out- lines of the figure. Indeed, many of the French models are of very fine muslin em- broidered in a floral design in very pale drab, while Valenciennes lace and insertion is liber- ally introduced between lines of very fine tucks, concluded by rows of fine gaugings. COQUETTE.

div.head: DEAD LOVE,
div.p: A DEAD LOVE,
BY MABEL COLLINS, Author of The Prettiest Woman in Warsaw," "A
Strange Visitor," &e.

Frank Ellerton was one of those fortunate persons who are liked by everybody and loved by a good many. As a child be was beautiful, and with naturally charming ways ; so that his father and mother and all his near relations worshipped him as a matter of course. At school he was called pgtty ; but a certain feline strength made itself fat beneath this prettiness. He was clever, and made others realise it. At college he became the idol, of a set of bright spirits, of whom he was the brightest. A great career was predicted for him, and he tried his hand at various forms of art —writing strange verses that lingered in the memory of those who read them, painting ,fasci- .:ating -"bits," and playing the violin nen for an amateur. But he grew tired of all these amuse- ments in turn, and took to collecting curios, very quickly developing a wonderful instinct for recog- nising treasures that it was worth while to possess. This occupation pleased him best of all ; it cost money, it passed away time, it was amusing, and it served to supply a topic of conversation in drawing-rooms. All this sounds as if Frank were a gentleman at large. Not so, indeed; though he had the appear- ance of it ,to the full. As a matter of fact, he was the spoilt and only son of a very successful London solicitor. This was all: and he had never tried to slur over the fact. It was useless, his father having had too many celebrated cases in his hands. Frank's college success had placed him in "society," some of his friends there being very grand people indeed. Frank's family was decidedly not in society, and dwelt just as happily at Brondesbury now as it did before he found it absolutely necessary to have rooms in Piccadilly, in order to own a decent address. Some hours

every morning he passed in his father's office. in 1 Soho, where ho shelved considerable aptitude for the kind of business which was there conducted. But he was not expected there after lunch. In the latter part of the day he went where it .pleased him. Sometimes it pleased him to go to Brondes- bury, for he liked being adored by his mother, and he enjoyed making love to Clare Waynefiete, his father's ward. He and Clare had been engaged, as they called it, before he went to school. When he finally came home from college, his parents consented to call it an engagethent. There had been a great deal of hesitation on their part, for very mixed reasons. Mrs. Ellerton thought her brilliant, beautiful boy, with . his womanish face and gentle manners, should marry some very grand person indeed, and she did not feel that there was anything to gratify her pride in his marriage with Clare. But his father looked at the matter very differently. He was anxious to be quite sure of Clare's feelings before be gave his consent; his conscience was exceedingly sensitive about this.

For Clare was the child'Of an old friend of his youth, who had left her large fortune entirely in his charge. He had fulfilled the trust righteously, and Clare was something of an heiress. He knew that it would be a rare stroke of good fortune for Frank if the marriage took place. For he was a man of the world, and did not think that any of the smart ladies who laughed and talked with Frank Ellerton at afternoon tea-parties would be at all likely to marry him. Clare's life had been so sheltered and spent in so profound a suburban seclusion that very few people realised her possessions. Her fortune was the least of these. She had rare beauty. and yei7 exceptional force and simplicity of character. She was very quiet in manner and reserved as to her thoughts, so that amonc, the good people of Brondesbury, especially among young ones, she remained an unknown quantity. Her old nurse understood her much better than did the smart persons with whom she took tea and danced; and old Mr. Ellerton had some very shrewd and creditable glimpses of insight with regard to her. He trembled with hope and fear as to Frank's ultimate success with her. He knew quite web that if Clare did marry him she would keep him straight. And he knew very well that he needed it. Clare had only one other serious admirer, and only herself and Mr. Ellerton had sufficient intelligence to recognise how very much in earnest this person was. He was a college friend of Frank's, and being so, thought it but right to keep himself in the background. For his world was one so far removed from Brondesbury that if Frank had not brought him to the Ellertons'.. bonne .he

would certainly never have seen Clare Wayneflete. So that he thought it due to Frank to give him every advantage; though he told himself he should never care to marry any other woman than Clare, and he believed he could win her love if he had the chance. But her whole soul was wrapped up in Frank Ellerton, and all her dreams were of him and his charming manner, his violet-blue . eyes, and his myriad accomplishments. Frank knew this, and felt perfectly safe. He gay. never a thought to Austin Montgomery, the severe- looking young curate with the cold, classical face, as a possible rival with Clare. But deep fires burnt .beneath that cold exterior of Austin's; and he was, like a fine race-horse, strong to endure. He was a curate at the East End of London, and had obtained permission to open mission-rooms, in which he did special work in the very heart of the, black poverty which is the 'disgrace of our nation. He had obtained this permission by the power of a long purse and great influence, for he was a poor curate only in seeming. He belonged to a rich family, and was free to do as he chose. His family was a good one, in the social language which was as unintelligible as Greek to the inhabitants of Brondesbury. So that when he came among them it was simply in the character of an East End curate. Fzank had been to visit at Austin's home in a far Midland county every year since their college days. The charm of manner and the brightness which had made him so popular in his boyhood had grown stronger as he reached man- hood, and the men who had delighted in his corn. panionship then delighted in it still more now, when he had many more things to talk about. There was no one like Frank Ellerton to brighten a country house-party or make a dull afternoon pass quickly. And as this personal charm and brightness, which di: so much to wile away the weary hours of crl.nv3ntional life, are always greatly in request, he had more invitations than he could possibly accept. He was a favourite at the Montgomerys', and his name was on the list for every sort of party. He went to them from Saturday to Monday when they were at their house on the river; he went to them for a week at a time when they were staying in Scotland; and when hey opened their house in town he was continually there. It seemed strange to Clare sometimes that she had never seen some of the most intimate friends of the man to whom she was betrothed; but the thought did not trouble her. Society, when it was composed of persons whom she knew nothing of, did not interest her. She did not consider, as many girls would have done, that the Mont- gomerys belonged to the great world, while the Ellertons sere suburban outsiders. When she thought of them at all it was as Frank's friends. For she loved Frank with a pure, simple, undis- guised love that was as fresh as the dew on a rosebud.

She was very like a rosebud herself, singularly fresh and sweet, with an air of remotenesa from the struggle of lite that was permanent with her. Nothing destroyed it, not even experience. She was not to be -tempted by the prizes that others fought for, and consequently her nature kept its precious characteristic of being but just unfolded, like a flower-bud, to the end. This was what Austin Montgomery found so intensely attractive in her, so unfailingly interesting. It was one afternoon in early summer, when they had been playing tennis, and sat tired and con- tented under the shadowy trees of the Brondesbury garden, that he told Clare this. He spoke in a low voice, in quick, earnest words; told her that he found her more interesting and more attractive than anything else in life; that his power for good would be infinitely greater if she were with him always, his friend and his love. He wanted her to be his wife—wanted it as we want only one thing in a lifetime. Clare was wise enough to understand something of the honour he had done her—to know that lie was greater in purpose than anyone else she had ever met, as well as "some- body" by birth—while the rest of her acquaintance were nobodies. All this was wonderfully plain to her, considering that she was a Mere girl and had wen nothing of the world but then she was very sensible and keenly intelligent. But in spite of understanding quite fully the honour done to her, she shook her head and refused it. She loved Frank Ellerton ; she considered herself engaged to him. This Austin had not known, and when he heard the engagement announced a few months later, he felt he had been foolish. This public announcement of the engagement would not have taken place—at all eveats, not at that time—but for an occurrence which all but ruined all Frank Ellertuo p hopes of future ease and comfort.

Atittin Montgomery was regarded as sufficiently intimate and important friend of the family to receive the news sneciallv from Mrs. Ellerton herdeir. Sh.e had na"twe for a moment thought or his possibly caring for Clare himself. He was so quiet that she did not look on him as a man likely to marry. And she had been well informed by her husband as to the Montgomery family, its position and its wealth. She knew that Clare's fortune would be no temptation to him, and she considered Clare no catch for anybody. So she told Austin the news in a very matter-of-fact way. He went quietly home to his East End mission-house and shut himself in his study, where he lit a pipe, and then fell into so deep a fit of thought that he let it out.

This thoughtful humour was broken up by the arrival of Frank Ellerton, who was admitted to the house as an intimate friend, and came knock- ing at the door of the study. He had never yet been shut out by Austin; and now, after a second's pause in which his face would have looked strange to Frank could he have seen it, Austin went to the door and opened it, with the same smile as ever. Frank hardly glanced at him, and would perhaps not have noticed had the smile been absent. He was full of himself and of his own affairs. He sat down in an easy-chair by the fire and began to talk.

"You've been told about the engagement, I sup- pose, old chap ? " he asked, as he proceeded to light a cigarette. Austin nodded gravely. "By George! ' Frank went on, "it's been touch-and-go with me this time. But it's all right now." And he drew a long breath as of great relief. "It's all been settled in a precious hurry," be said, in a rather discontented tone. "I always meant to do it some day, of course, but not quite so soon. Bachelor freedom over now! and it's our old friend Miss Sue Bacon that's responsible for it."
"What ? " exclaimed Austin. "How do you mean ? "

"Yes, indeed, pretty Miss Sue at the stationer's shop, that every one of us undergraduates tried to flirt with. Would you believe it—that she declared I had actually proposed to her, and threatened a breach of promise case?" „ _ _ .. . _
"Well !—and Miss Ilacon is a straightforward, independent• young lady, if ever there was oho! You must have flirted with .her pretty badly, Frank."

"0 lord! no—not more than the rest, I assure you." And Frank lounged back in his chair and laughed. But there was profound disbelief in the earnest look Austin fixed on him. He did not see it, but went on with his tale.

"The guy'nor's had to pay a precious lot of debts for me lately, and has behaved well over it, must say. I was having a very good time, when Miss Sue breaks up the harmony. After writing various useless and silly letters to me, which, of course, remained unanswered, because there was really nothing for me to say, she made an attack on the governor himself—wrote to him—made an appointment with him—came up to town and saw him, with her father. Of course, the results were disastrous. If only she had given me any idea that she meant business in that style I'd have given her some good diamonds to stay away. I've plenty of credit, and the guy'nor always paid sooner or later. But not after his interview with the Bacon family. He sent for me in the most formidable manner, and announced that he would pay not another brass farthing unless I effectually disposed of Miss Sue and got myself finally accepted by Clare Wayneflete at once."

"And you did it ? " "I did it. .I can always do a thing when I am put to it," said Frank, not boastfully, but in a pensive manner, with a modest consciousness of his talents. "I had a little conversation with Miss Sue, and a little conversation with Miss Clare; and though I must own they were both pretty hard work, lam proud to say they were both successful."

"Miss Wayneflete had not heard anything of the other matter, I presume? " said Austin, his voice taking on a curious dryness, in spite of all his efforts to prevent its expressing any kind of feeling. "Oh, yes. Sue took care pf that. But Clare forgave me, like the little brick she is. I assured her 1 was a mere boy, a- child, when I admired Miss Sue; and that from the time I first saw her- self, when she came to live with my people, I had never draught of anyone else. And she believed me. What angels women are ! " Austin smoked in silence, without responding to this burst of enthusiasm ; and he was so taciturn for the rest of the evening that Frank got rather bored, and went away early. _

About a week later Clare received a note from Austin asking her to come and visit his mission- rooms on a certain afternoon, when there was to bo a tea-party, and some prize-giving was to take place. "My sister, Mrs. 'Weir, will be here," he 'rote, "and she would like to meet you." Clare i.ook this as an honour consequent on her engage- ment to their friend, and wrote to accept with pleasure. She knew Mrs. Weir was a young widow, rich, very good-looking, and a very smart person. Mrs. Weir had never wanted to meet her before. She was very happy just then, proud of Frank, and very much in love with him. All good things that she had seemed to her to result from the fact that he had chosen to smile on her. The day came, and after lunch Clare went to dress herself, taking the greatest cure to please Frank's friends. She had a charming, instinctive taste in dress, quite unaffected by Brondesbury fashions or Mrs. Ellerton's ideas; and she made herself look delightful. She went off alone on the Sabbath day's journey from the north-west of London to the far east, after the madner of modern independent young women. Mrs. Ellerton did not approve of these ways, but Clare was very resolute in some things, though very quietly so. She found the mission itself with some difficulty, and was amazed a the sordid and horrible poverty which it stood amidst. She had not thought of the possibility of not being able to get a cab, and of having to walk through those dreadful streets; but this surprise was soon lost in amazement at the sights and sounds about her. She was glad indeed when she found the "hall, and saw Austin Mont- gomery just within the door. An exceedingly pretty young woman was standing beside him, whom he at once introduced as his sister, Mrs. Weir. Clare was interested in Austin's work, which was a wonder and a revelation to her; and she was delighted with his sister, who was very kind and sweet to her, and invited her to come and see her while she was staying in town. This invitation pleased Clare, and she tokl the others of it at dinner when she got home. Frank was there, and to her great surprise he did not seem pleased. He did not seem to like Mrs. Weir, and spoke, as Clare thought, unkindly of her. This impression passed away, however; later on, when they were alone, he admitted that Mrs. Weir was both charming and beautiful; and he liNie Clare not to mind his being vexed, assuring her that his love for her was so great that be was jealous of every- one who even liked her. And Clare was so much in love with him that this confession pleased her, and made her blush and smile. • Mrs. Weir took Austin home with her when she went away. "You must come and dine with me,' she said; and he willingly left behind the horrors and the hopeless problems which surrounded his mission, for a little while. Mrs. Weir's brougham came for her; and a quick pair of horses soon carried them down the dreary length of Mile End Road (where old-time romance is covered over with modern misery and sordidness, just as one smu-times sees fine old carving hidden with dirt— or worse, perhaps, with whitewash l) through the City, and presently to the comparatively fresh air of the Park. Close by Park Lane Mrs. Weir had a pretty little house of her own, which her husband had left her. She had some cousins stay- ing with her, so that she was not alone with Austin except during their drive, and in that time she learnt all Clare's simple story, so far as he knew it. -

"And she is engaged to Frank Ellerton! " she said at last, a world a meaning in her words. "That is why 1 wanted you' to see her," said her brother significantly. She made no answer. It did not seem necessary for her to ask the reason for this. The next. afternoon she drove out to Brondesbury and called on Clare, who, being very charmed by her new acfpaintance, was easily persuaded to drive back with her and stay to dinner. Mrs. Weir's cousins were dining nut that evening, so she had arranged a very special little party of her own —Clare Wayneflete and just other young woman. mi This other guest ca e n at dinner-time, in full evening dress. She was .handsome, with dark hair and hard, bright eyes. She wore black satin, made in a yery new. fashien, which Clare had never seen. Mrs. Weir introduced her as Lady Isobel Feversharn. Dinner was announced directli she arrked, and the three young women went, into the dinipg-room and sat down together at a table that was almost covered with winter roses. It was a new experience for Clare; she had seen nothing as yet of modern life, and she fancied dinner hardly existed where man was absent. Lady Isobel proved to be delightful company—bright, satirical, and rather bitter, yet always amusing. She shewed herself to be a sceptic and a pessimist of the first water long before the sweets appeared.
"isobel wasn't always like this," said Mrs. We:r to Clare; "she used not to scoff at everything. wish I could cure her of it."
"You never will now," said Lady Isobel. "I have learnt my lesson." . . . _ _ _

"Ah, but iC is foolish to judge all the world by a single experience." exclaimed Mrs. Weir. "1 am not so sure of that," said Lady Isobel. "One taste of sea-water is enough for most people.' Mrs. Weir laughed. "Will you tell us about your taste of sea-water after dinner? " "Yes, if you wish it," said Lady Isobel, "though it's a little unkind of you to ask 'tie to." "No," said Mrs. Weir, gently and earnestly. "I wish it. I have a reason."

"Oh! if lean save any other woman from believing the nonsense Men talk, well and good. Give me some moro peppered almonds, please; they are truly delicious with sherry." Mrs. Weir handed the little dish, laughing. "You are not dead yet," she said. "I should hope not ! " exclaimed Lady IsobeL "I was a fool to love and to believe—but I am not such a fool as to pine and regret ! There are still pleasures in life, you know—peppered almonds, and Wagner. Don't let me be late for the opera, will you, dear? I forget time and space when I tell stories."

They went back to the drawing-room and sat by the fire, and Lady Isobel talked. She chattered away, in her cold, bright fashion, of everything in heaven and earth; but presently Mrs. Weir reminded her of her promise to describe her "first taste of sea-water." She changed suddenly then, dropped her voice and spoke earnestly, with a pathetic cadence that sounded strange to Clare, who had only heard her mock and laugh. She told a tale of passionate love and of bitter dis- illusionment. "It is not every woman who would tell a tale like that out of her own experience," she said, meeting Clare's eyes fixed on her in wonder and sympathy, "but I do vhen I meet a young wdman who is likely to believe in some man's lies—as a duty—as an expiation," she added, with a sudden sigh. And Clare sighed too, for she felt how deeply Lady Isobel had loved. At that moment a servant Came to say that Lady Isobel's carriage was waiting; she rose, put on her silken wraps, and went away laughing, the same glittering, heartless creature that she had seemed when she arrived. •

Mrs. Weir came and put her hand on Clare's. "She did not tell you the name of the man," she said ; "of course not—she never speaks of him. lam going to tell you—no, do not stop me—l have a rel., on for telling you, of which she knew nothing. The man she loved was Frank Ellerton ! " Clare sank back in her chair, so white that Mrs. W air ran to 'her thinking she was going to faint. But Clare did not. She was not the kind of girl who faints easily. And she was so busy thinking that she had barely time to feel—yet! Mrs. Weir sent her home in her carriage, and her last words were: "I shall come and see you to- morrow. Try to believe that I have done this because I really like you." "Of course I believe that," Clare said "Why should I try? " "Can't you guess ? " said Mrs. Weir. "I my- self doubt myself sometimes. And never have I done so more than in this affair. For, as Isobel knows well, though she forbore to mention it in her list of crimes, Frank Ellerton made hot love to me last season, and I was on the eve of accept- ing him, when I gat to know her well enough to hear her story. And now I think—l believe I have not acted from revenge, but because I want to save you. Your love should be given to a man as single-hearted as yourself." Clare went away bewildered, full of strange and passionate thoughts. All the woman in her was awakened. When she reached the house Frank was at home, .and came out into the hall to welcome her; but she said she was too tired to talk, and passed on. Frank went back to the drawing-room with a very grave face. He had been delighting his mother by shewing her some curios he had been buying, and telling her about them. No pleasure or amusement the world could offer was so great to her as listening to Frank's voice, and watching his handsome. face when he chose to put on its charming expression for her benefit. That expression was gone now, alas! she saw at a glance that the pleasure of the even- ing was over for her, and she felt angry with Clare, whose fault it evidently was. The next day Clare did not appear until the afternoon, and then, hearing that Frank was in the house, she left' her room and went in search of him. It was a sunny day, and he was out in the garden. Clare joined him there, and they walked up and down a long gravel path in the sunshine. Mrs. Ellerton, looking from the window, little guessed how serious the interview was for her boy. He pleaded hard and passionately, and did not cease till Clare said: "It is useless, Frank. I cannot marry you; my love for you is dead." Then he turned on his heel and went quiCkly into the house. Clare lingered in the sunshine, feeling very tired and sad. Half an hour later Mrs. Ellerton found Frank shut in the library, crying like a child. "It's no use! " he said, "no use! The guv'nor will never pay my debts now. He's no idea what they are—l've never dared to give him an idea. I'm done for, mother ! " And so he' was. He had not the courage to face his father, and went abroad, hoping .the storm might blow over in time. But it did not. He had left his father to bear the whole brunt of it, and it was too much. Frank Ellerton ended his days as one of the melancholy army of ruined men. A year later Clare Wayneflete became Austin Montgomery's wife. Rich and free, though they are, they spend most of their time at• the little mlseion-house in the East End, where their presence is as the presence of angels. For Clare thorcughly enters into her husband's work. Her greatest friend is Mrs. Weir, who has since married again, and become a Countess. Lady Isobel has mado a great marriage, but the hard glitter in her eyes, left there by her love for Frank Ellerton, has never quite left them. (THE ,END. 1 WIDNES HERO- RECOGNISED.

On Monday evening at the Widnes Police Station Mr. S. Brighouse presented Mr. Alexander Wright, of James-street, Widnes, with the bronze medal of the Royal Humane Society. In January two boys fell into the river Mersey at Widnes. Wright immediately entered the water and succeeded in rescuing one of them. He dived into the river again in search of the other boy, but failed to find him. Wright had to be lifted out of the water in consequence of his exhausted condition. At the inquest he was complimented by the coroner and jury. It afterwards transpired that Wright bad previously saved three lives. On Monday evening his conducl was recognised for the first time.

div.p: THE THEATRE OF THE WAR.
THE WAR IN THE FAR EAST.

By the time these lines are in print the treat battle, which appears to be imminent Liaoyang, may have taken place, but, on 'the other hand, the Japanese have little to Tain by undue hurry and are certain to render their lines of communication thorough- 'ltY secure before fighting such a vital action, 'as they have the advantage at every point and cannot now afford to give a point away bY undue precipitancy. In the west we are, 'owing to strict censorship on both sides, -anything but well-informed about things in .the East, and even the exact balance of 'Power is uncertain. It would, however, 'aLppear impossible that General Kuropatkin ,nas more than too,ooo men concentrated at Liaoyang, which he seems to have taken up and fortified as his strategic position, though 'even now it is possible that he may find it advisable to withdraw on Mukden or Harbin. 'On the other hand, the Japenese seem to have ;between 300,000 and 400,000 troops with 800 Vins at their easy disposal of which the First Army under General Kuroki is ad- vancing rapidly from the victory of Kulien- •cheng, foo,ooo strong, and the Second Army 'of the same strength, under General Oku, is tasking. for Liaoyang from Takushan. Of the other troops available there is the Inysterious Third Army, of which not a -word of news has yet filtered through, 'which appears to be striking across Liaoyang 'towards the north and encircling the Russian troops with a view to a flank attack or 'cutting off their retreat. Meanwhile, New- hang has been abandoned, Vladivostok is oeing bombarded, with the remnant of the 12.11 • ssian fleet shut up, and Port Arthur has been " corked " at sea and cut off by land. e Japanese have landed in force on the -A-laotung peninsula at Port Adams, Pitsewo, .rld other poipts, and the Russians have ueen forced in self-protection to blow up alny, their great commercial harbour of the 'east, on which they have spent millions. .Irtogether, Japan has scored all along the . Ile, and, in addition, Russia has lost its Prestige, if not its pluck. The next few aYs may bring forth great events if Japan :axe ready to strike and Russia reluctant to etreat further.
STEVENSON AND DAWSON.

Since Christmas Dawson and Stevenson, the two great billiard champions, have been ftrigaged upon a rubber of test matches. The 41-st two resulted in a win for each after good tames of 18,000 up, and this lent an addi- licmal interest to the third, which was tarted a fort- night ago at 1h e Waterloo Itooms in Glas- 0w and drew large attend- ances through- 'out. Almost all through Stevenson led, shovvingparticu- larly brilliant form, especially 'during the -first week, -when amongst 'numerous big breaks he made One of 523, and the }Judders- -fi e 1 d man -started the second half of the match CHARLES DAWSON. with a large debit. For the first two days Stevenson held his lead, but Dawson, nothing 'daunted, played on pertinaciously and on the Wednesday began to pull up. By Thursday •evening he had practically wiped off his . deficit, and on Friday, for the first time, he assumed command, playing as -steadily as he did brilliantly. Starting the last day just over a hundred in front 413 f his' opponent, Dawson played magnificently and drew steadily away from his opponent, Illaldng one noticeable break of 398. Steven- Inn's luck was out, and towards the close 1,21;_s play became unsettled; and eventually 'tie Huddersfield man ran out a winner by 743 on the match of 18,000. It was a -characteristic game on both sides, and Proves once more what a steady and plucky Player Dawson is. He is never disheartened y his luck and plays on until he plays himself into luck. It would be difficult to two men better matched, and contests tween them are always fall of interest and -keenly followed by the public.

In due course regular watches are to be established, and each week a certain proportion of the men will live and sleep on board. The exact posi- tion of the Buzzard is about two hundred yards west of Blackfriars Bridge, opposite Temple Avenue, and the naval volunteers have already been nicknamed the "Black- friars Buccaneers." H.M.S. Buzzard will very shortly be " opened " with an imposing ceremony, in which the Lord Mayor and Corporation will figure; but she is already an established feature of London life.

• The opera season at Covent Garden nas IIOW been in progress a couple of weeks, and the sights to be seen there nightly have been brilliant and varied. The operas given during the past week have been Lohengrin ( twice), Romeo et Juliette, Tristan and Isolde, and Tan n- hauser,in which Mdmes. Kirby _ _

HERR HEROLD.

formance w a s that of Lohengrin, in which Herr Herold, the Danish tenor, made his first appearance in England. Herr Herold, it is interesting to recall has won golden opinions and awards at Copenhagen. His voice is a genuine tenor somewhat light in quality, tut musical and manifestly dominated by an artistic tempera- ment. Her Majesty the Queen, who was pre- sent, payed the singer a pretty compliment by subsequently receiving him in audience at Buckingham Palace. His reception by the Queen was very cordial, and Herr Herold was welcomed as one who had done credit to his country, where for ten years he had been a singer at the Danish Court. Welcoming him in his own language, Her Majesty ex- pressed the pleasure it gave her to hear him sing in England, and then went on to tell him that he ought to make it clear he was a Dane. She told him his King would be also very glad when he learned of the success obtained in Lohengrin, for Herr Herold has been a favourite singer at the Danish Court. Her Majesty did not conceal the interest and pleasure it gave her to see and hear a countryman of her Own at Covent Garden, and in her final remarks said, "I hope you will come sometimes and sing here in Danish. You must also go back and sing at home; my father loves to hear you."

For several days last week Mi. Tuittbe Grantham's Court, King's Bench Division, No. 5, was the centre of attraction in the Law C and great crowds of sporting man preaucirc, ally ousted the junior bar from their accustomed coign of vantage in a cause célèbre. The case was Sievier v, Duke, both well
owners of race- horses. Sir
James Duke,
Who was called
upon to defend a suit for libel, owns a good many horses,
but has never
figured so large-
ly- in the public eye as " Bob "
S-ievier, who, as owner of that
great mare, Sceptre, was for
a time one of the best known

men inEngland. Sceptre herself was dragged into the case, one of the points of the libel in question being with reference to her running in the Derby of 1902, when she started favourite and ran fourth, to the deep disap- pointment of the public. Mr. Sievier com- plained that Sir James Duke stated in the Raleigh Club that he, had had the mare pulled for financial reasons and was a richer man for the result, but this Sir James Duke denied. The other accusations complained of were that Sir James Duke had called the plaintiff a murderer, a thief, and a cardsharper —a pretty wholesale order in all! The de- fendant, who is a well-known member of the -..ommittee of the Raleigh Club, saw the plain- tiff in the club one afternoon last October speaking to Major Sellar, of the 4th Dragoon Guards. Afterwards he asked the officer in question whether he had introduced Mr. Sievier, and then went on to say what be thought of him in no measured terms, pro- testing that he was not a fit person to be in the club-house at all. The next day Major Sellar told the plaintiff that he could not ask him into the club, and, upon being pressed, gave the reason. Hence the action, which was full of interest, and revealed many strange details of Mr. Sievier's varied career. Mr. Eldon Bankes, K.C., led for the plaintiff, and Mr. Lawson Walton, K.C., and Mr. Gill, K.C., for the defendant; and Mr. Lawson Walton put Sievier through a merciless cross-exami- nation, which threw a lurid light upon his mode of life, Mr. Justice Grantham's sum- ming-up was equally scathing. and the jury, after a few minutes' consultation, brought in a verdict for Sir James Duke, adding that, should the law give the plaintiff a technical • verdict, the damages were to be one farthing, without costs. Thus ended the most sensa- tional slander case of the century, and the verdict has met with unanimous approval on every side. Sir James Duke was enthusiasti- cally cheered outside the Law Courts; but Sievier, who broke down towards the end, left by a side entrance unobserved/

div.head: TERRIBLE POSSIBILITY!
div.p: A TERRIBLE POSSIBILITY!

Suppose the operations of a railway goods yard went wrong. Trucks from the north were shunted on to the south line; goods for Scotland hitched on to a south express. Wouldn't there be chaos until matters were righted? Now if you have indigestion, your "goods centre" is disorganised. "Goods "—or rather nourish- ment, which should be sent to the brain is sent to the intestines. Substances which should be expelled from the body altogether, are turned on to tho main line, or, in other words, turned into the blood and allowed to run throughout the whole system. The blood is poisoned, causing headache. The liver is thrown out of order, and the bile elements are not abstracted from the blood. The stomach is filled with decomposing food, destroying all appetite, and giving rise to gases which distend the organ and cause intense pain. Bile Beans, applied to a system in this state, quickly correct it. They gently open the bowels and clear the system of gathered im- purities. Then they help the stomach to resume its work.; tone up the liver, which in turn purifies the blood; prevent formation of wind, and end flatulence. Health follows.

The well known Manx author, Mr. C. Frederix Wilson (author of " The Missing Will," " A Woman't Life," "Trump Cards," "Convict's Daughter," " Love and Life," etc), writes: "I recently suffered severely from indigestion. The pain after each meal was most acute. Wind also troubled me to such an extent that after food my body seemed quite swollen. A friend, who is an officer on board the " Medic," asked me why I did not try bile beans. On his recommendation I did so, and the result was most satisfactory. lam now quite cured andas well as ever I was in my life. lam convinced of the excellency of bile beans,and you can make full use of this letter if in any way useful to others." All who suffer from indigestion should find it useful, as pointing to a cure of this terrible disorder. Bile beans are purely vegetable, suited to the most delicate constitution, mild, yet effective. Of all chemists. Don't accept worthless substitutes and imitations.

div.head: POOR CHILDREN'S SUMMER CAMP. A Site Selected.
div.p: POOR CHILDREN'S SUMMER CAMP. A Site Selected.

Arrangements are already being sat on foot for the summer camp for poor Warrington children. A meet- ing of the committee was held at the old School Attendance Offices on Monday, under the presidency of Mr. Arthur H. Lee. The hon. secretary (Mr. NV. 11. J; Jenkins) reported on the steps taken to secure a site for the camp. It was, he said, very difficult to find a place possessing the combination of necessary features. A position dry and healthy, removed from objection- able surroundings, possessing an ample supply of good water (a most important essential), plenty of room for play and exercise, and with sea or fresh water bathinr, was not readily found. After correspond- deuce with eke Commissioners of Woods and Forests and land agents, advertising and making personal enquiry and research, there were only two places which he could mention for the committee's consideration. One was a disused battery north of Southport,now under the charge of the Coast Guard works department of the Admiralty. On this site were some buildings •which, with alteration might be utilized. The sea was a long way from the battery and its present intentions seemed to be to recede further. (Laughter.) Careful con- sideration should be given before this site was accepted. The other was a portion,, of land sea-frontage situate at Prestatyn, the property of Lady McLaren. It abutted on the seashore with practically an unlimited extent of good clean foreshore and sandy beach for bathing. It was sheltered on the north and west by sandy ridges, well covered with grass. On the north, and within easy walking distance, were high hills with charming rural scenery and exhilarating surroundings. Immediately adjacent was a large area of common land dry and beautifully situated adjoining the sea. Over this children could roam and play without let or hind- rance. There were natural grounds suitable for cricket, football and other games. There was a plentiful supply of good water which could be laid on to the camp at small cost. • This place he had inspected, and discussed the project with Mr. Linnell,Lady Mc Laren's agent, and the tenaat. He had made tentative arrange- ments for acquiring the site, and Mr. Linnell had written him that with Lady Mc Laren's approval the terms made provisionally might be adopted by the com- mittee. In his (Mr. Jenkins') opinion money spent on the site would be productive of the highest results and would never be regretted by those who had the child- ren's welfare at heart. After discussioniit was decided on the proposition of Mr. J. MOORE MURRAY, "That the necessary steps be taken for the establishment of a permanent camp at Prestatyn, and with a view to the same being used as a convalescent home for Warrington children, and that the Hon. Secretary take the necessary steps for that purpose." On the motion of Mr. J. W. PARKER, the Hon. Secre- tary was authorised to take steps for the raising of funds. It is estimated that a sum not exceeding £5OO will be required to erect and furnish a suitable perman ent camp.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

• Lynn Congregational Church. The Rev. D. Lincoln Jones, of Grosvenor-street, Manchester, preached the anniversary sermons at Lymm Congregational Church on Sunday. A service of song entitled "The Roll Call" was well sung in the after- noon the solos being taken by Misses A. Boden, Cissie Boond, and Easily Hughes. The story was read 'by Mr. Ernest Murnford, formerly of Lymm.

Cockhedge Congregational Mission. The Sunday school anniversary of the above place of worship was held on Sunday last, when the Rev. H. Wall, preached morning and evening to large congregations. The morning discourse was taken from the 14th chapter of Exodus and the 30th verse. "And Israel saw the Egyptians dead upon the sea shore," and the evening discourse, upon the "Faith of Abraham" from the 11th chapter of Hebrews Bth, 9th, 10th verses. In the after noon a service of song entitled "Pilgrim's Progress" was rendered by the choir, the connective reading being given by Mrs. H. Roberts. Special hymns and anthems were sung at all the services and the choir under the conductorship of Mr. W. if. Wallington performed in a praiseworthy manner. Miss Kitty Hall presided at the organ. Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. I The annual meeting was held on Sunday afternoon presided over by Rev. John Yonge, the President. He briefly introduced Mr. D. M. Main of Glasgow, who was in Warrington as a delegate to a conference of Rechabites. Mr. Main had a very hearty reception and spoke upon the benefits of Temperance to the individual as well as the community. He dwelt for some time upon the advantages of belonging to the noble Order of Rechabites, and gave statistics showing the marked longivity of their members, compared with other Friendly Societies, where they were not all total , abstainers. 116 could highly recommend the members ' of the P.S.A. to :join the Rechabite tents of the town. The Order of Rechabites would be a force to be reckoned with in the near future. The cause of temperance was , becoming stronger. Its influence was running into Society, notwithstanding the strong feeling amongst the publicans and their friends. The country would yet declare whether compensation was right, and say who should receive the compensation—those who ruined the people, or the people who were ruined. Mr. Bannister took part in the meeting. Mr. E. Smith delighted the meetingwith his rendering of "The Holy City, and the "Dream of Paradise." Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac., Ipresided at the organ. Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Sunday School.

The congregation at Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel celebrated the Sunday school anniversary on Sunday. At the morning service in the chapel, the Rev. J. Crompton Sowerbutts, of Southport, preached, the sub- ject of his address being the influence of women. In the afternoon a musical service was held in the Parr Hall. Mr. C. E. Parker presided, and the speaker was the Rev. G. H. Carnson. Mr. Frank Hickman played on the organ Guilmant's "Caprice." A pleasing feature of this service was the interpretation by the double quartet, consisting of Mrs. Taylor, the Misses Armstrong, Wilson, and Prince, and Messrs. Griffith, S. Hassan, Gough and Clay, of Hackett's " Magniflcat." The "Gloria" was sung by the children. The duet, "Now we are Ambassadors," was sung by Messrs. Hassell and Gough. Mr. Levi Richardson who con- ducted, gave a feeling rendition of" Suffer little chil- dren." There was an exceptionally large attendance at the evening service in the hall, when Mr. Sowerbutts spoke of the dignity of labour. Mr. Levi Richardson creditably interpreted "Be thou faithful" (Mendels- sohn). The "Nana Dimittis " was given in admirable style by the double quartet, and Mrs. R. H. Pearson sang with taste and expression "Glory to Thee" (Gounod). She was accompanied on the organ by Mr. W. H. Payton, Moe. Bac. The singing of the children was ably accompanied by Mr. E. G. Bickers. The collec- tions for the day realized £3l 10s. Rev. J. F. Matthews and Chinese Labour. " A Foul and Darksome Deed." At the Latchford Baptist Church on Sunday, the annual choir sermons were preached by the Rev. J. F. Matthews, pastor. In his sermon in the evening Mr. Matthews strongly condemned the introduction of Chinese labour into South Africa. He said: On Friday last one of the most tragic incidents of modern times occurred at the Foreign 03ce. Lord Lansdowne and the Chinese Ambassador signed the. Convention for indentured Chinese labour in South Africa. By that act Great Britain has sold herself to an ignorant, godless, unscrupulous, and self-seeking faction, which has no care for the purity and glory of the British flag, but is ready to prostitute the honour of our land to its greed and lust for gold. The only difference between it and the Arab slave raiders, is that the latter go in unholy ' gangs, and with lash and yoke and other instruments of torture, to capture their human prey and destroy their homes, while the former gets the British Government to do it by the aid of legal instruments. We in one sense are worse than the slave traders and raiders. They recognise no liberty for the black man; we on the other hand teach and preach the doctrine of the universal fatherhood of God. the brotherhood of man, and the solidarity of the human race. The men it is proposed to ship to South Africa under this ordinance will:be cooped up in cornpounds,and may be sold to any one master by another. If he runs away he will be captured and punished. He will be forced to work continually in the mines under the strictest surveillance. He has no remedy against the caprice and injustice of his employer. He has no rights, nor has he any liberty. This foul and darksome deed has been perpetrated in the light of day, by a so- called Christian nation, proudly boasting of her missionary enterprise and the liberty of her subjects everywhere. We have humiliated China in the eyes of the world, by the forced anti detestible opium traffic, and now we are degrading her manhood by forced slavery. I say deliberately, if ever China should rise in rebellion against this vile and infamous torture of her sons, and it were within my power to withhold the payment of taxes for war against her to compel her recognition of the Convention I should heartily rejoice at being able to do so. I hope whenever a general election comes, no burgess in this country will pledge his vote to any candidate who is not ready to sanction an immediate withdrgwal of the charter. If he does he will be a traitor tolnis country, to human liberty, and to God. The collection for the day amounted to .£9 Bs. 3d. Mr. Peter Harrison presided at the organ.

div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB. Secretary's and Treasurer's Reports.
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB. Secretary's and Treasurer's Reports.
A SUCCESSFUL SEASON.

The annual report of the Warrington Club has this week been placed in the hands of the' members. In a long statement the Hon. Secretary (Mr. H. Ashton) reviews the progress of the club through the season's engagements. The first team played 43 matches, 23 being won, 15 lost and five drawn. Referting to the final tie at Salford Mr. Ashton says: " Great hopes were entertained that our second opportunity to partici- pate in the Northern Union final would, on this occa- sion, terminate successfully. An indifferent forward display, however, shattered our prospect, and it is to be regretted that so few chances were afforded our splen- did back division, otherwise we would have wen—and that easily." On no occasion during the season has the club been fined for late start. The previous gate record of £257 versus Halifax on Good Friday last season was easily beaten in the cup-tie with Wigan, .£315 being recorded. Thirty-seven points in the League is also the highest total the club has secured. In a general retrospect the Secretary says that "The standard of play during the season has proved by results to have been of a very high quality, and without exaggeration we can claim that our team was second to none in the Rugby Union at the close of the season. At one period a very reasonable prospect of proving successful in the League Champion- ship was manifest, but lack of adaptability on the part of our forward line to withstand the vigorous forward play of their opponents on wet grounds, particularly at the latter part of January, was their undoing. During the cup-ties the form of our team was of a very high order, the only reg-ettable feature being the feeble display of our forwards in the final for the cup; though they were to be commiserated with somewhat in that illegal scrummaging was resorted to throughout the game. Rule 2 in the laws of the game states that a scrummage which can only take place in the field of play is when the ball is put down between the players who have closed round on their respective sides, and who must have both feet on the ground. Now by closing round on their respective sides, a strict interpretation of the rules means a scrum- mage must be parallel with the touch line,consequently I contend that a proper scrumma,r'e was not formed throughout the game. Only four forwards have scored tries out of 43 matches played, and between them six tries. J. Fish easily leads the way in the scores for the first team with 27 converted goals two penalty goals and 16 tries. Davies and Harris have each scored ten tries. Dickenson nine, Isherwood eight, and T. Hocken- hall five. The "A " team have once more enjoyed a very good season ; 26 matches were played 18 won, seven lost and one drawn, finishing fourth in the Lan- cashire combination. Kenyon heads the scorers with 16 tries,five converted goals and one penalty goal.
STATEMENT OF ACCOUNTS.

The Hon. Treasurer (Mr. Thomas Pemberton) in his financial statement states that "Subscriptions have in- creased by £36 19s. 6d.; 138 joining, 31 having resigned or failed to pay, leaving the number of members 649. The attendance at matches, considering the bad state of trade, has been very good, the gate realizing £1,727 18s. W. (exclusive of the cup ties at home with Swin- ton .£l6l us. 2d., and Wigan £915 11s.) made up as fol- lows :—lst team, £1,533 16s. 31d. A ' team, £194 2s. sd. The latter shows a decrease. The average tak- ings have been larger, but less matches were played. Cup ties at home and awayaccounted for £999 16s. id., of which we paid out £373 12s. lid. Assistance has also been given to junior football by the establish- ment of a Works League. We have been very suc- cessful in the trips during the cup ties, resulting in a further addition to the income of £46 2s. 101 d. for which we must thank our hon. se rotary. The annual sports again proved a large succe 1, showing a profit, of £lOB Os. id., against £ll3 7s. lid, last year. With regard to the expenditure, this has very much increased, owing to the greater number of matches, the renewing of the supports of the stand on the enclosure side, accommodation for spectators, ,a large increase in the wages; transfer fees, bonuses, and refreshments to the players; the insurance of the teams, Scc. lam sorry to say that the Works Competition was practically a failure, arid after paymlnt of expenses, there was only a small balance to hand over to the Infirmary." The total gate receipts were £2,727 14s. 9id., and the payment in wages, transfers, and bonuses were £1,417 Os. 2d. The balance on the season's working is a about £285.
The annual meeting will be held on Tuesday evening next. All the retiring officials are nominated for re- election, the only addition-LI nominee being Nlr. S. W. Jeffery for committee.

div.head: WARRINGTON GROCERS AND PROVISION DEALERS' ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON GROCERS AND PRO- VISION DEALERS' ASSOCIATION.
A Year's Work Reviewed.

The animal meeting of the Warrington and District Grocers and Provision Dealers' Association was held on Wednesday evening. Mr. E. Richardson (president) occupied the chair, and there were present Messrs. Gandy, Kay, Povey, Bowden, Owen, Reading, Gerravd, Stringer, W. Taylor and J. V. Gorst (hon. secretary). THE COMMITTEE'S REPORT.

Mr. Gorst read the third annual report of the com- mittee, which stated that theyl had a record to show of steady progress and substantial recognition of their work. Reference was made to the support given to the Bqtter Adulteration Bill introduced by the late Right Hon. R. W. Hanbury. The committee also wrote condemning the Greek currant monopoly. The com- mittee's representations to the Watch Committee re the striking of matches on shop fronts was duly considered and a byelaw had been framed to meet the complaint— the same to come into force on ;filly Ist next. Corres- pondence had also taken place with the Markets Com- mittee, recommending that the stalls should, in future, be let by public tender, as in most towns. The com- mittee did not consider the present position of this question at all satisfactory. The financial indebtedness of the Borough and the very heavy burden of the rates had been duly considered by the committee and they had taken steps to focus this feeling by asking other kindred associa- tions to unite with them in a meeting of protest, and to see what measures could be suggested by which the wanton financial recklessness could be cheaked. During the year Mr. T. S. Steel had been retained as the solicitor to the association and the committee felt sure that his appointment would be appreciated. The in- creasing activity of the Sanitary authorities in looking after the food supply of the public and seeing that they were protected from unscrupulous traders had the committee's warm approval. Correspondence with the traffic manager of the London and North Western Railway Company and the Cheshire Lines Committee had taken place and the result was seen in improved facilities by the cheap bookings from th 4 surrounding districts to Warrington on market days. A movement was initiated to bring about a closer union with the local Chamber of Commerce. It was hoped to form a committee of trades which might he affiliated with the older body. This it was felt would very materially increase the usefulness of the Chamber of Commerce. Thecommittee added that they could not conclude the report without a feeling reference to the great loss which the Associa- tion had sustai ted by the death at an early age of the* late Mr. S. G. Davey, one of the first vice-presidents. Mr. Davey's genialipresence was always welcomed. His good heartedness and kindly disposition endeared him to all. The committee also wished to place on record its indebtedness to the energetic and painstaking secre- lary (Mr. J. P. Gorst) and to the esteemed treasurer (Mr. Povey). The financial statement presented by Mr. Povey showed a balance in hand, after meeting all liabilities of £35 9s. 9d.
The reports were adopted on the proposition of Mr. GANDY, seconded by Mr. KAY.
THE PRESIDENCY.

Mr. KAY proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Richard- son for his services in the chair during the past year. The better feeling which now existed amongst the grocers of Warrington was largely due, he said, to the efforts put forth by Mr. Richardson, as president of the association. (Hear' hear.) Mr. GANDY said Mr. Richardson had not only gained their respect and esteem, but.also their affection. _

j Mr. POVEY supported' and said the association had been exceptionally fortunate in having Mr. Richardson I as president during the first three years of its existence. The vote was carried unanimously. In acknowledging the compliment, Mr. RICHARDSON said he had always held that the honours should go round,and last year it was understood that he was to be allowed to retire from the chair on the present occa- sion. He would therefore be glad to receive a nomina- tion for the position. I Mr. KAY said if it was still Mr. Richardson's de- sire to retire from th 3 presidency of the association,he would propose that the senior vice-president, Mr. John Gandy be appointed to the position. (Hear, hear.) Mr. OVEN seconded, and said in Mr. Gandy the asso- ciation would have an able successor to Mr. Richardsob. The proposition was carried with acclamation. IMr. GANDY, in accepting the position, said he took it as a great mark of confidence, and he would do what he could for the association. I TRE VICE-PRESIDEM, OFFICERS AND COMNIITTEE.

Mr. E. Richardson, Mr. Monks, and Mr. Page were unanimously elected vice-presidents. The following appointments were also made: Hon. Secretary, Mr. J. P. Gorst; hon. treasurer, Mr. j. Povey; hon. auditor, .Mr. Bowden; committee, Messrs. Owen, Reading, Gerrard, William Isaac, Bo wden, Stringer, and NV. Taylor, Matters affecting trade prices were then considerei.
