Mr. BALFOUR is a THE GOVERNMENT'S great tactician, and ESCAPE. tacticians are some- times forced to make fthemselves appear very Email. The issue raised by Mr. BLACK'S resolution and Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN'S amendment proved most awkward for the Government. At the last moment it was dis- covered that they were in danger of being left in a minority. To avert defeat, that tactical genius, thelPrime Minister, decided that the issue must be shirked. His amendment, as he said at question time, on Wednesday, was tantamount to the old device of moving the previous question. The House was invited to ignore Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S fiscal policy, also the policy hid down by Mr. BALFOUR himself at Sheffield, and the whole tur- moil created by both. The question of fiscal reform and the declaration of the Prime Minister at Sheffield, said this ingenious amendment, were not of the smallest consequence to the present Parliament. So all the House had to do was to express its "continued confidence in the pre- sent administration,land "proceed with the bus;_ ness proposed in the gracious speech from the Throne." Never has the party game been played with such cynical boldness. Mr. BALFOUR'S friends in the Press now excuse it on the ground that Mr. BLACK'S resolution was also a move in the party game. It was meant to turn out the Government, and Mr. BALFOUR had to fall back on the instincts of self-preservation. But the issue was of Mr. BALFOUR'S own making—his and Mr, CHAMBERLAIN'S. They have caused all this commotion. It is their threat to undo the work of Free Trade which has split their own party and alarmed the country. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN ex- pounded one policy; Mr. BALFOUR at Sheffield expounded another,which was an attack upon the principle of Free Trade scarcely to be distin- guished from the first. To say that all this does not concern the present Parliament because neither policy is to be submitted to it in legislative form is an audacious begging of the question. .Statesmen cannot be allowed to t ss these re- actionary proposals into the hat and then talk about proceeding with the business of the session as if nothing had happened. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S amendment was sufficiently evasive, but it did take note of the Prime Minister's willingness to make a change in our fiscal policy. The plain implication was that such change was in the direction of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S views. This claim by Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN to the Prime Minister's soul threatened the Government with the defection of so many Unionists that Mr. BALFOUR found it expedient to evade Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. It was now perilous to discuss even the Sheffield declaration. So the only resort was to ask the -Unionists to give the Government a blind vote of confidence. Mr. BALFOUR said to thorn in effect, 1 "you support the measures we have introduced this session: There is nothing in our present policy 0 which you take exception. We are not asking now for the taxation of food, or for any- ! thing to which the Unionist Free Traders are opposed. How can you consistently vote in such emanner as to turn us out of office ?" By taking this line at no small sacrifice of dignity, Mr. BALFOUR turned to his own advantage the natural , reluctance of many Unionists to give the finishing stroke to a Government that has made such large demands upon their toleration; but this was the largest demand of all.. , Mr. BLACK'S:TOSOIUtIO/1 accurately expressed the views of every man who is not an out and out backer of Mr. Chamberlain. It expressed the views of those ministers who in the debate on the Address soundly affirmed that they were against the taxation of food for the purpose of Protection 1

Mr. GERALD BALFOUR, for instance, speaking in his brother's absence, was perfectly frank on this point; but, according to the Prime Minister's argument last night, this frankness was irrevelant and even improper. The whole fiscal question belongs to some future day, of which all that can be said is that it may be more convenient for Mr. BALFOUR than the present. The sole duty of man from their point of view, is to keep that politician in office and enable him to present a semblance of unity in his party. It is not an edifying exhibi- tion and we fancy that the moral effect of the debate is to make many good Conservatives fee to-day that Mr. BALFOUR'S tactics are poor sub- stitutes for courage and straightforward dealing, The Prime Minister has contrived to escape defeat but he has not escaped dishonour. We do not believe that the majority of 5 5 which the Govern- ment secured can bring satisfaction to any self- respecting Conservative.

The clauses which have been inserted by the Manchester Ship Canal Company in their new Bill for the protection of the river rights of the Warrington Corporation and traders appear to be adequate and generous. They may appropriately be; termed the Magna Charta of Warrington's rights on the river. Practically all the points raised in the recent action and decided in favour of the Corporation and traders by the late Mr. Justice Byrne have been conceded by the Com- pany and embodied in the clausea inserted in the Bill. We trust that the agrurnent arrived at marks a new era in the relations existing between Warrington and the Manchester Ship Canal Company. The antagonistic attitude which has hitherto existed has been detrimental to the best interests of both parties. The only outstand- ing ddlerence is the settlement of the action at law, now pending in the House of Lords. The many concessions made by the Ship Canal Company have left very little to fight for. The question of costs is, of course, .an important one, especially for the ratepayers, but this should not prove an insurmountable barrier to a speedy settlement of the litigation. The Town Clerk and the Parliamentary agents of the Corporation have solved greater difficulties than this during the past few days and they are to be congratulated upon tne successful results of their efforts. The crowning point would be a friendly agreement with the Ship Canal Company on the action now pending in the House of Lords.

There can be no question that the construction of the works proposed by the Manchester Ship Canal Company, which will. provide Warrington with a dock nearly two miles in length and a con- stant depth of 8 feet of water, will greatly facili- tate traffic on the river within the Borough. The possibilities are great, and the manufacturers and traders of Warrington will show a surprising lack of enterprise if they do not take full advantage of the benefits which will be obtainable from the full use of the dock, when constructed. Attention is repeatedly being called to the advan- tages which would accrue from a wider and freer use of our rivers and canals. There is scarcely a town in the kingdom more favourably situated for doing a large carrying trade by water than Warrington. Standing midway between two such important seaports as Liverpool and MancheAer, with ample facilities for cheap water carriage,there is scope for a much larger development of our export trade. The construction of the proposed dam should give an impetus to a freer use of the river and canal by manufacturers. There seems no reason why in the course of a few years, the whole length of the new dock should not be bounded by wharves and warehouses, and become the centre of a large carrying trade.

The Water Committee having reduced their charge against the Ragged School to £1 per year, opportunity was taken by the school managers last Saturday to open the bath again after several years' disuse. It is still felt, however, that the Water Committee should, as was suggested in this column, forego any charge for the water used in such a manner, seeing the great advantage to the town from a sanitary point of view. The Committee ought really to be glad to provide water free to all and sundry who will interest themselves in the cleanliness of poor neglected children. What joy the Ragged School boys manifested on Satur- day when the big bath was re-opened! In a surprisingly short space of time the tank Was full of lads who fairly revelled in the wholesome luxury of a bath. Mr. Skelland and Mr. Owen super- intended the arrangements and had no difficulty in maintaining order. Oa several nigh ts during the week, other ragged children have baen permitted to use the bath. The Ragged School Committee has also decided to renovate the whole of ,the school premises. The debt on the building fund has been removed, and the renovation which has been :so long delayed, will be taken in hand at once. in connection with the Walking Day festival, it has been decided to purchase a new banner.

There is every prospect, we are glad to say, of a permanent summer camp for the poor children of Warrington being secured. Arrangements have been practically completed for acquiring a site near the sea at Prestatyn. Mr. W.H. J. Jenkins, the hon. secretary of the Poor Children's Summer Camp and Convalescent Horne,informs us that the situation is an admirable one in every respect,being surrounded by beautiful sc3nery, and abounding in every requisite for giving the slum-waifs a healthful and happy time. From very smail beginnings this charitable proj3ct has been pushed along m(3st enthusiaitically and successfully, and . greatly to the cred.t of Mr. Jenkins and Mr. Arthur H. Lee, the prime movers. S )mething like £5OO is DOW required for the provision of a permanent resort at Prestatyn, and we hope the efforts of the organisers to raise this sum will meet with a gratifying response. Charitable people could not find a more admirable outlet for their surplus cash. They have only to reflect that every shilling contributed makes some poor child healthier and happier, to, we are sure, t41c.3 a real joy in giving. It is intended among other schemes, to organise a band of boy collectors, who will thus be able to perform useful service in uplifting their poorer comrades.

The conscientious objector des ns-it have an enviable time whoa he appears before the magis- trates for his certificate of exemption, and we should imagine that the Warrington County Petty Sessions is about the last place he would desire to go to for the purpose. A R.xton farmer who applied there on Wednesday was bluntly told by the Clerk (Mr. H. Greenall) that he WiLS an idiot, because .he thought the preventive measure of vnccination worse than the disease. It seems, from the evidence, that the applican t has a neighbour with two children. One, which i has been vaccinated, s seriously ill, while the other unvaccinated, is ".one of the finest in the country." Hence the anti-vaccinator, and hence Mr. Greenall's impatience. We are generally inclined to sympathise with the individual who applies for an exemption certificate, but in this case we marvel that an exemption was granted. such evidence, could hardly have The Bench, on been satisfied that .. the applicant had a "con-
scientious objdction."

The claims of Rechabitis m have frequently been urged before the Warrington publio, and the i important conference held n the town on Satur- day should serve a further educational purpose. For many years the Order has been doing much to train juveniles in the paths of sobriety, and it was this side of its work w hichthe Conference specially considered. The juvenile tents have proved a splendid recruiting ground for the adult branches. As Brother Wells-Smith pointed out in his highly interesting paper, there have been over 40,000 transfers during the past twenty years, and in many other directions the movement has made great strides. The Order nrist be a distinA power for good in the lives of maay young people, and the workers are deserving of every encour- gement.

Judge Edge is, we are glad to note, not one of those legal luminaries who are content to mer.ell deplore the amount of perjury and deliberatelrh.g in the courts over which they preside. His wora.nlP feels so strongly on this question that he is taking practical steps to -bring litigants and their vot- nesses to a proper appreciatiJn of what taking the oath means. Speaking with regard to his Owe Court at Clerkenwell ha says that "perjury occ11r! in this court some four or five times a day, anu. the offence is committed in from 70 to 80 per oh; of the cases tried." A statement like this shoultt give us all pause, for what takes place every day Clerkenwell is only indicative of the state of thinge all over the country. Go into any court you like Warrington PAce Court will do—and if you ere, not amustomed to what goes on you will belaniazeu, at the amount of "hard swearing."We were convere ing only the other day, with a clergyman who fre" quently visits the courts,and he commented sedlYci on the callous disregard of the truth displaY! by so many of the people who appeared in °E; defendant and witness boxes. No amount Christian teaching appears to avail, and stern Pre" ventive measures are required if this grTv- mg vice is to be checked. Judge Euge has, on his own authurity, committed two or three witnesses for perjury uttered before him, but the difficulty of folio Ring pp such cases prevents sc'd drastic a step being taken as often as it is demand° His Worship's excellent and practical sug,gee. tion is this: That judges " should have the power to at once commit a person for perjury by givillg him in charge to appear immediately before a magistrate; and that the judge he allowed te direct a solicitor from his Court to prefer the charge in the magistrates' Court." The fear of the law would persuade people to tell the truth nothing else might avail, and we hope that judiele,' powers on these lines may very soon be conferrea If the magistrates themselves were given si!flilar. discretion it would be a further step in the righw direction.

- Wesleyans will regret the departure of the Rev. James Dunk from this circuit—he having accepted an invitation to Watford as superintendent for 1905. The rev, gentleman delivered an eloquent address at a public meeting held at Bewsey Road church, last week in connection with the Liverpool district synod. Lord Gerard who has been appointed second- lieutenant in the sancashire Hussars Imperial Yeo- manry, joins the corps which his father was command- ing at the time of his death, and from which he was seconded for service in South Africa. The new officer is 21 years of age this year. Miss Mabel Reaney, only daughter of the late Rev. G. S.Reaney, formerly pastor of Wycliffe Church, and Vicar of Christ Church, Greenwich, at the time of his death in 1901,was amongst the number who were pre- sented with the Degree of Bachelor of Science at the Presentation of Degrees of the University of London which took place on May the 18th. At the annual movable conference of the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows, lo be held at Manchester during Whit week, the Warrington district will be repre- sented by Bro. R. H. Halford, the present Grand Master of the district, and Bro. Thomas S. Steel, a P. Prw. G.M. of the district.

A deputation has been appointed by the Warring- ton Property Owners' Association to wait upon the Finance Committee of the Corporation for the pur- pose of discussing the financial position of the town and the rate question in order to see whether there is any way of reducing the present high rates.

Mr. and Airs. J. W. Tanner, of Thynne street, War- rington, celebrated their golden wedding on Sunday last. At a gathering of the members .of the family and a few friends, hearty congratulations were offered to the aged couple, which congratulations will un- doubtedly be endorsed by the wide circle of acquain- tances which Mr. and Mrs. Tanner have made during their long residence in the town of Warrington. At Emmanuel Church, Bold street, Warrington, a special service for men only was held on Sunday after- noon last, this being the first of a seri& of services to be held on the third Sunday of each month. The Rev. F. Vaughan (curate in charge) preached froM Jonah 1, 6, his subject being "The man who wouldn't." The service was of a most interesting and helpful character and was attended by a goodly number of men.

H. M. AsirroN's LIFF/ To'sro is the KING of Tolsacs.--63. SA.NKEY-sTREET, Warrington.--.Advt. Fire at Monks, Hall and Co's. Works. At 10.30 on Wednesday morning a fire broke out at Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co.'s tubs works, Liverpool-road. Crosfield's fire brigade turned out and on arrival at the works found that the fiam3s had been got under control by employees.. Jets were got to work and the fire was soon extinguished, the damage being slight. It is supposed that the outbreak was due to excessive heat from the furnace setting the woodwork of the roof alight.

BaCE BOOTS FOR ALL.—UNDER. THE CLOCK.—Xclvt Secondary School Entrance Examination. It is announced that an entrance examination for the admission of boys and girls to the Secondary School will beheld at the school on Friday, June 24th. Intending scholars must be over 12 years of age on the Ist September. An examination of 23 scholar- ships (value £5 and free tuition at the school), offered by the Education Committee for competition to the children of residens or ratepayers who intend to become pupil teachers, will ba held at the school on Friday and Saturday, June 3rd and 4th. Candidates must not be less than 14 years of age on or before July 31st.

LADIES BEST GLACE BOOTS and SHOES, UNDER the CLOCK, BRID GE-STREET.—Ad7t. A Determined Anti-Vaccinator. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wed- nesday, before Captain Withintgton and Mr. T. Halton Arthur Woodall,farmer, Rixton, applied for a vaccina- tion exemption order. Asked what his conscientious objection was, applicant said a neighbour's child was seriously awhile his eldest child,who was not vaccin- ated, was one of the finest in the country. He would sooner his child have any disease that be vaccinated. The Clerk: You would rather it die then ? Applicant: Yes. The Clerk: You are an idiot thea. The Bench granted the order with some reluctance.

FOR CLASS AND CFIINA. of every description try J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. The Ambulance Corps. The annual inspection Of the Warrington Corps of the St. John Ambulance Brigade, took place on Friday last at the Ambulance headquarters, the Gymnasium Dr. George Thomson, of Oldham was the inspecting officer. Fifty officers and men presented themAelves. After the inspection, Dr. Thomson expressed himself in the highest terms possible with regard to the smartness and efficiency of the corps, and stated it was a pleasure to inspect such excellent men as had been presented to him that evening. The men who were not on parade were absent by leave caused through evening employment, sickness, and being out of town. tOne member is still on active service in South Africa. BASSINETTES AND MAIL CARTS in latest art shades.—J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—AdVt. The Health of Cheshire. A report to be presented to the next meeting of the Cheshire County Council states that in the adminis- trative county last year there were registered 16,296 births, and there were 8,642 deaths. The birth-rate per 1,000 in the municipal boroughs was 27.6 in the other urban districts 27.5, in the rural districts 24.3, and in the administrative county 26.8. In the whole of England and Wales the birth-rate for 1903 was 28.4 per 1,000 of the population.—The death-rate per 1,000 in the municipal boroughs was 16.2, in the other urban districts 13.8, in the rural districts 12.4, and in the _administrative county 14.2. In the whole of England and Wales the death-rate for 1903 was 15.4 per 1,000 of the population, the lowest rate on record. As to zymotic diseases, the • mortality from each. except scarlatina, was lower in Cheshire than in the large towns. As compared with the whole country the mortality from measles, fever, and diarrhcea was very low in Cheshire, and the mortality from scarlatina and whooping cough was just in excess The Cheshire mortality from smallpox and diphtheria was equal to the average in the whole country.
H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF TONICS.-63, SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. Wilson Barratt in Liverpool.

I After an absence of about fourteen months from I Liverpool, Wilson Barrett will make his welcome re- appearance at the Shakespeare Theatre next week, I commencing Whit Monday evening, when he is I assured of the heartiest reception in a round of the most popular plays in big extensive repertoire, sup- ported by his company of 100 artistes. Wilson Barrett opens his week's visit at the Shakespeare with ' a performance of "The Silver King," which will be played on Whit Monday and Thursday evenings. On Tuesday and Wednesday evenings, Wilson Barratt will present a new and grand revival of" Claudian " in celebration of the coming-of-age of this remarkable I play which Ruskin so much admired. On Friday evening, for the first time in Liverpool, Wilson I Barrett will be seen in his new comedy entitled " In ! the Middle of June," which is quite pm innovation on ! the part of the famous actor-author and presents him in a new light as a comedian of rare resource and humour. Wilson Barrett's visit to the Shakespeare will appropriately, though regretfully, terminate on Saturday,May 28th, with two performances (afternoon and evening) of his world-renowned play, "The Sign of the Cross," which it is estimated has been seen by !twenty minion people in all parts of the globe, and has I proved the closest alliance between church and stage. ; It is worthy of note that, notwithstanding the immense expense entailed by this engagenent, ordinary prices for admission will prevail. Proposed Chess Club. It is proposed to form a chess club at the Bridge street cocoa rooms and the promoters would be glad if anyone willing to join would hand in his name to the manager, Mr. Starkey, who is the secretary pro tern, and who would be glad to give all information. Pollee Changes at Lymm. Acting-Sergeant Sharp, who has been stationed at Lymm for the past two years, has been promoted to the rank of sergeant, and has been transferred to Sale. P.C. Frost, who has been stationed at Shaving- ton, near Crewe,has been promoted to acting-sergeant to succeed Sergeant Sharp at Lymm.

Apollo Choir's Success'. At an eisteddfod in connection with the Welsh Church at St. Helens on Saturday, the Warrington Apollo Choir, conducted by Mr. Harry Berrey, won the chief choral competition. The test piece was " Britons " (Prothero). Mr. Percy George's party (Warrington) secured the prize in the quartette coin- petition.

Music in the Park. The Volunteer band gave the opening performance of the season on Sunday and an excellent programme was submitted in the presence of a large assembly. Next Thursday evening, commencing at 7-15, Mr. T. J. Down's military band will occupy the stand. The following programme has been arranged : March "Russo," Ganne. Overture " be Fidble Berger,"... Re Corporation Contracts. At a meeting of the Amalgamated Society of Cabinet Makers it was unanimously agreed to protest against the principles embodied in Councillor Maginn's motion being introduced into the business of the Warrington Town Council viz., "The lowest tenders be accepted by all committees of the Corporation for work done for that body." The Society protests on the ground that it will bring into competition, firms who do not work under fair conditions *ith firms who pay the standard rate of wages and work to conditions agreed upon by the various societies concerned, which competition will have a lowering tendency in the standard of living of the working class citizens.

The failure of the Company to give such counter notice within two days as aforesaid or the finding of the said Surveyor that the said channel is not in accordance with the provisions of this Section shall be conclusive 'evidence of the default of the Company; (11) If after any such complaint as aforesaid the sur- veyor shall certify that the Company has failed to maintain the said channel in accordance with the pro- visions of this section so that the navigation thereof shall have become obstructed or impeded or if the Company fail to give counter notice to the Surveyor as aforesaid thereupon and until the said Surveyor shall have certified that .the channel has been restored and the navigation thereof has been rendered unobstructed and I uoitnpeded the Corporation and the traders shall have full right for vessels to pass through Walton Lock and to navigate in both directions the canal betweenl Walton Lock and Eastham or any part thereof together with the use of Eastham Lock Walton Lock Old Quay Lock Runcorn and of that portion of the River Mersey referred to in sub-Sections (6) and (8) hereof free from all tolls dues and impositions whatsoever. Provided that the Corporation and the traders shall not be entitled to the right of free navigation in this Section provided if the Company (after such complaint by a trader followed by the certificate of the Surveyor or failure by the Company to give such counter notice as aforesaid) shall forthwith commence to dredge and continue to dredge the aforesaid channel to the reason- able satisfaction of the Surveyor. In the event of any failure by the Company to comply with the provisions of this sub-section so that any trader becomes entitled to the right of free navigation as herein provided such right of free navigation shall be without prejudice to the right of such trader to proceed against the Company in respect of any damage which he may sustain, but the amount of tolls which would have been payable if such freedom had not been conferred shall be taken in reduc- tion of any such damages; (12) In addition to the rights cnd privileges con- ferred by Clause 2 sub-Clause (a) Of the scheduled agreement the traders shall be entitled to the use of the Old Quay Lock Runcorn for the purpose of entering and leaving the Canal without payment of any additional tolls or dues in respect of the use of the said lock. (13) Any vessel passing through the said river diver- sion (Work No. 5) destined for or coming from any point on the River Mersey to or from which at the passing of this Act right of free navigation exists and the passage of which vessel along the natural coarse of the said river shall be prevented by the dam across the said river (Work No. 6.) shall be exempt from any toll or charge in respect of the passage to or from such point. (14) The Corporation shall for the purposes of this Section be deemed to be traders; (15) Any trader mayenforce by action the provisions of this Section so far as such provisions affect him. (16) The Company shall reasonably use the sluices and Works and Work No. 5 by this Act authorised so as not to exclude the tide flowing up the said river to Warrington Bridge but this shall not prevent the Com- pany from keeping the lower portion of the said sluices closed against the incoming tide. When the tides be- low Work No. 5 rise to less than 13 feet above Ordnance datum the Company shall if required by the Corporation on tides by which the canal is influenced by tidal action permit water to flow into the river from the canal through the existing Waken sluice so as to give as far as practicable the benefit of the additional tidal height. And the Company shall also (except when prevented by flood) so operate and use the said sluices on the ebb tide as to reduce the water level at Warring- ton Bridge to ten feet above Ordnance datum within thirty minutes of the time at which a corresponding tide would reach such level under existing circumstances (17) The Company shall construct through Work No. 6 two culverts each having an internal diameter of not less than three feet with suitable penstocks and regulating gear at such position and at such levels and otherwise as may be agreed between the Surveyor and the Chief Engineer to the Company or in the event of diffaience between them as shall be decided by Sir John Wolfe Barry K.C.B. or other Arbitrator to be appointed unless otherwise agreed on the application of either of the parties by the Board of Trade. The Com- pany subject to other the provisions of this Section shall at all times use the said culverts to their full capacity so as to pass through the same as much of the upland flow of the River Mersey RS the same will take and the sluices to be constructed in the river diversion (Work No. 5) by this Act authorised shall not be opened for discharge down river unless the said two culverts are open to their full capacity, and the sluices shall remain open only during the time when the said culverts are open as aforesaid. For the further protection of the Corporation of War- rington the following provisions with reference to the construction and use of Work No. 7 shall have effect (that is to say) : (1) The rising main or sower (Work No. 7) shall be constructed under the supervision and to the reasonable satisfaction of the Corporation and in accordance with plans and sectioas to be previously submitted to and approved by them and shalt be com- pleted before Work No. 6 is commenced. (2). Until the corporation shall divert the sewage of the Borough from the river so as to treat and puri- fy the same, the company shall pay to the corporation such sum as shall be reasonably expended by the Cor- poration upon the working, cleansing, maintaining, and upholding the said rising main or sewer and all plant and machinery in connection therewith. (3) For the purposes of this Section the rising main of sewer aforesaid shall mean and include all works in connection therewith for the purpose of lift- ing ejecting or discharging sewage from the sewers diverted into the said rising main or sewer. (4) The Company shall carry or continue the said rising main or sewer to a point to be agreed between the Company and the Corporation below Work No. 6 aforesaid and as approved by the Acting Conservator of the River Mersey. (5) Upon the completion to the satisfaction of the Corporation of the said Work No. 7. the same shall vest in the Corporation and the Corporation shall be- come and shall continue to be entitled to discharge the sewage therefrom into the tidal waters of the River Mersey. (6) If any difference shall arise between the Cor- poration and the Company as to the true intent and meaning of any of the provisions of this Section , relating to the said main or sewer or as to anything to be done or not to be done thereunder such differ- ence shall be determined by an Arbitrator to be appointed (unless otherwise agreed) on the application of either of the parties by the Board of Trade and the arbitration shall be subject in all respects to the pro- visions of "The Arbitration Aa, 1889."

div.head: Death of Mr. Charles H. Longshaw.
div.p: Death of Mr. Charles H. Longshaw.

The death occurred on Saturday- morning last of Mr. Charles Henry Longshaw, only son of Mr. Charles Longshaw, builder, &c., of Folly-lane. For the past five years the deceased was a victim of locomotor ataxy, but it was not until a few weeks ago that the progress pf this peculiar and painful disease of the nervous system prevented him from getting out of doors. He was 34 years of age. By his kindly and winning disposition he had made a large circle of friends, and atfthe funeral in Grappenhall Church- yard on Wednesday, many of them attended to pay a last tribute of respect. Numerous floral tributes were sent.

Football Team Entertained. Warrington's victory in the South-West Lancashire Competition was celebrated on Tuesday evening,when the members of the team, together with a large num- ber of friends, were entertainAd at dinner by Mr. and Mrs. Hackney, host and hostess of the Roan Cow, Knutsford-road. A capital repast was served, and Mr. H. Ashton presided. In proposing the health of the host and hostess, the Chairman took opportunity to congratulate the team on their achievement ta winning the South-West Lancashire Cup for the second time, and also the bold front they presented in the League tourney. Reference was also made to the Northern Union Cup final and valuable advice was offered to the players. During the evening songs were given by Messrs. J. Fish, Elliott Harris, Dai Davies, and Thomas.

Certificated Class Teachers' Association. A general meeting of the Warrington Certificated Class Teachers' Association was held in the Municipal Technical Institute on Thursday evening. The President, Mr. Isaac Bowen occupied the chair and there was a good attendance. The transaction of ordinary routine business having been completed, Mr. Thomas Edden read a most interesting and instruc- tive paper on "English Place-names.' Taking four periods of English history, viz. : British, English, Danish and Norse, the essayist gave the origin of many well-known names. Especially interest- ing was that portion of the paper dealing with South Lancashire and Cheshire names. On the proposition of Mr. S. W. Jeffery seconded by Mr. F. H. Longshaw and supported by Mr. F. J. Emson a very hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the essayist. The next meeting of the association will take the form of a picnic, in July, the arrangements to be made by the committee.

Salvation Army Bazaar. This bazaar in the Co-operative Hall was brought to a close on Saturday, when it was announced that the receipts for the three days amounted to about £215. At the opening ceremony in the afternoan the Rev. J. F. Matthews presided, in the absence of ' Mr. C. E. Parker. Adjutant Everness apologized for the absence of Mr. Parker, who had, however, sent them 1,5, with a note expressing his admiration of the work of the Salvation Army. (Applause.)—The Chair- man said his sympathies were with the Salvation Army in Warrington. He had always had a warm admiration of the spiritual side of the work, and an equally warm admiration of the social work which had been accomplished during the past 15 or 20 years. The Army had come to stay, and they all felt it was doing a work which, perhaps, the combined action of the churches could not accomplish. Whether it was their greater simplicity or the elasticity of their organization he did not know, but they had certainly got down to the submerged tenth, and below it, and by the power of the grace of God had been largely successful in raising many into the kingdom of His dear Son. (Applause.) He was glad to learn that they fully appreciated the value of music, which was an agency in their work, and that one of the objects for which the sale was being held was to secures new instruments for the band. He hoped the effort which was being made would be eminently successful. (Applause.)—Miss Bessie Dutton, in declaring the sale Open, remarked that the Salvation Army had been most usefally established in the town for a long period now, and if there was any danger of the public becom- ing oblivious of Christ in any measure, it had been banished by the Salvationists' recent laudable efforts to feed the hungry families of the unemployed. Local Betting Dispute -

At the War—rington- County Court on Thursday before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., an application was made by Mr. Browne in reference to, a claim entered by Messrs. J. It. Rowsen and Com- pany, commission agents of 18, Old Burlington-street, Burlington Gardens, London, against Mr. G. T. Heyl Dia, of Stretton for £3O, the amount paid by the plain- tiffs for the defendant at his request.—Mr. E. Draper (Messrs. Robert Davies and Company) represented the plaintiffs and Mr. A. Browne defended. At the outset Mr. Browne applied for the hearing of the case to be transferred to the Westminster County Court on the ground that,it could be more conveniently tried there. An affidavit was read, stating that Mr. Heyl Dia was Low residing in London where all his business was conducted. He had not resided in Stretton br several months and would not return to Stretton until August. The subject matter of the claim was a betting transaction upon which there was a dispute. The de- fendant alleged misrepresentation. It was further stated that the cause of action arose in London, and that the defendant was confined to bed as the result of a surgical operation.—Mr. Draper opposed the ap- plication, and submitted an affidavit, alleging that the defendant was in a fit state to proceed with the case. It was further stated that it would be necessary to subpcen four witnesses residing in the. Warrington district to rebut the charge of misrepresentation.— his Honour did not think sufficient reason had been given for transferring the case to a London court. He would, however, adjourn the hearing of the case in the Warrington Court to Thursday, June 9th.

div.head: DETAILS OF THE AGREEMENTS.
div.p: DETAILS OF THE AGREEMENTS.

The Manchester Ship Canal Bill was completed by a House of Lords Committee on Thursday, and was ordered to be reported for third reading. Satisfac- tory clauses for the protection of the Warrington Corporation and traders have been inserted.

The three firms of Messrs. Monks Hall and Com- pany, Messrs. Joseph Orosfield arid Sons, and Messrs. James Fairdough and Sons who petitioned against the Bill, have secured independent clauses providing for the payment of compensation in case of specific darroge. The clauses which the Corporation have obtained are given below in extenso. They are for the pro- tection of all the traders and may be termed the Magna Charta of Warrington's rights with reference to the river. Stripped of their legal phraseology, the most important clauses provide that there shall be constructed a dam, lock and sluices at Bank Quay. These works will have the effect of converting the river for its own length within the Borough, into a dock in which at all times there will ba not less than 8 feet of water. This advantage should greatly facilitate the navigation of the river within the Borough and give to all persons having rights of frontage on the river great facilities for Lading and unloading, and the use of wharves. In order to prevent the apprehended nuisance caused by the water beinglimpounded above the dam, two culverts are to be constructed of three feet internal

diameter which will .'always be open to allow the upland waters to flow through, except when tides are flowing up the river, when they will have to be closed in order to prevent silt from being deposited above the dam. These culverts will also prevent the water in the dead end becoming brackish. All tides rising above 13 feet will fl3w ever the proposed sluices and pass on to Howley weir as they do at present. The Ship canal Company have undertaken at their own cost to construct a rising main or sewer which will pick up the four outfall sewers now discharging into the river at Bank Quay. The sewage will then be forced by means of compressed air and the use of ejectors through the culverts to a point below the proposed data so as to reach the tidal waters of the river. The company have also undertaken to bear the cost of working and maintain- ing this rising main until the Corporation are com- pelled to take the borough sewage out of the river for the purpose of purifying the stream: When that event arises the proportion of cost to be borne by the Corporation will be settled by the Local Government Board. It is very unlikely that the Corpora- tion will be called upon to pay .the cost of construction or tin maintenance of the sewer for many years to come. The company, it will be rememberea, refused to entertain the idea of bear- ing the cost themselves when asked to do so in the preliminary negotiations. The estimated cost of the culvert is £30,000 and the annual cost of maintenance There is to be no arbitration in future on disputed points. The Borough Surveyor is to be the sole judge whether. the Ship Canal Company have or have not carried out their obligations. This will involve ad- ditional work on the Surveyor but the cost of arbi- tration proceedings will be saved. The Borough Sur- veyor's decision is binding on the company and in de- fault of non-fulfilment of the obligations, a private trader may go to law and sue for damages on the strength of the Borough Surveyor's decision. This will obviate the necessity of arbitration proceedings. If the safety of Warrington bridge is endangered the depth may be reduced if agreed to by the Com pany and the Corporation. In default of the navigable depth being maintained, the traders are to have right to pass down the Canal free of toll. Hitherto the traders have been compelled to enter and leave the canal at Eastham. In future they will be able to leave or enter by the Old Quay Lock at Runcorn.
It is probable that an effort will now be made to bring about a settlement of the action at law which is now pending in the House of Lords. TERMS OF THE AGREENIENr.

div.head: JUNIOR CONSERVATISM. Liberals as " Dast Throwers."
div.p: JUNIOR CONSERVATISM. Liberals as " Dast Throwers."

Mr. Roger C. Parr presided at the sixth annual meet- ing of the Warrington Junior Conservative Association held on Saturday afternoon last. Mr. Parr was re-elected president of the Association and in proposing him, Mr. DRAPER said their opponents were active now and were doing everything they could to increase their power. They were advertising them-, selves in all sorts of ways and in connection with all sorts of objects, but he believed that as long as they had gentlemen in office like Mr. Parr, they would be able to repel any attack their opponents might make on them. Mr. W. L. Williams was re-elected chairman and Mr. S. Thorley, vice-chairman. Councillor WILsoN, in proposing the re-election of Mr. Brooks as treasurer, and Mr. Hayes as secretary said the Liberals were working tooth and nail now, as they wished to defeat the Conservatives.
The President paid a high tribute to the admirable services rendered to the Association by Mr. Herbert Hayes, and the proposition was carried unanimously..

Richardson, while the representatives on the Club Committee appointed were Messrs. W. L. Williams,Stanley Thorley W. C. Brooks, W. Gibson, J. Strettle and J. Seed. The mover was Mr. F. WEBSTER, and the seconder Mr. M. ALLEN.

Mr. H. J. WESTBROOK obServed that Mr. Hands had asked the meeting, not to be deceived or sold. 'He quite agreed with him, although it was hardly necessary to tell Conservative workingmen that it was the other side who ought to have that advice given to them ; and his authority was the statement made the other evening by Mr. Howes in the Parr Hall. Mr. Howes was a Radical lecturer, and it wis always amusing to read Radical speeches. He (Mr. Howes) then claimed that the Radicals were the party of progress, but it struck him (Mr. West- brook)that it was rather a large order for a man to take upon himself when the same evening the audience had been asked to tie the town to doctrines 60 years old. (Laughter and applause.) If Hr. HOWQ3 would get his information from decent books and not from a certain source the speaker named he would find that the party of Progress was the party to which those present belonged. The Radicals were adepts at misrepresentation, but if the Radical working man would only think for himself, and not be bought by bribes, he would see how hollow it was to talk about Chinese slavery and conscience. It would not be slavery, but perfect freedom and liberty. Why, the very document on which it was possible to make an agreement between this country and China was brought into existence not by a wicked Unionist Government but by a Liberal Government in the year 1860. It was also a fact that out of 50 odd different ordinances promulgated over 20, or nearly one-half, had been effected by the Liberals, so that it did not lie in their months to talk about the question at all. The Liberals were the champion dust throwers and red herring drawers. They were not running this question on behalf of the working man, it was really An election dodge.. The Chinese agreements were entered by the free will of the natives, and would their own Minister in London allow them to be entered into if they admitted of slavery ?. ("No, no," and applause.) Counciilor HULSE seconded the motion, and spoke of the Conservative party as a progressive party. They were not heterogeneous but a homogeneous, and they clung to each other for their own prosperity.
NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

Warrington thoroughly deserved to win on Satur- day, and it is safe to say that had time permitted they would have pulled off a victory at Wigan. Most of their batsmen were in grand form and the score had reached 213 with only 7 wickets down when the closure was applied. At close of play the Wigan players had responded with 107 for the loss of 6 wickets. This was the first meeting of the teams for several years and Warrington had no reason to feel dissatisfied with their display. The record for the first five weeks of the season—which is alike gratifying and creditable—is four victories and one draw.

The Warrington Captain, E. A. Connor, is to be congratulated upon his splendid innings. He hit freely, but without a single faulty stroke, and placed 61 (not out) to his credit. His chief hits were ten fours.

W. H. Podmore also wielded the bat in brilliant style, and by dint of hard, clean hitting knocked up 50. Next on the list comes J. Callon with 26, whilst P. B. Hawtin was responsible for an excellent 25. T. Wright, who figured so successfully in the Bootle en- gagement, compiled 23.
H. G-. Rushton was the top scorer for Wigan, his innings realizing 32. Wright bowled him with a fine ball. Halliwell hatted steadily for 29 and Broughton put together 19.
Podmore and Übsdell come out best in the bowling department. libsdell look 1 wicket for 5 runs, and Podmore 2 for 23.

Warrington's cup-fighting footballers were to be seen displaying their prowess with the bat and ball at Arpley on Monday and Tuesday evenings. As a complimentary benefit to G. Hampson, who has kept wicket for ten years, the Warrington eleven arranged a friendly match which attracted fairly-large gates. It was a novelty to see Jack Fish at the wicket, but although try-getting is more in his line he did not appear at all perturbed at taking the field in such an unusual role.

The cricketers did not take matters seriously, and the result was that their visitors from Wilderspool triumphed by five runs. Fish and Cook had quite an escort of juvenile admirers when they retired to the pavilion, and the cheering youngsters reminded one of" grate fites " ett Wilderspool. G. Jolley made the best innings or the footballers, and he was closely followed by Harry Ashton, the popular secretary, who gave quite an exhilarating display.

It is fitting that athletics should be encouraged among the Secondary School students, and we are pleased to note that a cricket club has been formed. The members had the satisfaction of placing a victory to th6ir credit on Saturday when they tried conclusions with Rylands's office staff. There was nothing re- markable in the scoring,W.floughton being at the top with 10.

Sankey Wire Mills entertained High Legh and wm by 8 runs. Woodcock exhibited fine form with the bat and knocked up 22, whilst R. Cook bowled well. R. Ashbridge (18) was the visitors' highest scorer and Lowe did good work with the ball, capturing 8 wickets.

G-rappeuhall made short work of Winnington Park 294 whose combined efforts produced only 18. The visitors scored 127 for the loss of 7 wickets, their most successful batsman being J. Pearson, who ran up 36. To Watson belongs most of the credit for the early dismissal of the visitors; for he captured 7 wickets at the ridiculously low cost of 2 runs.

Warrington Grammar School experienced a heavy d3feat at the hands of their }Jaime visitors, who had a margin of 39 with 5 wickets to fall. Lindley gave a fine batting display, and compiled 29 (not out.

Penketh seem to have struck a had vein and lost at Hough Green by 11 runs. Their best batsmen were S. Hobson who contributed 20, whilst Upson knocked up 15. Penketh " A also fared badly, Rainhill " A " gaining the victory by 13.
Appleton and Stretton had the best of their meeting with the Cable Company, and St. Paul's accounted for Hels!3y, there being no double figures in either Football.

The football season really closel on Saturday last when St. Helens played their extra match with Hol- beck for promotion to the Senior League. Though they were drawn away to Huddersfield the Saints played up so manfully that they obtained a lead of seven points early on and maintained it to the end. The South West Lancashire clubs are all once again participating in first-class football and diere will doubtless be even keener comnetition between them in the future.
Oa returning home the victorious S tints Avant e.l masse to the house of their popular skipper, Billy Briers, who was prevented from playing by illness, and gave him a hearty sort of serenade.

The annual general meeting of the Northern Union at Huddersfield, in July next, will be the scene of an interesting discussion. Not only will an attempt be made to carry the twelve a-side resolution, but another of an equally important character will be placed before the meeting to be •voted upon. This will be a pro- posal to abolish the working clause, which makes it compulsory for all players playing under Northern Union rules to be in bona-fide employment. Should the new project be enforced, it will mean out-and-out professionalism for the wealthiest clubs in the Northern Union League. It may not be carried out on so large a scale as is the case under the " Soccer" code, but still it is quite apparent that if the working clause is eliminated, it will only be a matter of a season or two when out-and-oat professionalism will be adopted. Broughton Rangers, who suffered from the vagaries of the working clause rule last season, will, I hear, propose the resolution at the annual meeting to abolish the working clause, while Hull have promised to second the motion. Salford, Swinton, Oldham, Hull Kingston qpvers, and other prominent clubs, including those in Northumberland and Dur- ham, will support the innovation and there will be a strong endeavour to obtain the three-fourths majority necessary to carry the proposal.

The Wigan Football Club balance sheet just Issued denotes remarkable progress on the part of the club which has had a record season. Ab3ut £4,500 has been taken at the gates, viz, first team £3,532, and "A," team £696, with £251 for a county match. There is a balance in the bank of £690.

The Yorkshire vote, taken on the whole, may be the means of throwing out the intended new policy, but everything will depend upon whether the much belated twelve-a-side game is adopted. Should this be the case, the abolishment of the works clause would likely follow, and the pure professional element be instituted. The working clause undoubtedly ha 4 its advantages and disadvantages, and there will be much to say on both sides. It is understood that Mr. Joseph Platt, the hon. secretary of the Northern Union, is bitterly opposed to the proposed elimination of the works clause, and unless his vote and sympathy can be secured there is strong reason to think that the pathway to professionalism will be bldtked up for at least another season. All the same, the situation is mast interesting,and developments are eagerlya waited.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

At the time of writing the prospects for the Whit- suntide holiday are decidedly cheering. The weather during the whole of Friday was delightful and cyclists are looking forward to a grand time this week-end. , Tours to favourite holiday haunts are being organized, and if only the present congenial weather continues the country lanes will be alive with wheelers. As usual, the members of the Warrington Cycling Club will divide themselves into two parties. The far-famed Vale of Llangollen will be visited by one section, and the other will explore the Ellesmere district. The Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Club have arranged runs to Vale Royal to-day,and to Macclesfield on Monday.

The unpromising weather of the early part of Satur- day afternoon kept many cyclists in town. The War- r' ngton club run was to Delamere, but only half a dozen members turned out. The roads were in splendid condition after the rain, and the outing was thoroughly enjoyed. Warrington was reached about ten o'clock.
1 Tuesday evening was rather dull and stormy, but the roads were all that could be desired, and 16 mern- i

bers oycled to Glazebury. Several interesting games of bowls were played on the green attached to the Raven Hotel, and afterwards an impromptu smoker was held. Songs and recitals u ere given by members and the gathering was a great success.

The Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Cycling Club, which has a membership of between 30 and 40, is carrying out a most attractive programme this season. Owing to the unsettled weather, there was only a small turn- out for Saturday's run to Cranage. The officers of the club are :—President, Councillor James Dodds; vice-presidents, Mr. W. Pacev., Mr. J. Wadsworth, and Mr. S. Blythe; captain, Mr. T 7 Barlow; sub-captains, Mr. J. Davidson and Mr. W. Webb ; hon, treasurer, Mr. E. Jones; hon. secretary, Mr. E. Graham; com- mittee, Messrs. R. Graham, C. Bromley, F. Hardy, O. Gough and J. Harding.
Cyclists should light their lamps to-night at 9.12.

Bowling. The works competition increases in interest as time goes on Rylands's No 1, had no difficulty in disposing of Vernon-street tannery on Saturday. The match between Firth Company and Cheshire Lines was more keenly contested, Chcshire Lines triumphing by 15 points. Artingstall's failed to turn out a team, so London and North Western Railway, the cup-holders had a walk over.

div.head: SUGGESTED LABOUR CANDIDATE Meeting Last Night.
div.p: THE SUGGESTED LABOUR CANDIDATE Meeting Last Night.

• A meeting of trades' unionist representatives was. held in Bold street WeSleyan schoolroom last evening, under the auspices of the Labour Representation • Committee, to take into consideration the advisability or otherwise, of selecting a labour candidate to con- test the Borough at the next general election A.. gentleman recommended by the National Labour Representation Committee was in attendance, but at the close of the meeting the press representatives were informed that no information could be divulged. We understand that no definate decision was arrived at.

div.head: TO-DAY'S HORSE PARADE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S HORSE PARADE.

To-day the annual May parade of horses will thke place and the event promises to be a great success. There are 120 entries in the ordinary classes and 25 for the three cup competitions. Two silver cups are pre- sented by the President (Sir Gilbert Greensll, Bart.), for the best light lurry or van horse and for the best light horse respectively, and Mr. Peter Davies has again given a silver cup for the best heavy or cart horse. The President and Reception. Committee will meet the judges at the Lion Hotel at 11 15 and proceed immedi- ately to the ground, in Arpley fields, where the judging will begin at 12 prompt. Lady Greenall will present the prizes to the successful competitors. Non- competing turnouts must be in Slutcher's-lance at 1.30. The procession will leave Arpley punctually at 2 o'clock and proceed along Parker-street, Sankey-street, Butter- market-street, Chnrch-streret, rlund the Lamp, Church- street, Mersey-street, Bridge-street, Horsemarket-street Winwick-street, Tanners-lane, Froghall-lane, Priestley- street, Powys-street, Bank Quay, Sankey-street, Bold- street, Wilson Patten-street. The following will be the order : Corporation Fire Brigade. Ambulance. Walker's Band. Class 1. Brewer's pair horses. la , single horses. ~ 3. Builders, Merchants. 79 4. Contractors, and Carters. 2, „ 5. Tanners. stield's Band. , ft Engine. , Escape and Brigade. Class 6. Corporation vehicles. „ 7. Coal Merchants and Dealers. 8. Corn Dealers and Millers. Borough Band. Class 9. Butchers, Bakers, and Grocers. „ 11. Heavy miscellaneous. • „ 12. Light miscellaneous. „ 13. Pair horse miscellaneous. Pioneer Band. Class 14. Fish Dealers and 31ilk Dealers. „ 15. Farmers. ', 16. Covered Furniture Vans. Non-Competitors. A collection will be taken along the line of route in aid of local charities. -
Admirable arrangements have been made by the com- mittee with Messrs. George Venn and T. H. Pretty as hon. secretaries.

div.head: VOLUNTEER HORSE RACES.
div.p: VOLUNTEER HORSE RACES.
An Interesting Programme for Whit-Monday.

Warrington will have a' great Bank Holiday attraction in the regimental horse races promoted by the local Volunteer Battalion. The event will be unique, inasmuch as this is the first time such races have been held at Warrington, and a great deal of interest has been aroused. A large field off Wilderapool Causeway has been secured, and stands have been erected for the accommodation of the sPectatators. The afternoon's programme embraces seven races, commencing at 2.20 with the men's flat race, for which there are 22 entries. This race will be open to the Ist. V.B. South Lancashire Regiment only, and there will be three prizes of £3, £1 10s., and 10s. respectively. At three o'clock the officers' steeplechase will commence, and this too is confined to the first South Lancashire Regi- ment. Colonel Reid Walker has presented a silver cup as first prize, and the second award is a silver cigarette case. A race open to all comers within a radius of 15 miles of Warrington should prove an interesting event, the first prize being .C 5 and .the second £2 10s. For the Mounted Infantry Challenge Cup steeplechase there are 19 entries and no doubt the contest will be keen. The winner will reaeive a cup presented by Mrs. Avery and £1 in cash, and there will be a second prize of £l. Other events will be the officers' flat race, Victoria Cross Race, and driving competition for regimental transport. In the Victoria Cross contest the competitors have to race about one mile over hurdles on the flat course. They have also to dismount under fire, and pick up and carry a dummy over the last. hurdle past the winning post. There are 15 entries for .the race, and the first prize is a cup presented by Captain Crosfield, and .£l. During the afternoon the Regimental band will play selections. Captain A. F. Bundock, the adjutant, will be the judge. After, each race Lady Greenall will present the prizes to the successful competitors.

div.head: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.
ENDING MAY 14th, 1904.

Daring ths waak, th 3 following births and deaths were registered :—Warrington Registration District births, SU; deaths, 31. The excess of births over deaths was 28. The birth-rat& was equal to 45.0. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 21.0 per 1,000, against 18.8 the average of the previous 4 weeks and against 8.5 the corresponding period of last year. The death-rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal to 7.6 per 1,000, against 4.9 the average rate of the previous 4 weeks and against 2.3 the correspond- ing period of 1903.
The ages of mortality were:- 0-1 1-5 5-15 15-21 25-35 65—up. °rota 6 8 IL 16 31
The deaths included 2 from measles, 1 from scarlet fever, 7 from whooping cough, 2 from tubercular diseases, 2 from lung diseases, 3 from heart diseases, 14 from all other causes.

The following cases of infectious disease have been reported during the week :—Small-pox, 2 cases; scarlet. fever 29 cases; diphtheria, 1 case; enteric, 1 case. Total number of patients in hospital, week ending May 14th, 103. MET RORO LO G Y.—The mean temperature was 47 Fah., and therefore the same as the preceding week. The maximum temperature 62 F., was recorded on the 11th inst, and the minimum temperature 47 F., on tie 10th inst.
The rainfall measarei .15 inch. The general direc- tion was S.W.
J. GUEST GORNALL. Medical Oilicer of Health.

div.head: GRAPPEN HALL.
div.p: GRAPPEN HALL.

DEATH OF MRS. ANN MAINwaRiNG.-,--Mrs. Ann Mainwaring, an old inhabitant of Grappenhall, died on Thursday evening after a somewhat short illness. Deceased had reached the ripe age of 80 and had spent most of her life in the vallage. The interment takes place on Monday next at three o'clock.

- THE CRICKET- CLUB.—The two elevens have now played two matches each, the Ist eleven proving victorious twice and the 2nd once. The game last Saturday against Winnington 2nd turned out a very hollow victory. Watson, for Grappenhall, etas in rare form, taking seven wickets at a cost of 2 runs, the visitors being dismissed for the smill total of 18. The home players gave a good display with the bat, seven batsmen scoring 127 runs. The best scores for the winners were, Pearson 26, Carter 27 and Ellis 21. The 12nd eleven visited Altrincham, their opponents being I St. George's and returned discomforted. The bowling of the home eleven was much too good for the 2nd who only made 9 St. George's replied with 49 and ran out winners somewhat easily.
