div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

BROKEN BOTTLE LEADS TO CAPTURE. James Leonardy, a notorious character, appeared before the Warrington Bench on Wednesday on a charge of being found on the, enclosed premises of Ann Holloway, 53, Bewsey-strest, at 3.30 that morning, with intent to commit a felony.—P.C. Edwards stated that he was on duty in Bowsey-street when Mr. Harry Holloway told him that a man was in the house. On making search he found prisoner in the washhouse and took him into custody.. On the way to the Police Station he was very rough.—Mr. Harry Hollo- way stated that he was- awakened by the smashing of glass and on going downstairs saw a man in the yard. He went for P.C. Edkvards who found prisoner in the wash-house. There was a broken bottle on the stairs in the house, and it appeared that in going to the lumber room prisoner had knocked the bottle over and caused the noise which aroused witness. —Superintendent Monaghan said the prisoner would not work and was a loiterer. That was his 33rd appearance. —He was sentenced to three months' imprisonment with hard labour.

div.head: Warrington Borough Police Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Police Court.
Minor Cases.

SATURDAY.--=Before Messrs. Birchall, Hayward, Wright R. T. Fairclough, Geddes,and Alderman Smethurst. HURDLES STOLEN FROM A FlELD.—Three youths, named Patrick Price, 35, Golborne-street • George Ellis, 22, Elizabeth-street, and Charles Steele, Aikin- street, were charged with stealing from a field at Arpley, iron hurdles, value 10s., the property of James Bowcock, butcher, Horsemarket-street.—The Chief Con- stable said that for a considerable time the neighbour- hood of Arpley had been the" happy hunting ground" for a lot of petty thieves and people who did wilful and wanton damage. About three o'clock on Friday after- noon Mr. Bowcock went to see his land at Arpley. Upon arriving there he found the three youths filling a handcart with the iron hurdles which protected his land. Their intention was to sell the iron. Information was given to the police, and P.C. Clough made inquiries and apprehended the youths.—The Chief Constable described the prisoners as" rank, rife, pilferers."—Prisoners were fined 30s. each with the option of a months' in:yrison- ment. • A "TAP "AND ITS RESULTS.—James Crank,l7,Dicken- son-street, was summoned for having illtreated his child aged 22 months in a manner likely to cause it un- necessary suffering and injury to health on the 4th May. Mr Browne who appeared to prosecute on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C. said the prisoner was charged with haying hit the child on the left side of the face, either with his fist or his open hand. The side of the face was bruised and was one black IBMS. Prisoner would not work— Mary Crank, wife of prisoner, gave evidence, and said -the prisoner " tapped " the child with his hand.—Dr. Peacock said that when he examined the child he found a distinct discolouration of the face, which was also bruised. No slight tap had caused the bruises and dis- colouration, and considerable violence must have been -used—lt was stated that prisoner was in the habit of thrashing the child, and Edith Millington, the next door neighbour, said she had heard the blows whilst in her house. She considered it terrible cruelty to strike the • child as prisoner had done—Prisoner admitted striking the child but said he was in drink at the time. He was sent to prison for a month. DISGRACEFUL CONDUCT IN BUTTERNIARKET-STREET.— Patrick MacDonald, Gleeson's Lodging-house, Bank- street, was charged with having been drunk and dis- orderly in Buttermarket-street the previous night, and also with having wilfully damaged a lady's blouse and skirt, to the amount of £2.—The evidence showed that • whilst under the influence of drink prisoner chased his wife into the shop of Mrs. Smith, milliner, 31, Butter- market-street. A struggle ensued between them, and a jug of beer, which the woman was carrying, was spilled over a blouse and dress. The goods were ruined. P.C. Gibbs came upon the scene and prisoner was taken into .custody.— [his was his 28th appearance and he was sent to gaol for three months. _MoNDAY.—Before the Mayor (presiding), Alderman Smethurst, Councillor Thornton and Messrs. Birchall, Wright. and Hayward. MILITARY ABSENTEE.—Thomas Hardacr, last from -Manchester, was charged with being an absentee from the 4th Battalion King's Liverpool Regiment, stationed at Altcar since 1897.—P.C. Holland said he saw the prisoner in Horsemarket-street, and on account of his military appearance questioned him. Ultimately he admitted that he was a deserter.—Prisoner was handed •over to an escort, and, on the application of the Chief Constable, the constable was recommended for the usual reward. AN OLD OFFENCE.—John Kelly, Dannett-street, was charged with having been drunk and disordei ly at 10.40 p.m. on Saturday night. He was also charged with having committed a breach of the peace by fighting on August 27th. 1902.—The Chief Constable explained that prisoner failed to appear in answer to a summons issued in 1902 for the latter offence and he had not been since -seen until his apprehension.—P.C.'s Reddington and Cooper (26) proved the cases—Prisoner was fined ss. and costs and bound over to keep the peace. CRUELTY TO A HoßsE.—James Kilduff, 24, Marsh- straet, was summoned for having ill-treated a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state.—P.C. Turner said that on the 9th inst. he saw defendant in charge of a lurry. Upon examining the animal he found a large wound under the saddle round which there was a quan- tity of matter.—Inspector Taylor corroborated.— Inspector Gibson, R.S.P.C.A. said the horse had under- gone an operation and was put to work too soon.—The magistrates considered the offence was due to lack of foresight and ordered defendant to pay the costs (6s. 6d.) SUNDAY GAMBLING.—Thomas Stringer, 44, Howard street, was summoned for having tossed for money in a passage at the rear of Aitkin street, on Sunday Bth inst. —P. C. Clough spoke to having seen the defendant along with three companions tossing coins in an entry at the rear of Aitkin street. When the officers ap- proached the men made off, but Stringer ran into the arms of P. C. Jones. He refused to give his name and address and had to be brought to the Police Station— The Chief Constable said Sunday gambling was becoming .alarming.—A fine of 55., and costs was imposed.

div.head: DIABETES AND CONSUMPTION
div.p: DIABETES AND CONSUMPTION

Every case completely Cnred in two months without leaving home. The causes of these complaints have been discovered by MR. SPARKS, SPECIALIST, 36 WAKE- FIELD ROAD, STALYBRIDGE, and they can be cured sooner and safer by his treatment than any other. Every case of an.Tmia and general weakness cured no matter who you have been under. Mr. Sparks knows more about the cure of consumption than any other known man.

DISORDERLY CONDIICT.—James Lee, labourer, 19, Back Crossley-street, was fined 55. forhaving made loud and unseemly noises in Winwick-street, on May Bth. P.C. Baxendale said defendant was shouting and "try- ing to sing." ALLEGED GAME T RESPA SS.—Richard flughes,labourer 15. Plumpton-street, was charged with being unlawfully in possession of game, and also with having gaming nets and pegs in his possession on the previous. Wednesday.— Se rgeantE vans said he was on Atherton's Quaylin company witha man named Kent and saw the defendant at 5.25 on the morning in question coming from the direction of Sir Gilbert Greenall's land. He ran away, but was sub- sequently caught and a net and pegs, as well as a rabbit, were found in his pockets. He had dropped another.— Defendant who had previously been before the magis- trates for trespassing was fined 10s. and costs, • the nets and pegs to be confiscated. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Birchall (in the chair), Alderman Hutchinson,and Mr. Geddes. , THEFT OF A. Bans.—William Wilson or Percival, of ' Cadishead, was charged with stealing a whitewash brush, value 4s. 9d., the property of Mr. Hamlet Houghton, ironmonger, Bridge-street.—Prisoner was seen by Eliza Andrews to take the brush from the shop-door. The police were informed and he was arrested with the brush in his possession.—Prisoner said the brush pro- duced in Court was more valuable than the one he stole. —P.C. Phillips stated that the brush produced was the stolen one.--A fine of 20s. and costs, with the alterna- tive of a month's imprisonment, was imposed. THEFT FROM A. SCHOOL.—Amy Holland, a stranger, was sentenced to a month's imprisonment for stealing from the porch of Cairo-street schools, a jacket of the value of 55., the property of Miss Ella Wilson,a teacher. —Superintendent Monaghan stated that when the jacket was missed the police were informed and it was ascertained that prisoner attempted unsuccessfully to pledge it at the shop of Mr. Houghton, Mersey-street. , In the evening she was arrested by P.C. Clough and on I being brought to the Police Station denied all know- ledge of the theft. Ultimately she admitted to him I (the superintendent) that she had stolen the jacket and sold it to a; woman named Duckworth in Ellesmere- street for 4d.
THURSDAY.—Before Mr. John Fake,lough (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst,Nlessrs. C. White. Hepherd, and
Geddes.

WOULD NOT WORK.—William Berry was summoned for neglecting to maintain his family, whereby he, his wife, and five children became chargeable to the War- rington Union.—Mr. B. Shearer said the prisoner and his family sere admitted to the Workhouse on May 16th. Prisoner was employed at Whitecross and was in regular work, his last week's wages amounting to 275. He deliberately gave up his employment and went into the Workhouse. Mr. Shearer added that the house was getting full of such cases and he. asked the Bench to make an example of the m tn.—Mr F. Aukland, relieving officer, said prisoner's employers informed him that the man left work for no other cause than to get his back pay and go on the spree with ft.— Prisoner was sentenced to a months hard labour.— Henry Riley, who was charged with neglecting to main- tain his wife and five children, expressed sorrow and said "it was all through drink."—He was sent to gaol for a month with bard labour. "WANTED SOMETHING TO EAT."—Eliza Rowlands was charged with stealing ashawl,of the value of 7s. 6d. from the shop of Edgar V. Morton, pawnbroker, St. James's street.—The Chief Constable said prisoner stole the shawl from insidelhe shop door and pawned it at another shop within a short time. She made a very ingenious statement as to how she came in possession of the arti- cle, and gave the name of a well known customer of the pawnbroker. When arrested prisoner said she would not have stolen the shawl had she not wanted something to eat—Detective Barlow said prisoner belonged to, a respectable family but for some time she had not been living at home—Oa prisoner promising to go home the magistrates discharged her after recordin,g la con- viction. ABSCONDING FROM A WOR,KHOUSE.—Meredith Jones was charged with absconding from Wrexham Work- house with clothing belonging to the Guardians on May 17th.—P.C. Gibbs stid he was on duty in Arpley- street when prisoner came to him and said he wanted to see a doctor. On being questioned he said he had ab- sconded from Wrexham Workhouse. Prisoner was re- manded until the %Vrexham authorities could send for him. A FORGIVING COMPLAMANT.—Thomas Wells was charged with assaulting Ann Ball, with whom he lodged on May 18th.—Mr. Steel defended.—Cornplainant said defendant used foul language, and when she told him to desist he struck her on the head with his fist. She was however, willing to withdraw the case.—Mr. Steel said the affair was quite an accident.—Phe case was with- drawn on payment of costs. FRID tY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alder- man Smethurst, Coancillors Roberts and Thornton,

and Mr. Hephet=d. FACTORY ACT PROSECUTION.—John Walker and Co., Bewsey-street, were summoned for employing a boy named William Henry Perry, aged 14, at 9.25 p.m. on May 6th, contrary to the previsions of the Factory Act. —lt was stated that the offence had been committed inadvertently, as there was no need for the lad to be at work.—A line of ss. and costs was imposed. UNHAPPY MARRIED LlFE.—Samuel Silcock, 27 Cartwrighestreet, was summoned for having deserted his wife, Margaret Silcock, 10, Brew street, •St. Helens. —Mr. Steel appeared for the complainant and Mr. E. A. Connor defended.—The parties had previously been separated, but complainant went to live with her hus- band again in January. In april she had to summon him for assault and he was fined. Complainant alleged that after the case had been heard she went to the house but was refused admission. —For the defence, Mr. Connor stated that complainant had repeatedly left her husband of her own free will— in fact she had spent about nine of the past ten years away from home. Defendant denied having refused to admit her to the house—After hearing evidence on both sides the magistrates granted a separation order with ss. per week alimony. An advocate's ee was allowed. WOMEN'S SQUABBLE.—Annie Large, 59, Plumpton- street, was summoned for assaulting Mary Jane Cope, 15, Hesketh-street, on the 16th inst.—Mr. Steel defended —Complainant said defendant struck her in the face,and pulled some of her,hair out by the roots.--In cross-ex- amination complainant admitted that she pulled Mrs. Large's hair—Mr. Steel : It was a regular tearing match —On behalf of the defendant, Mr. Steel characterised the case as "a petty squabble between two women, emanat- ing from a lodger.' —A fine of ss. and costs was in- flicted. HUSBAND APPLIES FOR A SEPARATION ORDER.— Alfred Glover, 26. Victoria-street, applied for a separa- tion order against his wife on the ground that she was an habitual drnnkard.—Complainant said defendant had been of drunken habits for the past twelve months, and appeared to go worse every week. He had done every- thing possible to try and reform her, but without avail. She was continually rambling about the streets, and he doubted whether she really knew what she was doing. She was not living with him.—The case was adjourned in order that the defendant could appear before the Court.

div.head: BETTER THAN MONEY IN THE SAYINGS
div.p: BETTER THAN MONEY IN THE SAYINGS
BANK.

The working man to-day gives more attention to the food he has to eat than his forefathers gave, as he reali.es that his health—his bank—depends very largely upon the properties of what he eats and drinks. It follows, then, that the popular article of food is that which is easy to digest ; but more popular still are preparations which are found to aid and strengthen the digestive organs, and also to act as an energiser for the whole system. Dr. Tibbles' Vi-Cocoa is such a food. It places a means in the hands of everyone to build up and maintain a strong constitution, which enables its possessor to travel his life's journey without the aches and pains which are in many cases preventable. Thus we come round again to sound commonsense based on experience.

LIVERPOOL AND NORTFI WALES.—Whitsuntide Sail- ings.—The Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Company announce special railings for the Whitsuntide Holidays by their new palatial saloon steamer, "La Marguerite," also by the splendid paddle steamer "St. Elvies," and the favourite saloon steamer "Snowdon." Until Wednesday next the Snowdon will keep on the Liverpool service for Llandudno, Be.aumaris and Bangor (connecting for Menai Bridge.) "La Marguerite" (with a passenger-carrying capacity of over 2,000 people) will make her maiden trip on' Saturday, 21st, and take up the daily sailings (Sundays and Bank Holiday included) during Whitsuntide Holi- days. finishing 29th May, when the" St. Elvies "will take her place for a brief period. On Saturday, 21st inst.,the " St. Elvies" leaves for Llandudno and Menai Straits, returning direct from Menai Bridge to Liverpool. This is a most delightful sea trip, and is sure to be . well patronised at the low fares advertised should the weather be favourable. Residents at St. Helens will be pleased to bear that the South Lancashire Tramway Company bave agreed to run a through car to the Pierhead leaving St. Helens (Bridge street) at 7.30 a.m., thence to Prescot (King's Arms) at 7.55 a.m., passing Knotty Ash at 8.15 a.m., and proceeding along the usual route to Pierhead. From the above announcement it will be observed that nothing is wanted except fine weather to enable the company•to reap the benefit of their enterprise by placing such a fine steamAr as "La Marguerite" upon the North Wales service, and giving such unequalled passenger accommodation at the same popular fares as heretofore. •

FAILURES IN ENGLAND AND WALES.—According to " Kemp's Mercantile Gazette," the total number of failures recorded in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, May 13th, was 180,viz.:—New Bank- ruptcy Proceedings published in the London Gazette, 87; deeds of arrangement registered, 93. The res- pective numbers in the corresponding week of last year were : Bankruptcies, 77 ; deeds of arrangement, 83— total 360; being a net increase in bankruptcies of 159, and a•net increase in deeds of arrangement in 1904, to ate, of 230.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, May 21 1904
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, May 21 1904

said he believed it was a fact that the lowest tender was not accepted, but it, was not known until after- wards, when a personal explanation was given by some members of the committee, that it was the lowest. He did not think the sub-committee had made a mistake; the mistake was on the part of those who sent in the tender. Mr. Harry Fairclough's tender—and he thought Mr. Fairclough was referring to that—was for £lOB. For that amount he undertook to remove the counter supply new fittings but no mention was made of linoleum. If the committee had thought the tender was inclusive they would have accepted it. He contended that, even in trade terms, linoleum was not a, fitting. It would perhaps be better for the Borough Surveyor to draw up a form of tender to avoid any mistakes in future. Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH said it was not intended by the Association to specify every artiele needed but simply to state what the job was. That ought to be distinctly understood by the committee. Councillor WILKINSON did not wish to stultify the action of the sub-committee, but the Surveyor had issued a specification for the work, and if Mr. Harry Fairclough had only said "I am willing to perform the work according to the specification" it would have been sufficient. (Hear hear.) He hoped the little slip on the part of the sub-committee which had resulted in a loss of £l7 would be a lesson to all other committees. Councillor LORD understood the work was in hand. He would have liked to have moved that the matter be referred back, but it would be no use doing so. Councillor TINNION said the work was very urgent. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH : I think the Finance Committee empowered the sub-ccimmittee to give the order. The matter -then dropped. MR. JOLLEY AND "BASELESS SUGGESTIONS." Mr. JOLLEY took exception to Councillor Wilkinson's admonitory tone. The sub-committee, he contended, did not make a slip. In regard to Mr. May's objections, if the committee could give figures which would enable, the real comparison to be made they would do so gladly, but it was impossible to do so at the present time. Mr. May's suggestion in regard to the secondary school had been made in terms which he (Mr. Jolley) considered unfair. Mr. May knew as well as he did that the school was not in existence in May of last year. It was only started in September. Yet Mr. May deliberately sug- gested that the old Technical Instruction Committee could give particulars. He (Mr. Jolley) wished to take strenuous exception to two words, one of which 'was frequently used, namely, the word " farce " and the word" harsh." He (the speaker) had had the honour of presiding over many committees, and the use of the word farce as applied to a committee consisting of five members of the Corporation and five selected members with the chairman and vice-chairman, was an insult which ought not to be allowed tb pass month after month.
Mr. MAY : I protest against such an inference. The CFIAIRM AN : You have had your say, Mr. May. Mr. MAX: I made no such insinuation.

Mr. JOLLEY, continuing,said that the suggestion made month after month, ever since the committee came into existence, that the Finance Committee were trying to keep the full committee in the dark was utterly base- less and unjustifiable. On several occasions he had not commented on Mr. May's remarks, but as silence did not seem to stop these offensive comments he took the opportunity of saying a word or two in defence of the action of the committee over which he presided: so that the general body of ratepayers might realize that although the members were patient and long-suffering, they were not going to tolerate, even from Mr. May,re- peated_insinuations of such an offensive kind.
4 Mr. MA.Y rose to explain. The CHAIRMAN ; You must sit down, please. Mr. May: I did not apply the expression to the COMmittee. .
The CITA.IRMAIsT : Now Mr. May, are you going to sit down? There is an end of it.
The minutes were then approved. SCHOOL NIANAGENIENT CONINIITPEE. THE HOLIDAY QUESTION. •

The Ray. MORLEY STEVENSON, in moving the adoption of the minutes of the School Management Committee, referred to the reconsideration of the resolution with reference to the head master of the mixed department of St. James' school, Latchford, which was notapproved by the Education Committee. The matter had again been very carefully co nsidered,he said,and the committee by a very large majority determined to reverse their previous decision, and had fixed the salary at the rate of £3OO per annum. By the resolution relating to holidays it would be seen that the committee proposed a change with reference to the Whitsuntide holiday. The follow- ing dates had been fixed:— WHITSUNTIDE: Elementary schools, Friday evening, May 20th, to Monday morning, Mty 30th. 'Secondary school, Friday evening, May 20th, to Tuesday morning, May 31st. WALKING DAY: Elementary schools, Wednesday evening, June,29th, to Monday morning, July 4th. Secondary school, Thursday evening, Sane 30th, to Monday morning, July 4th. MIDSUMMER: Elementarfschools,Friday noon July 15th, to Monday morning August 15th. Secondary school, Friday noon, July 15th, to Monday morning, August 29th. _ . .

The Rev. Morley 'Stevenson pointed out that the resolution with reference to Whitsun- tide must be read in conjunction with a succeeding resolution, which read as follows :—That the practice of granting a half day's holiday on the occasion of H.A. Inspector's visits to the schools be discontinued, and, in view of the extended holiday granted at Whitsurutide, the managers be asked t ) en- deavour to curtail as far as possible the occasional holidays. Mr. Stevenson aided that the practice of granting a half day's holiday on the occasion of H.M. Inspector's visits was when such visits were a great strain on the teachers and children, but now, when the inspector's visit was not so much in the nature of an examination, practically that strain had ceised to exist and it was felt that the half-holiday might be discon- tinued. The frequent practice of giving occasional holidaysacted very badly on the school attendance. A half-holiday at one school was immediately telegraphed to another and the consequence was that the attendance at the other school was diminished. The committee felt it would be some advantage to the Borough and the rates if a week's holiday were given at Whitsuntide,and managers were requested to discountenance, as far as possible, the practice of giving occasional holidays. (Hear, hear.) Mr. UPSON seconded. AN APPLICATIO NOT ACCEDED TO.

Colonel BUCKTON moved al an amendment, that the following resolution be referred back for further consideration :—"An application by the managers of the Fairfield National School for the appointment of an additional assist ant mistress was not acceded to." He stated that he was one of the managers of the Fairfield School, and it did not quite appear on the face of it what the facts were. A teacher, who had been serving her apprenticeship, completed it at the end of December and had been teaching since. She passed third class in the King's Scholarship Examination and therefore could not enter a training college. She had the option of going to the pupil teachers' class, but she did not see her way to do so, and accordingly the committee did not see their way to keep her on. This was not an application for an increase of the staff, but that they should have another teacher in the place of one who was leaving. The work of the school it was true had been reduced by no cookery being taught, but those who knew the school would admit that it was a good one. He might be prejudiced, but he believed it. was second to none in Warrington. He hoped it would maintain that position and not be hampered by a reduction of the staff. The head teacher was already taking one standard and unless the staff were increased she would be called upon to take two. That would militate against the efficiency of the school. Councillor ROGERS seconded.

The DIRECTOR explained that the reason there was no cookery was that there was no room for it. It was not in consequence of the action of the committee, and it was only fair that that should be stated. Mr. MAY supported the amendment on the ground that it would ba an undue increase in the cost of educa- tion to proven.; pupil teachers who had passed third class becoming teachers in the town. By insisting upon all teachers befog certificated,the committee was placing itself in the hands of the Teachers' Union. ("No, no.") While teachers were scarce why should they not go in for pupil teachers, because in many instances those pupil teachers were better than certificated teachers ? They took more interest in their work.

The CHAIRMAN : You are departing from the subject altogether. Mr. MAI( said he supported the amendment because he thought they were going on the wrong tack in forc- ing girls out of the schools by an arbitrary rule. It was because a girl was not allowed to continue in the ser- vice of the committee that she was forced out of the school.

Mr. UPSON did not think that what Mr. May had said should be allowed to pass without comment. It would be well if the full committee understood how they stood in the matter. Instead of forcing teachers out of the school they had provided exceptional facilities for girls to improve their professional standing. These third class teachers had just passed the lowest stage of the King's Scholarship Examination—a preliminary examination to their professional training. The com- mittee offered these teachers 10s. a week, half time in school, free tuition at the classes and free books, so as to qualify themselves for their future career. Where was compulsion exercised to the detriment of the girls? It was the truest economy to have the most highly qualified teachers in the schools. (Hear, hear). Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH did not see why teachers should be sent away when there was an insufficiency of them. The teachers to whom reference had been made were recognized by the code, and until they got a better class their services ought to be continued. Councillor LORD: Are the Fairfield schools under- staffed ? Mr. C. H. UNSWORTHAaid he had made inquiries, and had found that the school in question had well over the staff required by the Education Department. On that

div.head: EDUCATION COMMIT:a.
div.p: EDUCATION COMMIT:a.
MR. MAY'S CRITICISM OF THE FINANCE COMMITTEE.
The School Holidays.

Mr. F. Monks, J.P., presided at the monthly meeting of the Education Committee held at the Town Hall on Monday evening. There were also present :—Alderman Bennett (vice-chairman). Rev. Morley Stevenson, Rev. John Yonge, Rev. E. J. Willcocks, Councillors S. Davies, Hulse, Rogers, Ellison, Dodds, Tinnion, Craik, Wilkinson, Lord, Roberts, Messrs. R. T, Fair dough, T. May, C. H. Unsworth, J. Fulton Smith, J. D. Backton, E. J. Guest,W. Bibby,J. Upson, E. Plinston, A. J. Jolley, G. Walker, R. T. Fairclough and J. Moore Murray (director). MR. MAY AND ECONOMY.

COMPARATIVE STATEMENT OF EXPENDITURE WANTED. The adoption of the Finance Committee's minutes was moved by Mr. A. J. JOLLEY. Councillor TimoN. seconded. Mr. MAN- proposed that the minutes be referred back for the purpose of inserting a statement of the cost of education for the corresponding month of last year,so as to show a comparison. He was under the impression that that was going to b 3 dons this month,and as it had not, he had taken the trouble to insert the particulars in his own copy of the minutes. He found that the School Attendance Committee during April last_year— which was the first complete month under the Educa- tion Committee—spent £l3 3s. 6d., and that this April they had spent eiactly the same sum. The CEINIRMXN pointed out that according to the rules, Mr. May ought to have written out his amend- ment and sent it up before making his comments. He was really out of order.

Continuing, Mr. Max stid the expenditure of the School Management Committee had diminished from £435 to £ls6—something like two-thirds less. Then they hail the item for elementary school teachers' salaries,which for this year was £2,015,as against £1,560, being an increase of about £5OO on the month. The expenditure on the secondary school was a new item for which they had no compare ,unless the old Technical Instruction Committee condescended to supply the information—which he had no doubt it would be within their power to do. The accounts passed this month for the Secondary school and) School of Art totalled 2111 and £25 respectively. The main item was, of course, the increase in the elementary school teachers' salaries. As he had said on previous occasions, it seemed to be the chief work of the School Manage- ment Committee to increase salaries, and now they had a result of it. They had, however, no compare with the cost of the old denominational management. Doubtless they had froth in their minds the fiasco created by members of the Council who, in the Council Chamber, voted against what they had previously voted for several times in committee. It was fully time that the committee-should know how they stood from month to month, and instead of wait- ing until the end of the year before they took a fit of economy they should watch over the expenditure as often as they could and have comparative statements. Of course, he could say a great deal more—(kear, hear) —about economy and the farce they had in the town of very powerful organizations being formed in order to protest the ratepayers from their representatives. (Hear, hear.) Leading ratepayers and property owners had formed such an organization and he had the honour to be a member of a special committee elected for that purpose. It was therefore only rigut that he should bring up this question of increased expenditure. They did not want to be kept in the dark, and they had heard gentlemen with much greater experience than himself say that it was only reasonable that they should have the comparative statement he suggested. Councillor ELLISON seconded, and said he thought the statement would be a great convenience to the mem- bers. _ . _

Mr. A. J. JOLLEY : I submit the amendment is out of order to start with. It is in neither of the two forms prescribed. Councillor DODDS said he did not think the com- mittee would mind giving last year's figures for pur- poses of comparison. The CIIAIRNIAN : Of what practical value would the statement be at present? Councillor DODDS : At present I don't think it would be of much value. _ _ _ _ .

The CRAIRNIAN : It would be of no more value than the fifth wheel to a coach. The expenditure last year was purely exceptional and it is not to be compared. After consult 'lion with the dire3tor, the chairman ruled that the amendment was out of order. There ought to be a definite proposal that the minutes be ap- proved and adopted with the exception of a certain item. He thought Mr. May would get what he wanted a little later on, in the respect of the expenditure of all the committees. Councillor TINSION : We ought to have a standing order to meet amendments of this kind. Mr. MAN' said he was content to leave the matter in the hands of the committee, on the understanding that particulars would be supplied later.
APPOINTMENT OF CARETAKERS. THE POSITION OF SCHOOL MANAGERS.

Councillor DODDS called attention to a resolution that an advertisement be issued for the appointment of a schoolkeeper for Eleathside school. He would like to ask whether that was quite in harmony with the rules, as he understood that the managers of the school usually nominated someone, and the committee then appointed that person if suitable. The DIRECTOR then read the following letter from the Rev. W. Bracecamp :—" I understand that at the last meeting of the Finance Committee it was decided to advertise for a caretaker for Heathside Schools. At a meeting of the Eletthside School mmagers,Las chairman of the managers, was asked to write to point out that there must be some mistake, as we quite understood that the previous arrangement between us and the education authority would hold good in this case, particularly as we understand all other appointments have been made in this manner' viz., we nominate the caretaker, and you appoint. If this is so surely it is a waste of time to advertise, when we have plenty of applicants, and even should you still decide to advertise we respectfully point out that we should have the right to consider the applications and nominate to you for the appointment." Councillor DODDS moved an amendment that the reso- lution be not approved. I Councillor ROGERS seconded. _ _ _ _ _

Councillor TINN. lON remarked that he voted for the resolution because he thought there was a principle in- volved. He understood from the Director that the appointment of caretakers was absolutely in the hands of the education authority, and that any rights that the various school managers might have had under any agreement or in law were surrendered by a more recent agreement with the education autho- rity,and, therefore, in supporting the resolution he did it just to test the principle. On the occasion on which the resolution was passed, they had many applications, and several of them, so far as abilities were concerned, were equal, except that he understood that the man- agers had recommended one man. Because of that re- commendation, and purely on that account, it was thought that that applicant should have the appoint- ment. They should settle the principle of whether the committee were to make the appointment or the school managers, as it was practically giving the managers the appointment if the committee allowed them to nomin- ate and then accepted their nomination. Councillor DAVIES thought that if they adhered to the committee's resolution they would be taking away power which properly belonged to the managers, who ought to settle a matter of that kind. The CHAIRMAN said that as fur as he understood it the school managers suggested the appointment. If there was any valid reason for not confirming the appointment, the committee had a perfect right to decline to do so. Otherwise, as an act of courtesy, and wishing to avoid friction, the committee might fairly accept the nomination of the managers. (Hear, hear.) They might ride a principle to death. Councillor TINNION: You may starve it to death too. Mr. JOLLEY said he believed in principle, and wanted to adhere to it. He ventured to submit that this amendment—which he was prepared to support—was practically in accordance with a rational principle. It seemed to him that the legal right to appoint the caretakers now rested with the committee as the local authority, but it had hitherto been the practice of the committee in every instance to accept the nominations of the managers, which seemed to him to be in accord- ance with principle, as they did not own the premises of the schools which they maintained at the present time. If the committee, instead of passing the resolution, had accepted the suggestion of the managers they would only have been doing what had been done in es/ery other case and what was done immediately afterwards in the case of another school.So long as the person suggested by the managers complied with the general conditions laid down by the committee, there was no departure from principle in appointing that person. The Rev. JOHN YONGE asked why a distinction had been made between Heath Side and St. Ann's school in regard to the anpointment of caretakers. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY : I cannot get inside the heads of other members and ascertain their motives. (Laughter.) The amendment was carried unanimously. A QUESTION OF THE LOWEST TENDER. The Finance Committee had passed the following resolution :—A report of the sub-committee appointed to consider and accept tenders for the work to be done at the new education office, that they had accepted the tender of Mr. R. Lockerbie, amounting to £125, for the cupboards, shelving, linoleum &c., required, was sub- mitted, and it was resolved that the action of the sub- committee in the matter be confirmed. Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH said he was not going to move an amendment but be thought it should be known that several tenders were sent in, and one was lower than £125. It was submitted on a contract form drawn up by the Association of Builders, and if that contract form was wrong it ought to be altered as it was at pre- sent ia use by most builders in the town. Councillor TLNNION, a member of the sub-committee,

ground he did not see why the Fairfield school should be treated in a different manner from other schools. Councillor DAVIES sad that since he had ientered the room he had ascertained that there was a sufficient staff for 230 children, and yet at the present time the latter only numbered 212. Was that correct? Mr. JOLLEY replied that the committee had refused the request for an additional teacher as the school was already adequately staffed. Councillor CRA.IK said he understood that some additional information was to be brought before the committee. He did not;follow Mr. Buckton in his remarks about the pupil teacher, because she could not be considered a member of the staff, and therefore the managers were not applying for another assistant in place of a memoer of the staff. Mr. BUCKTON said his point was that another teacher was required to take the place of the one who had left. The Rev. M. STEVENSON said the teacher, who had been an ex-pupil teacher since last December, was pre- viously a pupil teacher, but neither as a pupil teacher nor as ex-pupil teacher had she been accounted upon the staff. Such help as she had been able to give she had given, but such teachers were not reckoned as members of the staff. They must treat all schools alike, and the committee, therefore, did not see their way to grant an additional teacher. For his own satisfaction he had paid a visit to the school that day, in conjunction with the correspondent and the headmistress, and he was bound to say that there were, in his opinion, circum- stances which rendered, it not staffed as efficiently as it demanded. it was a school that was giving a better education than the majority of the elementary schools in the town, such 'as French and mathematics, which were extra subjects, and that meant a better staff. If, therefore, Mr. Buckton had moved an amendment to the effect that the matter be referred lack for further consideration, in the light of the special circumstances of the school, and after what he had seen, he should have supported it. After a consul- tation with the Director, owing to the publication of the new code, it seemed to him almost certain that the whole question of staff and curriculum of the schools in the borough would have to be considered very shortly, and very seriously too, and in all probability before the next school year began after the summer holidays. They would very probably have to lay down entirely different regulations froln those which existed at the present moment, and then would be the time to consider what would be best for Fairfield School which was fulfilling a most useful work in that part of the town. He under- stood that the headmistress did not press for the new assistant until after the summer holidays. The CHAIRMAN suggested that in the circumstances the amendment should be withdrawn, and Col. BUCK- TON, with the approval of his seconder, consented. COUNCILLOR DODDS AND OCCASIONAL HOLIDAYS.

Councillor DODDS said he would like to emphasize the necessity of asking managers to curtail occasional holidays. The question of occasional holidays was most important, and he hoped the managers, as well as the committee, would do all they could to get rid of them. For instance some of the schools were closed last Thurs- day and he questioned whether it was a wise procedure. He had as great a reverence for Ascension Day as any- one, but he tried to remember it at hiS work, and he thought they should take that view of it. To waste the whole of the day was not fair to the ratepayers. He had no objection to the children attending a short service on that day but there was no necessity to give a holiday. PLAYING WITEI THE COHAIITTEE.

Mr. E. PLINSTON referred to the following resolution: —"The committee considered a letter from the managers of the Trinity National School, with reference to cer- tain complaints contained in entries made by H.NT. Inspector in the log book of the mixed department of that school. The managers' explanation being con- sidered unsatisfactory, the Director was instructed to request them to furnish the committee with specific explanations, of the complaiuts by not later that Satur- day, the 14th May, and also to intimate that, unless these explanations are reteived, and the correspondence in connection with the management of the school is considerably improved, the committee will have to con- sider the desirability of bringing into operation the powers conferred upon them by the Education Act,1902." He 'contended that the committee ought to have a thorough understanding why this particular school was allowed to play with the committee. He did not know why it was, but the ;L" rinity National School appeared to be playing with the committee week after week. He would like to know whether the necessary information had been furnished.

div.head: USE OF SCHOOL PLAYGROUNDS.
div.p: THE USE OF SCHOOL PLAYGROUNDS.
ALDERMAN BENNETT COMPLAINS OF PLAY- ING IN THE STREETS.

Alderman BF.xxErr drew attention to the following resolution :—" A letter from Mr. %V. J. Wilson, sug- gesting that the playgrounds of the various schools in the borough,be opened in the evenings during the sum- mer months for the use of children, was submitted, but the committee could not see their way to take any action in the matter." Alderman Bennett contended that there was a great deal in what Mr. Wilson sug- gested, although the committee did not see their way to adopt it. He desired to emphasize the extreme de- sirability of affording whatever facilities they could for children in the crowded p‘rts of the town finding opportunities for recreation which were so desirable. He lived in one of the best classes of streets, bat his life was made a continual burden by children playing at cricket and football—not that he had any objection to these sports—iu the streets. If they lived in some streets the children would be hauled before the magis- trates and fined. The better class of streets were not looked after with that rigid vigilance which was be- stowed upon the lower parts of the town. He was not objecting to cricket and football, but he objected to having them played before his window. rhe CHAIRMA.N : Alderman Bennett never did such a wicked thing himself. (Laughter.) Alderman BENNETT said he was brought up in the country and was able to play in the fields. He would prefer children to play in the school grounds rather than in the streets. Councillor WILKINSON said the committee had no power to make managers of schools accede to the sug- gestion. Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH observed that with reference to the National School, Church-street, he paid £l2 for repairs last year. There was a bill for this year for re- pairs to the ground, which the managers had to pay for. The committee ought to pay a certain proportion of the repairs to the playing ground. The Rev. M. STEVENSON, replying to Mr. Plinston's question, said the correspondence was not yet complete but the committee were alive to the importance of the matter, and would play their side of the game to the best of their ability. With regard to Alderman Bennett they had all the greatest sympathy for the motives which actuated him in his remarks, but the playgrounds were not the property of the comniittee, but of the managers of the schools, and the committee had only rights over them during school hours and three evenings in the week for the evening school. Therefore, it was not in the power of the committee to turn them into playgrounds as suggested. If children were turned lbose, without superintendence, a great deal of mischief would be done, and Mr. Fairclough would have a bigger bill to pay than he had at present. (Laughter). The minutes were then agreed to. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COHNIITTEE. THE INSPECTORS.

The School tt3ndance Com nittee at a recent meet- ing considered the desirability of filling the vacancy caused by the dea,th of the School Attendance Inspector (Mr. William Jones). It was resolved, "That a senior school attendance inspector be appointed to act as the prosecuting officer of the committee, to prepare the reports for the weakly rota meetings, in addition to undertaking the charge of a district, and generally to ar...t under the instructions of the Director ''; that "Mr. William Bamber be appointed senior school attendance inspector, at a salary at the rate of £llO per annum; and that he ba temporarily appointed to the position as from the Ist M5,y,1901"; and that "an advertisement be issued inviting applications for the position of school attendance inspector thus rendered vacant, at a commencing salary at the rate of 215 per annum, rising by £6 10s. p3r annum to a maxi won of £9l, the appli- cants to be not less than 21 nor more than 30 years of age." Councillor ELLisoN moved the confirmation of the minutes, and pointed out that Mr. Bamber was no t appointed temporarily, as stated, but permaftently. The DIRECTOR said it was necessary to insert the word temporarily, in order that the salary might com- mence from May Ist. If it had not been inserted, the salary could only commence from that evening. snoormys AND APPLICATIONS FOR SIT CATIONS.

COUDCMOr DODOS cimmentel upla the form issued by the committee on the occasion of a boy applying for a situation. He said that last week one of his assist- ants received an application from a boy for a situation. A form was brought from the Education Office, and he was asked to put down the rate of wages the lad was going to be paid before the lad could get a certificate of exemption from school. He did not think employers ought to be asked to state such a particular, although he WaS not ashamed of the amount of wages so far as his firm were concerned. Mr. MAY pointed out that in one case it was pr3posed to give a boy 2s. p, week, and the form gave the com- mittee power to object to unsuitable situations. (Hear, hear). THE ATTENDANCE NOT SATISFACTORY.

UpsmsT said 58 one who had criticised the com- mittee he would like to congratulate the committee on the increase in the average attendance, 86 against 83, but still 86 was not Ideal. They ought to be able to cent., and it would mean an immense get above 90 per amount of additional grant earned by the children and cut off that class of children who ultimately formed the "corner-men of the towns. Those who to-day were the " co rner-nrn " had been the children who ir atten4ance at school. were irregular in the Mr. PLINSTON said he could assurethem that the sub- committee were not satisfied with the percentage, fully alive to the important work of although they were the sub-committee every Thursday afternoon. They did not allow any further latitude than they could help, but after the special plea give to which they had to listen they were bound to give some consiaeration to the parents. He repeated that they were not satisfied with

the percentage, but that they were doing their utmost to raise it. A difficulty would arise between the sub- comrnitteeand the Medical Officer and the Health Com- mittee, as the latter had put their restrictions on the children as to the time for attending school after ill- ness. That was a cause of a great deal of the absenteeism.

Mr. FAIRCLOUGH said that no proper system was adopted, and instanced the case of a number of children being sent from school as they were suffering from ring- worm. There were other children in the family, and he should like to know if they were separated. Councillor ELLISON, in reply to Councillor Dodds, said a child between 13 and 14 years of age was not required to attend school if it showed to the satisfaction of the department that it was beneficially employed. The CHAIRMAN : The question is whether the ques- tion with reference to the wages should be considered in regard to the words beneficially employed. Councillor ELLISON said Mr. Upson had already been answered. The committee did their best to raise the average attendance. There were still over 1,000 sick children.
The minutes were passed. THE SITES FOR THE NEW SCHOOLS.

At a meeting of the Sites and Buildings Committee the Education Department having inquired how far the Sites and Buildings Committee had proceeded in the matter of supplying the increased school accommoda- tion required in the Latchford district, the Director was requested to intimate, in reply, that the committee hope to be able soon to submit a plan of a site for a new school in that district for approval. The Director submitted tracings of certain of the proposed sites for new schools, and the committee decided to view the sites, and the inspection took place on Monday. Mr. FAIRCLoUGH, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said the committee want round the town and viewed the different sites, When the matterlhad been sufficiently considered it would be brought up again. They were proceeding slowly but, he thought, safely, and he hoped they would get the sites as economically as possible. (Hear, hear). Councillor TINNION seconded, and said the committee commenced their work at a quarter to two, and with other work they had on hand they were engaged until 5.30. They did not walk; it was impossible. (Ironical cries of" Shame," and laughter). He understood the committee were likely to be surcharged with the cost of the vehicle. Councillor Dodds preferred to pay his own expenses, but he (Councillor Tinnion) was not going to do so, and also give his time to the service of the committee. Surely their work was of sufficient value to pay for a couple of horses for ten of them to view the sites, instead of having to walk round the borough. The CHAIRMAN : That is not on the minutes. (Laughter). Councillor Tinmon : To be forewarned is to be fore- armed. If-we are surcharged it is not my intention to pay. (Hear, hear, and laughter). 'r he minutes were carried,and the Council rose.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
A MONTH FOR BAD LANGUAGE._
A Runcorn, on Monday, Joseph Bushell. an old offender, was sentenced to a month's hard labour for using obsceneand profane language on Sunday morning.
DEATH OF MrCACBARKER.

• On Thursday afternoon Mr. Michwl Barker, a native of Huyton and consulting surveyor to Runcorn Urban District Council, died after a prolonged illness at the age of eighty years. He had been surveyor to the Run- corn Local Authority for over fifty years, and had snperintended the building of the whole of modem Runcorn, and had never once involved the town in legal proceedings. DEATH OF MR. THOMAS LEWIS.

The remains.of the late Mr. Thomas Lewis,of Bradley, near Frodsham were interred at Overton Church on Monday afternoon amid apt imposing demonstration of respect and esteem. The deceased wag one of the best known gentlemen in Mid-Cheshire,and took a prominent part in public affairs for upwards of thirty years. He was a member of the Runcorn Board of Guardians and Rural Council and was held in high regard by the mem- bers of the authorities. FORGING SCHOOL ATTENDANCE ENTRIES.

- --- Au extraordinary case of forgery came to light at Runcorn, on Monday, when Mrs. Keen was summoned for the irregularity of her daughter's attendance at school. A book was produced containing entries pur- porting to be made at the Wesleyan School, Worsley, and signed by Miss Grundy. These Miss Grundy, the head mistress at the school, declare I were forgeries. The defendant protested that she could not read nor write, and did not know who had made the entries. The woman was severely lectured and fined 'is. (Id. SAD WIDNES CASE.

On Monday, at the Widnes Police Station, Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest on the body of John Bentham, infant son of Mary Bentham, Nelson-street. On Thurs- day night Mrs. Bentham went to sleep with the child by her side. Another child, James, aged two years, was put to sleep at the foot of the bed. At four o'clock in the morning Mrs. Bentham wakened and found that James had crawled from the foot of the bed and was lying on the younger child. The child was afterwards found to be dead. The jury returned a verdict of " Acci- dental death." • _

div.head: -WIDNES LIBIII,. ASSOCIATION.
div.p: -WIDNES LIBIII,. ASSOCIATION.

_ Mr. Max Muspratt presided over the annual meeting of the Widnes Liberal Association, at the Liberal Club, on Monday evening. There was a fairly representative gathering.—ln his opening address, Mr. 'Muspratt spoke of the good work done by the association in the various districts throughout the division. At Huyton progress was made in particular, many old Radicals coming back to the fold.—The formation of committees for Widnes. Ditton, and Cronton was then gone into, and the following prominent representatives were selected :—Farnworth : Messrs. H. Mercer, J. Whitfield, F. Wooley, F. Horner, and J. Caldwell. Halton: Messrs. Owen, and F. Wright. Simms Cross: Messrs. T. Cosier, J. Sadler, and E. Devlin. Victoria: Messrs, D. Lewis, A. E. Calvert, F. J. Poole, and P. Quinn. Waterloo: Messrs, D. Brennan and G. Owens. West Bank: • Messrs. F. Hartland, r. J. Peters, and J. Williamson. Ditton and Cronton : Messrs. P. Whelan and P. Gow. The following were chosen on the Central Committee :—Messrs. D. Lewis, A. E. Calvert, D. Cosier, J. Brady, H. Mercer, F. Hartland, J. Sadler, P. Quinn, D. Brennan, and W. Horner. The members pre- sent afterwards had a chat on organisation matters.

div.head: ST. HELENS
div.p: ST. HELENS
CALLOUS Sr.' HELENS FATHER.

Frederick Gillebrand, a bottle-maker, of Bath-street, was summoned by the Prescot Board of Guardians, at St. Helens, on Monday, for deserting his four children. Mr. Thompson, relieving-officer, said Gillebrand had been twice sent to prison for three months on the same charge. His children had been in the workhouse since August, 1902, and had cost the guardians over £7o. Prisoner said he had been out of work, but the re- lieving-officer said that drunkenness was the sole cause of the trouble.—Mr. C. Sharpies (chairman) said prisoner ought to be ashamed of himself. They were sorry they could not give him more than the three months' maximum imprisonment. GAS PROFITS AND ST. HELENS RATES. The working of the St. Helens Corporation Gasworks has been even more successful than usual during the past year, and the profits amount to over £ll,BOO or £2,800 more than last year. For several years the com- mittee have devoted a share of the profits to help to re- duce the borough rates, and as there is this year a prospect of another increase of 3d: in the for educ%- tion the economists on the Council will no doubt make a great attack on the gas profits. The Gas Committee held a special meeting on Wednesday, and decided to lizind over £5,000 of their profits to the borough fund,as against £3,000 last year. The education rate last year was about 51d in the poand ; this year about 10d in the pound is required.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

SUDDEN DEATH AT EARLESTOWN. The Earlestown police report the sudden death of Lawrence Taylor, forty-five years of age, of Porshaw's lodging-house, who died on Saturday evening after i being picked up unconscious n Cross-lane, apparently in a fit. HAYDOCK THEFT CASE. At Warrington County Petty Sessions on WednesduY, John Platt was charged with stealing 135., the money ' of George Keith, 78, Blackbrook-road, Haydock.—The evidence showed that the men lodged together and ell the morning of the 13th inst Keith went to work, leav- ing the prisoner in bed. On returning in the evening he found the cash had beenstolen from a box in a drawer P.C. Carroll arrested the prisoner who admitted taking the money to spend it at Haydock park races.--He was lined 15s. with the option of 14 days imprisonment.

"Weil, then, just settle yourself in that easy chair, place your feet upon the back of the nearest cat, and listen,"

"It was a beautiful warm afternoon about the end of June. I sat in the front sitting room bay window, smoking a cheroot, and reading a few stray items in the morning paper. I had promised repeatedly for a month to go for a row up the river witinny friend Cunningham As I looked up from my paper between whiffs at the passers by, I saw Barry Cunningham in the distance, making his way towards my diggings' and I knew that the promised row would take place that day. I do not love womankind, in fact I hate them, and in my zeal against them, I had stated at the Club some time before, that I would never marry, for there wasn't a woman in Christendon whom I could trust sufficiently to make her my wife.
Harry Cunningham bad heard of it, and, unknown to me, bad sworn that he would, within three months, either get me engaged to be married or provide a new set of chessmen for the Club. _ _ _ _

_ I decided to go with him for the row, and as we sauntered along towards the distant boathouse,Cunning- ham began to unfold tome his love trouble. Up to lately, he said, he had been the acknowledged lover of Winifred Edgerly, and theattachment had been so plainly seen by everyone, that rumours had begun to shape themselves Into definite form, and the day of the wedding had been fixed,—that is, in the minds of the gossips. But, as often happens, the usual 'slid twixt cup and lip' was not missing from the romance of this case. Old Farmer Edgerly had began to pull up his nose at Harry, because, as he said,a booking clerk at the station was hardly good enough match for a well-to-do farmer's daughter. And to make matters worse, Harry said that Winifred herself had begun to be cool with him, and it was beginning to drive him to desperation. In fact, I began to be afraid for him, he seemed so unlike his usual self. I had all sorts of forebodings of our row up the river. Sometimes I pictured us rowing gently along, when all at once Harry jumped overboard and was drowned, and I had to figure on an inquest at a little countryside inn. _ _ _

At last we reached the boathouse, and, selecting our craft, we made a start up the river. It was a lovely day, and az we flew along the smoothwaters, our spirits rose, and Harry seemed to forget his love trouble. I was glad of this, for it would mean that I should not have to figure on an inquest,at all—a thing abominably detest. _ _

What a beautiful river the Dene is. I have never been up the Rhine, but if it can beat our Done—well, it is welcome to the victory. As we were pulling nicely past an enchanting spot, Harry caught sight of a group of picnic makers seated on the grass, partaking of a spread which they had evidently brought with them. There were two young men an two maidens; and at the sight, Harry caught his breath and nearly lost an oar. Once more the vision of an inquest rose before my mind's eye, and with the speed of lightning I seized the vanishing oar and pulled with all my sttength to straighten our little craft in the stream. Harry saw that he had made a mistake and made amends for it by pulling with all his might away from the place where he had been reminded of his trouble. At the same time I vowed to myself that if ever a woman looked at me with eyes to allure, I would strike her dead with a glance. And so we went on up the stream until we reached our destination. It was a lovely spot, the prettiest on the river. There was a little cottage standing in the midst of a beautiful garden. Around it on the left were trees, and on the right was an open space of green fields. The flowers were a sight to behold. Nowhere have I seen such richness of colour and such abundance. We sauntered about till at length we reached a group of trees to the extreme left of the garden. There midst the cluster was a little sheltered arbour. It did not seem to be more than six yards square, and was enclosed ny wooden palings. Right from the middle of the soft grassy carpet with which the ground was covered, there grew a huge pear tree, with branches spread out and reaching over the wooden palings. There was a rustic bench as well, placed alongside a table of similar struc- ture,—in truth a peaceful little haven, where even the most irritable reader might bring his book and be at peace: At the farther end of this arbour, and leaning against the pailings, were two ladies' bikes. At the sight of them I would have drawn back and led my friend away, but he had seen them too, and with his long forefinger pointing, he would fain call my attention to them. Evi- dently anything appertaining to the other sex reminded Harry of his trouble, and it was with great persuasion that led him to the cottage and ordered tea. We were greatly surprised to find that although we had telegraphed up to them, asking that tea for two might he provided, at that moment every bit of space in the cottage was occupied, and if we were to take tea there, we must partake of it under the pear tree in the garden. Harry readily acquiesced in the arrangement, and tea was laid forus on the table under the pear tree, and in close proximity to the two bikes. We had not proceeded far in the process of demolish- ing the eatables spread before us, when there came tripping down the path towards the place where we were, two gaily clad girls of about twenty and twenty- two summers. The taller of the two was dark, and possessed of a healthy-looking countenance. She bad a fine figure, and altogether made up an attractive person- age, at least, so thought I, but then a woman-hater could not judge of female beauty. The second was not much shorter in stature, but very much lighter in complexion. Her hair was loosely fastened, and, as the wind caught it and blew it about her face, it seemed to add to her beauty. An utter carelessness of conventionality char- acterized her ; and, as she came along carolling the air of a pleasant little song, I could not help thinking to myself that if all women were as attractive as she, I, even I, did not wonder that some men lost their heads. But at the sight of us, sitting eating our tea under the pear tree near to the spot where their bikes were lying, the song stopped, and with quite a sedate and womanly manner, they came forward to claim their belongings. I bent lower over my meal. It had never been my cus- tom to enter into conversation with womankind without I was forced to do; and now I thought the circumstances did not warrant me taking my attention from my enjoy- able meal. I was startled someAluit from my reflections by n faint little scream from the corner where the bikes were. Harry too, was roused, and with more display of concern than I, rushed to see what was the matter. It was but the work of a moment for him to be informed that the tyre of one of the machines had punctured. With the air of one who understood the subject, be began to examine the faulty tyre. He enquired for repairing materials, and found out at once what had caused the scream. It -,as the sight of the flat tyre, and the thought that neither of them possessed a repair- ing outfit.

_ Harry at once set to work to do the best he could under the circumstances. But it was all to no purpose, for after labouring a considerable time in a manner I could not understand. he gave it as his verdict that the tyre was unfit, and that the fair rider would have to choose another way home than on the faithless bike. After more conversation, he got the inform- ation from them that they lived at a village we had passed on our way up the river, and that they had been for a few hours' spin round the neighbourhood. With quite an abundance of chivalry, Harry offered on behalf of himself and me, to carry both them and their bikes to their home on our way down the river.

I felt, as I heard him, that I would like to punch his head, but being on my best behaviour before ladies, I acquiesced, and with the most courteous attention, we escorted them down to the riverside. Placing them safely in the stern of our boat, we commenced our return journey. Whether it was the weather, the beautiful serenity of that long June evening, the romance of the situation, or even the re-action in the life of a cynical man, I cannot say. Certainly some influence was at work that evening. Before we had reached the halfway of our journey, we found ourselves enconsced under the overhanging branches of the trees by the riverside, each of us in earnest conversation with one of the fair bike riders. Harry, with his usual audacity, bad appropriated the taller of the two ; but this did not trouble me,for the one with the fair counter- ance was a most enjoyable companion. Once rtwice my conscience pricked me, and I looked rather timidly at the banks of the river,expecting every moment to see an accusing fiend step forward out of the trees. I was, or bad been, a woman hater, and I remembered it, and it troubled me. But more strange still than all this, as we landed them at their village, the night being yet young, we were invited to moor our little boat in one of the sheltered nooks Of the river and walk up with them to their home. They suggested this, they said, that we might be personally thanked for the care we had taken of them, by the dear kira, old dad who would be so pleased to see us. I began to excuse myself, but Harry being determined to pursue the adventure further, I had to drop my scruples and go on with the affair. I shall never forget that walk from the riverside up to the village. I felt all mv antipathy to women gradu- ally disappearing, until, RS I neared the door of their home, I began to think that, after all, if I ever did think of getting married, I might seek a worse wife than the one with whom I had walked up from the river.' It was a merry little party that met in the sitting room of dear old dad that night. We all enjoyed our- selves—every one of us ; and before we left, I had promised to visit them again on the following Sunday. There was one thing I did not quite understand. Dear old dad seemed to have known Harry all his life. Of course Harry has a frank open manner, and that would account, no doubt, for some of the freedom with which

they conversed. But still that did not account for it all, and I could not make out the mystery. But mystery it was not to remain for long, for, as I rowed home with Harry in the dusk of the evening, the revelation came, and with such force, that I could hardly keep my seat in the boat.

Thinking that Harry was inconsistent with Winifred Edgerly, by his flirtation with the girls up the river, I began to mildly chide him for it. What was my con- sternation, when he burst out with a peal of laughter so loud that it disturbed the birds in the trees as we passed them. I did not charge him with callousness, as I felt at first inclined to do, but waited and tried to smother my anger somewhat. At last he spoke, and began the unfolding of such a tale, that I venture to give it in its entirety. The very harrowing love trouble with which he regaled me on our way to the boathouse was all the imaginings of his own mind. Farmer Edgerly and his daughter had never existed, but had only been called into being by Harry, to assist him. in taking my attention from the real state of things. Harry, it seems,had been engaged for some time to the Wier of the fair bike riders. She was in the plot, and, on his instructions, had arranged with the good woman at the cottage to plead a full house and put us under the pear tree for our tea. Then she had led down her sister into the enclosure where we were regaling our- selves. She trusted to Harry after that to carry the plot further. Under the pretence of examining the makes of the bikes,bef ore they arrived on the scene,he had slipped from the bench where we sat, and, unscrewing the valve of the tyre,had allowed all the wind to escape. Then he had screwed it up again. I had cone on eat- ing, not dreaming- of the plot which was thickening about my head. To come unprepared with repairing materials was one part of the duty of Harry's fiancee, and the little scream she gave as she set eyes on the supposed puncture of her sister's tyre, was very well done.

And so I had been led into the pleasant little trap, from which, as Harry saw, I had no inclination to escape. Ashe related his story, between fits of laughter, I could not help thinking of all that had happened that afternoon.

In imagination I could see him again gasp for breath as he saw the little pleasure party. And as I told him of my thoughts of an inquest, I thought that in reality it would come to pass, for he nearly choked with laugh.- inE _

then as I related to him that I would have given any- thing at the time, for him not to have seen the bikes and thus spare his feelings, off he went again, and the work fell to my lot of rowing the boat home, for he could not keep from laughing. And so the Club, although losing the set of chessmen which would have been its property if Harry had failed to fulfil his task, now have a beautiful ivory set; for I have presented them with one as a n emento o f my marriage, which took place at the little church in the village up the river, and at which dear old dad was prominent, and Harry Cunningham as wall."
