div.head: Flogging Boys.
div.p: Flogging Boys.

Sir,—The magistrates who ordered the boy, Herbert Hocknell, of Howarth-street, Runcorn, to receive twelve strokes of the birch for stealing, ought to be ashamed of themselves. Even if the statement of the superintendent of police be true that Hocknell was a bad boy, and had .given his parents much trouble, it does not follow that he will be changed into a good boy after being brutally punished in such a disgusting and foolish manner. Is this the kind of treatment we are to continue to expect from magistrates in the twentieth century? It was the boy's first conviction, apparently, and he was subj ected to the detestable treatment that we inflict on those criminals colivicted'of robbery with violence.

If the magistrates and police in other districts can deal with such young offenders without degrading them with this kind of indecent brutality, why not at Run- corn? I hope that other readers will strongly protest against this abominable treatment of boys.—l am, &c., OLD RUNCORN.

div.head: " Twelve Millions of People on the Verge of Hunger."
div.p: " Twelve Millions of People on the Verge of Hunger."

Sir,—So said Joseph Chamberlain, discussing his fiscal proposals in a speech at Birmingham on the 12th Inst., and the speaker was probably not far off the truth. But as the causes are local and not external neither tariffs nor free trade can provide a remedy. People are not hungry in England through a scarcity of food or money in the country, for there is more than enough of these commodities to provide liberally for all the inhabitants. It is not assuredly shortage of supplies but unrighteous monopolies which produce the sadden- ing and shameful state of things to which Mr. Chamber- lain refers. So long as some men, under cover of law, are permitted and encouraged to levy blackmail on the land and minerals, and others pile up fortunes for them- selves and their offspring out of the hard earnings of the poor, so long will poverty and hunger be numerous and permanent dwellers in the land. Even should tariffs or other arti- &lal devices increase manufactures and trade generally and the methods of distributing profits remain as at present, the advantage that would accrue to the workers would be infinitesimal as compared with the gains of the capitalists. Nor let the working classes indulge in the delusive hope that some day a Tory or a Radical policy will bring them salvation. These polices are only classism 'in disguise, and "classism "should be sufficiently well known by this time to be discarded for ever. The hope of the workers should lie in the policy of the Gospel,and in that alone. When law makers and employers of labour have been brought to realise the fact that doing unto others as they would expect to be done to is nota mere pulpit platitude but a Divine law binding upon every man who palls himself a Christian, a change for the better will assuredly come. Under this i rule justice and mercy will supersede the party politiciann the government of the nation; em- ployer and employs will deal with one another as brethren 'having equal rights to the natural gifts of God ; and cries for a living wage " will no longer go -up to heaven from the pit, the fields, the manufactory, or the forecastle. Nor will it be possible for a spurious philanthropy to glorify itself by the giving away of cheques for which it never toiled nor spun. And, once more, war, that enemy of God and man, and carnival of the devil, will no longer disgrace and beggar a people professing Christianity,forits incentives—greed,cruelty and ambition—will no longer find dupes to operate upon. In short a loyal obedience to" the golden rule" will do much to bring in the reign of" Glory to God, and peace and good will to men." Yours truly. lONA. May, 7904.

div.head: TRIALS OF JURYMEN.
div.p: THE TRIALS OF JURYMEN.
A Twice-Postponed Inquest at Sankey. CORONER BLAMES THE RAILWAY COMPANIES..

" I have to congratulate myself that I have got to Sankey at last "said Mr. S. Brighouse the County Coroner, in opening an inquest at the Chapel House, Great Sankey, on Wednesday, on the body recovered from the St. Helens and Sankey Canal on Thursday of last week. The twelve "good men and true "who formed the jury,were originally notified to attend at the Chapel House at 6.30 on Monday evening. Mr. Carr, the Coroner's clerk, put in an appearance, but a telegram was received from Mr. Brighouse postponing the inquiry as he had missed his train at Liverpool. Later the inquest was fixed for 10.30 on Wednesday morning and the jury- men were at the hotel promptly to time. Mr. Carr, who cycled from Ormskirk, was again in attendance, but the Coroner, who travelled by rail, telegraphed that the train to Liverpool was late and Ile inquest would have to be put off until 11.15. The jurymen waited patiently and on arriving the Coroner explained the reason for the postponements. He never knew, he remarked, that Sankey was so far from Ormskirk, or so difficult to get at. On Monday evening he was walking into Central Station Liver- pool. to catch the 5.36 train, and the station claCk stood at 5.30. He thought he had lots of time but whbn he reached the platform the train was just steaming out. It appeared that the clock had been out of order and it was attended to on Monday afternoon, but it stopped again. That morning he left Ormskirk at 8.49, but instead of arriving at Liverpool at 9.8 the Lancashire and Yorkshire Company landed him there at 9.30. Con- sequently he missed the train to Sankey. The foreman of the jury (Mr. Knowles): I understand you have put a few workingmen to great inconvenience. The Coroner: I have not; the companies have. I cannot help it. I know what inconvenience it has put you to, and I am also inconvenienced by these people. Mr. Nightingale (a juror) : I think it is a shame that the Government should require men like us to waste time in this way. The Coroner: You absolve me from any blame. Mr. Nightingale I don't blame you at all. The companies are to blame, but they have so soul.

The inquiry was then proceeded with. It appears that the body was seen floating in the canal by William Warburton, 8, Hood-lane, who,with assistance,recovered it and informed the police. P.C. Dugdale, of Collins Green, gave the description of the body which was pub- lished in our last issue. No evidence of identi- fication was forthcoming. Papers bearing Wake- field addresses were found in deceased's pockets, and correspondence with the Yorkshire police had resulted in the receipt of a letter from the Chief Constable of Bradford stating: "The description given is thatof a man who gave the name of Gladstone and who lodged for a fortnight with Mrs. Kitson, 3, Hirst- street, Bradford. He left on the 29th ult. with the intention of walking to Lancashire in search of employ- ment. He was very reticent regarding personal matters and I have been unable to learn much,but it is said that Gladstone was a tinner by trade, and that his father is a commercial traveller in Wakefield. He also spoke of brothers in Grimsby and Southport." A verdict of" Found drowned "was returned.

div.head: SORDID STORY.
div.p: A SORDID STORY.
Saturated with A1c3I:o1.

At Widnes, on Thursday morning, Rose Ann Michael, residing in Water-street, was charged with neglecting her three children in a manner likely to cause them suffering and injury to health. Mr. Knowles prosecuted on behalf of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, and said the case was a very sordid one, due to the defend- ant's strong addiction to drink. She was in receipt of good wages, which for the most part were spent in drink. Her home was filthy, upstairs in particular be- ing unfit for human habitation. The beds were desti- tute of covering the children were ill-fed and badly clothed, and their condition in the court that morning suggested starvation. Dr. Hutchinson, in stating the woman's condition, said that drink had become adisease, and he did not think she could resist it if she tried. She was a chronic drunkard, saturated with alcohol. Further evidence was given by Police-constable Mosley and Inspector Hobden. Acting-Superintendent Strickland gave the record, -which showed that she had been sent to gaol three times for similar cases.
She was committed to gaol for six months with hard labour.

Earl Rocksavage, son and heir to the Marquis of Cholmondeley attained his majority on Thursday,and the event was celebrated by the family and tenantry at Cholmondeley Castle, Cheshire. The Earl, who is in the 9th Cancers, returned from India last week. About seven on Wednesday evening a man riding a motor cycle in Beckenham-road, Penge, knocked down Mr. Young, a local curiosity dealer. Several bones in the latter's foot were broken, and after Dr. Devene had • tendered first aid Mr. Young was conveyed on an ambu- lance to the hospital.

div.head: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]
div.p: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]
SOCIAL SERMONETTES FOR WORKING MEN,
BY JOHN TAYLOR. Author of "Search Lights on. Land, Labour and Social Problems."

div.head: HOW WE GOT OUR. NATIONAL DEBT.
div.p: HOW WE GOT OUR. NATIONAL DEBT.

"Debt, grinding debt, whose iron pall the widow, the orphan, the sons of genius, fear and hate; debt which consumes so much time, which so cripples and disheartens a great spirit with cares that seem so base, is a preceptor whose lessons cannot be foregone, and is needed most by those who suffer from it most." —EMERSON.

When you tell your children that in January, 1819, the National Debt of this country amounted to the appalling sum of £1,230,295,567, and the interest on this debt amounted to £49,187,350, or nearly a million pounds every week, you must expect those children to ask you some queer questions. They will want to know hoW this big debt was incurred, and how the money was spent, and what we have got to show for it, and why they ought to pay either the principal or the interest, seeing that they were never consulted about it. And they have a right to know, for you have no business to swindle, and plunder, and rob generations yet unborn. Think of the magnitude of that debt in 1819. There were less than twenty millions of people in the United Kingdom in those days, sc) this debt works out at £6l per head for every man, woman, and child in England, Scotland, Ireland and Wales. And the interest averages nearly a shilling a week for every one of them,ornearly fifty millions a year. I.—THE FOUNDATION S OF OUR NATIONAL DEBT WERE LAID BY SPEND-THRIFT MONARCHS.

These reckless adventurers spent all their revenues, and then borrowed money from their own subjects, and never repaid it, and the first step in our wrong-doing was when Parliament took the responsibility of the "King's Debt," and gave security for the payment of the interest.

Cobbett, who hated" loan-mongers" as he hated the devil, never would admit that the nation was in debt to anybody. He said, "You talk about the King's army, and the King's realm, and the King's throne, and the King's navy, and the King's palaces, but why don't you talk about the Ktng's debt? All the wealth, and pomp, and power, and dignity of the State you give to the King, and yet you say the debt is ours. Those who have had all the land, and money, and privileges, and possessions of the nation should take the debts too. But you lay this great war debt on the shoulders of meawho never:contracted it,and who are bitterly opposed to it, and you call it a' National Debt.'" Our earlier monarchs "lived on their own." Their lands and estates, that belonged to the nation, produced a sufficient revenue to supply all their ordinary needs. It was only when they quarrelled with other nations, and involved us in costly and bloody wars, that they had to come down on their people for" aide," and "ser- vices," and" relief." Wehad no standing army, and we had no regular navy, and the whole revenue of the kingdom from the days of Henry VIII. to James 11. hardly over reached two millions a year. And yet with this small inco-ie the nation paid its way and managed to keep out of debt. Our earlier Kings were sometimes hard up, like ordinary mortals and then they raised money by forced loans. King John compelled a rich Jew at York to lend him money by the simple process of knocking out one of the Jew's teeth every day till the money was paid. The Jew had a suspicion that when his teeth were done his head would go next, so he parted with his money to save his life. James I. and Charles I. raised vast sums of money by selling the Crown lands, and putting up honours and titles and seats in the House of Lords for sale. Chalks and James IL were always in debt and difficulties, but they indulged freely in women, and wine,, and gambling,and these are said to be expensive amusements Between them the worthy pair ran up a" King's debt" of £644,263, and when James fled to France the King's creditors had small chances of ever seeing their money again, because the nation had never assumed the res- ponsibility for that debt. When William, Prince of Orauge, came to the throne, in 1688, the entire revenue of the country was only £2,001,855 a year. But William had some axes of his own ta grind. He wanted a standing army and navy, and heaps of English gold, that he might fight the French and settle his Continental quarrels at our expense. So the manorial lords agreed to pay a land tax of four shillings in the pound for the land they governed, on condition that the land should be their own: and if the King would grant them this very small favour they would assume the responsibility of the King's Debt, and find him an army and navy and plenty of money. So you and I lost our country's land and we got the King's debt in exchange for it, and a standing army into the bargain.
It-THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A STANDING ARMY WAS OUR SEuOND STEP IN WRONG- DOING.

When William got his army he did not care a fig what became of the country. The land tax fell from four shillings in he to three shillings, and then to two, and finally, by dishonest assessments and evasions, it fell in some places to nothing at all. To raise the money that the land grabbers ought to have paid, the King and his Parliament imposed taxes on births, and marriages and deaths, and heaven knowns what besides. They also raised money by loans on exchequer bills, and lotteries, and gambling schemes, but the money always went faster than it came.

At last a Scotchtnan named Paterson, hit upon a device for tapping the wealth of the aristocratic land thieves by persuading them to lend sums of £l,OOO each to the Oovernment at 8 per cent interest. These promissory notes they received in enchange afterwards became Bauk of England notes, and in a few years this scheme flooded the country with depreciated paper money.

When the King got the ships, and the men, and the money, too, he fairly went the pace. Within one hun- dred years from the establishment of a standing army and national debt, Christian England contrived to kill 1,820,000 men in battle and squander £3,383,000,000 of money in war. This works out at more than £l7l per head for every man, woman and child in the Kingdom When you think of the rivers of blood we shed, and the heaps of gold we squandered, you will probably ask me what it was all about and what we have got to show for our money to-clay.
lIL-OUR NATIONAL DEBT IS ESSENTIALLY A
WAR DEBT.

The money was spent in insane attempts to oontrol the destinies of other nations, and to enable us to " boss " the whole•world. The whole story is so sordid and selfish and shameful that lam almost ashamed to tell it. When William 111. came to the throne he was involved in a bloody war about the right of succession to the Spanish throne. We had no more right to meddle with the Spaniards in the choice of a King than I have to tell you what brand of tobacco you shall smoke. But he did meddle, and in 1690 his Parliament voted him four millions, "the vastest sum that ever a King of England had asked of his people," to prosecute the war. We were fighting in Scotland, and Ireland, and Flqinders, and France till 1702, when %William died. He fan up our "King's debt" to £12,750,000. No man living to-day can tell us why we shed all that blood and spent all that money, or what we were fighting about. We had got a standing army of our own, and, like the festive Irishman who had got a new shillelagh, we were bound to crack every skull with it. But we got neither profit, nor honour, nor glory out of these wars Smollett tells us that the long and bloody war which ended in the Treaty of Ryswick " had drained England of her wealth and people, it almost entirely ruined her commerce, it debauched her morals by encouraging venality and corruption, and entailed upon her the curse of foreign connActions,as well as a National Debt which was gradually increased to an intolerable burden." Queen Anne succeeded William, but she had neither principles nor policy of her own; so the Ministers of those days practically ruled as they pleased. She married Prince George of Denmark, and he was reck- oned one of the biggest fools in Europe. That witty monarch Charles 11. said of him: "I have tried Prince Georg) drunk, and I have tried him sober, but, drunk or sober, there is nothing in him." . . .

With two such rule f; as these we had fine times. The Duke of Marlborough fought cur battles, and took com- missions on the pay of our hireling troops and on the very bread they had to eat. His wife Sarah, Duchess of Marlborough, used to " cheek " the Queen and plunder her to her heart's content. We set all Europe in a blaze about the Spolish succession, and we fought many famous battles in Flanders and in Spain, but what they fought each other for no man has yet been able to make out. We ran up our debt to £37,000,000 when Anne died, and she left a nice crop of quarrels for her successor ; and those "states- men "who left us with thest quarrels ought to have been hanged or shot, for they were far more dangerous than wild beasts.

George I. was in Germany at the time of Anne's death, and he had hardly enough money to pay his expenses over. He was as poor asa church mouse when he succeeded to the throne of England, andhe could not speak a word of English; but he knew the value of English gold, and he knew how to appropriate it to his own use. He persuaded Parliament to vote enormous subsidies for the defence of his Hanoverian dominions, and he introduced a whole harem of German harlots to plunder us, while he kept his own wife shut up in a dungeon for more than thirty years. When he died in 1,727 he had run up the debt to £52,500,000. During the reign of George ll.the same insane policy of meddling with other nations was steadily pursued, and we squandered our blood and treasure in fighting other people's battles, and neglecting our own interests. We took a great interest in the affairs of Maria Theresa. the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, and Empress of Germany. She was one

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, May 21, 1904
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, May 21, 1904

of alp noblest women in Europe, and was affectionately called the "Mother of her people." We spent £43,000,000 of our money in fighting for her, and then we changed our minds, and spent another S:82,000,000 in fighting against her. So the debt went up merrily, and we had some stiff battles for our money; but what they were all about nobody knows, and nobody cares. In 1775 the debt was £126,000,000: and then George 111. began to make the money fly. He insisted on tax- ing our American colonies without giving them repre- sentation. They threw a cargo of his taxed tea into Boston Harbour, and invited him to come on. Hecheer- fully accepted their invitation, and poured thousands of hireling foreign troops into the colony to cut his people's throats and burn their homesteads. The wild Indians were let loose to scalp and tomahawk the colonists, and for seven long years we had a war that cost us £97,000,000 in hard cash, and in the end we lost our possessions, for we acknowledged the independence of the United States in 1783.

In 1792 our debt stood at £237,400,000. Then there was trouble with France. The French Revolution was aimed at a tyrannical King and an oppressive aristoc- racy. We had no more right to meddle in that quarrel than you have to dictate to your neighbour where he shall buy his groceries or his drapery goods. If we had left those Frenchmen alone they would have worked out their own destinies in their own way.

But we set all Europe in a blaze as usual, and we carried fire and sword through France, and Spain, and Portugal, and Belgium, and our share of that butcher's bill was £831,000,000. This works out at £4l per head for every man, woman,and child in the three kingdoms; and you will agree with me that this is a big price to pay for the privilege of preventing Frenchmen doing as i they please n their own country. If we had beedl ruled by jabbering idiots, or raving lunatics, or howling mad- men, w& could not have been more outrageously mis- governed or more shamefully betrayed. Of course we had to borrow most of the money to pay this big war bill,and then the Rothschilds, and Barings, and Goldsmiths, and the money-lenders of those days had their innings. No nation under heaven was more shamefully tricked,and duped, and deceived,and robbed, than this dear old England of ours. The thieves who had stolen our land became money-mongers and usurers. Old Shylock was not in it for ways that are dark and tricks that are mean. Bat I will tell you the rest of this disgraceful story another day. Meanwhile let me ask you to realise, if you can, the havoc, and misery, and poverty, and suffering that a century of this policy inflicted on this country. It is easy enough to say that we slaughtered nearly two million able-bodied men in our mad lust of empire, and that we squandered three thousand, three hundred and eighty-two millions of money in wicked and wanton wars, and that we ran up a debt of £1,23C,000,000. But what was the good of it all? We might just as well have flung our gold into the depths of the sea. The money was worse than wasted—it was used to uphold tyranny and oppression, and to kill freedom everywhere. And the same evil spirit is among us yet, and we are exposed to the same perils every day. Any super- annuated idiot, who calls himself a statesman, can plunge us into another costly and bloody war, as we have no law to hang him or shoot him on the spot. And John Bull tamely and meekly submits to such rulers, and permits them to tax him, and fleece him, and fool him to their hearts' content.
"He must be a thorough fool who can learn nothing from his own folly."

div.head: IN AND AR3UND WARRINGTON.
div.p: IN AND AR3UND WARRINGTON.
Tha Libra' Party and the Labour Party
Ei3l: TIIB FREE CRITIC.]

Some of the impulsive members of the Labour Party are very anxious to have an Independent Labour candidate for Parliamentary hcrnours in Warringtonlat the next election. Although lam personally in sym- pathy with most of the objects of the Party, believing that tho greater part of the fulfilment of their creed will lead to the uplifting and further emancipation of the people, yet after all it would be a most suicidal act in the present position of the political parties in Warrington to run a candidate at the forthcoming General Election. Besides the Labour. Party in War- rington should recognise the fact that most of the objects they seek to attain will have the support of Mr. Arthur Crosfield and also of the Liberal Party. The time is not ripe in Warrington to run an Inde- pendent Labour candidate and it is simply courting defeat and playing into the hands of the enemy, viz., the Conservative Party, to attempt to do so. . _ _ _

The fact should also be recognized that most of the objects aimed at by the Labour Party have the practical support of the Liberal Party and on main issues you cannot separate the two pirties. The time will come in Warrington as well as elsewhere when the Liberal Party will be called upon to support the Labour Party -but that time is not now—and therefore if the Labour Party is wise they will throw their whole might and strength in support of Ur. A.rthur Croefield.

It is one of the devices of the Conservative Party to set the Liberal Party and the Labour Party against each other, but they are silly and igiorant birds who are caught with such poor chaff as is scattered about by those who work political mischief for. their ,own particular ends and aims. I have been amused at :reading some of the—par- don me for saying so —silly speeches that have been made lately at that active political club known by the name of the Junior Conservative Club. " Junior" is an apt name for it, for the remarks made showed that their political and life experience was on the youth- ful side. When they have lived a little longer and read more they will have seen the folly of their ways. Fancy the audience being told that it was the con- servative Party and not the Liberal Party who were the friends of the working classes. Does it say any- thin,' for their knowledge of English history—pa-it or modern—to regale th&r hearers with nonsense of that kind?

One can understand a Lord, Landowner, Clergy- man an-1 Brewer being a Conservative, but a working- man never. Is not the Conservative Party the natural protector of what it calls the vested interests of the Land, the Church and the Brewing Trade? Have you never noticed that legislation by the Cmservative Party is always on behalf of,a class and very rarely on behalf of the people as a whole? Is it not very often, to quote Mr. Winston Churchill,whose eyes have at last been opened, that the Conservative Party's legislation is for the classes and not for the masses and for the millionaire instead of the million? For a working man to vote for a Conservative is a most stupid act and he • is simply helping to hinder the true progress of the race.

Recent events apart from what has happened in the past should alone convince him. Let in ask himself these simple questions: How is it that it costs 'me more to live than it did a few years ago? Is my position one jot or tittle better than it was a few years ago ? Has not the price of food, tea included;the poor woman's solace and comfort,as well as luxuries, even including such a common thing as tobacco, ivne lip ? Has trade improved or gone ? And has not for some time now the Conservativ3 P.trty had the reins of office in their hands? And have they not brought a lot of misery and disz;xnfort io.t) the homes of the working classes and als of the po )r? How can they 'forsooth therefore .c!aim to be th) " friends " of the working classes ? Verily, thy remind one of the fable of the wolf in sheep's clothing.

div.head: DROWNED WHILST CATCHING "JACKSHA,RPS." – -- Sad Ca3a at Lower Walton.
div.p: DROWNED WHILST CATCHING "JACKSHA,RPS." - -- Sad Ca3a at Lower Walton.

Mr. Dobson conducted an inquiry at the Stag Inn, Lower Walton, on Tuesday, on the body of Peter Cliff, son of Alfred Cliff, 2, Eastford road, Lower Walton a labourer. Captain Waring was present on behalf of the Manchester Ship Canal Company. Mrs. Cliff, the mother of the deceased, identified the body and stated it was that of hersou who was 81 years old. She last saw him alive at 6 o'clock on the previ- ous night. He was then in Eastford road, playing with a tin can, to which he had a piece of string attached. Ile was brought home dead at ten o'clock the same night._

Mrs. Barlow stated that her son, George Barlow, aged five years, told her he was with the deceased on the previous night. They were on the Ship Canal bank and deceased left him to go and catch "jackshar_ps." Barlow last sight of him amongst the bushes. It was about nine o'clock when Barlow returned home. Mrs. Cliff came to inquire if he had seen Peter and he told her he had left him on the canal bank.

George Brown, carter stated that he went about 9.30 to search for the deceased. From what he heard of Mrs Brown he went on the canal bank and noticed a child's cap in the water of the old pump hole which forms part of the Shin Canal and is at the bottom of the slope at Lower Walton. He grappled for the body and recovered it. There was a fence along the canal bank and the pump hole was also securely fenced. It was possible for the boy to climb round tip end of the fence. No one had any right to go there. The jury returned a verdict that the lad was drowned by accidentally falling into the Manchester Ship Canal at Lower Walton.

A young lady named Sexton, aged 16, died in the Cork Infirmary on Wednesday, from injuries sustained in a bicycle accident. She was riding her machine through a principal street on Monday when she was run into by a jaunting car, on which were two policemen who were conveying a prisoner to gaol. The horse attached to thecal. trod upon the unfortunate cyclist inflicting severe internal injuries.

div.head: SENSATIONAL BURGLARY -- CHARGE.
div.p: THE SENSATIONAL BURGLARY -- CHARGE.
Full Details of the Attempt on the
Stores.
A LOADED REVOLVER FOUND.

Full details of the sensational burglary case, briefly reported in our last issue, were unfolded at the War- rington Police Court on Thursday. A crowded Court awaited the reappearance in the dock of the prisoner, Joseph Hudson, who had been under a further remand at Strangeways since Saturday. Two charges were now preferred against him,namely—breaking and entering the house of Mr. William Ford, cashier to thg Warrington. Co-operative Society, 37, Froghall-lane, and steal- ing £2 12s. 3d. in cash, two bunches of keys, and a cash bag; and being found by night armed with a dipdly and dangerous" weapon, to wit a loaded revolver, with intent to break and enter the lock-up shop and office of the Warrington Co-operative Society in Sankey-street.

The dhief Constable said the charges against the prisoner were very grave, and unfortunately the bench could not deal with them that morn- ing in any way except to commit to the Assizes. If he made out a prima facie case on one or both of the charges—and he was sure he would—he would ask their worships to commit Hudson to the Assizes. He differentiated between Assizes and Sessions for the reason that the Burglary Act of 1896 distinctly specified that in any case where .the circumstances were of such a serious or important nature as would dis- tinguish that case from one of less importance, it would be well for the magistrates to commit to the higher tribunal. In the present case there was an ele- ment which distinctly showed that the prosecution stood forth from ordinary cases—it was that of prisoner having carried a deadly weapon, loaded, whilst com- mitting burglary and attempting shop-breaking by night. Stating the facts, the Chief Constable said the prosecu- tor was the cashier at the stores in Sankey-street and lived at 37, Froghall-lane. His son, Walter John Ford, lived with him and had a shop in Buttermarket street. These two gentlemen retired to rest within a short time of each other on May 6th. The ton left his jacket on the sofa in the kitchen, and the pockets contained a cashbag with over £2 in money, keys and other articles belonging to the shop. His father, on going to bed,left his trousers, containing 2s. in money, some small articles and the keys which belonged to the office of the Co-operative Society, on a chair at the bedside. He went to sleep peacefully and shortly after four o'clock he awoke. He noticed that his trousers were not where he had left them, and he at once made an examination of the pockets and found they had been rifled. He aroused the household and on a search being made, the cash bag containing over £2 together with some keys were missing from the pocket of Mr. Walter Ford's jacket. The house had been entered by means of the back kitchen window, and it was evident that a very daring burglary had been perpetrated. Not by any means daunted or aghast at the discovery, Mr. Ford went down town. His immediate and first thought was for his employers' interests, and he at once proceedad to the stores Some bakers were at work, and he informed them of what had taken place. They went to the yard in Cairo street, and to their great astonishment saw the prisoner rush from one of the side wings and climb over the wall. He dropped into an entry and an exciting chase was immediately commenced. Prisoner dodged like a fox hard-pressed by the hounds, but in the meantime Mr. Walter Ford had given information to the police, and acting Sergeant Foster, and Constables Stuart and Gibbs joined in the chase. Prisoner was practically hemmed in by his pursuers and did not know where to go. He was finally cornered at the back of 14, Museum street where he was pounced upon by P.C. Stuart as he was endeavouring to open a gate. He had not time to make any sort of struggle, and said "I give in. I am fairly caught." Fourteen yards from the place where prisoner was captured, and on the premises of the magistrate's clerk (Mr. G. F. F. White) a loaded revolver, fully cocked and ready for immediate use, was found. Prisoner was searched at the Police Station, and in his pockets were three cartridges which fitted the revolver. Mr. Daintith, gunsmith, of Bridge-street, would tell the magistrates that the weapon only required a slight pressure of the trigger to fire it, and that the cartridges found on the prisoner were the facsimiles of those with which the revolver was loaded. Prisoner did not deny having had the revolver in his possession. He gave the name of Hudson, which was not, however, his proper name. That, he (Mr. Talbot) would tell their worships in private, as he did not want to inflict suffering on innocent people by saying anything about prisoner's family affairs. The police had traced his history from early life. Prisoner had quite a miscellany of articles in his possession. There was us. sd. loose cash, a rolled gold watch, a gold ring, an electric torch, a gim- let, and two pieces of wire. The gimlet was used for the purpose of boring the sash of the window, and the wires were then put through thejaole and used to force back the catch. In addition prisoner had in hia pockets two pocket-knives, anda table knife (the latter also being usedito force back window catches).The articles bore the trace of considerable use, so that the prisoner was evichiptiv not a novice in his profession. Prisoner also had a microscope. ,Burglars, explained Mr. Talbot, were generally fastidious and did not care to burden themselves with worthless lumber. They therefore examined the hallmarks with a microscope. Other things in prisoner's possession were a slip of paper •bearing a train time, a pair of silent rubber shoes (worn out of consideration for his clients, because he did not want to waken them), and a pair of gold spectacles which obviously belonged to himself as he was short- sighted. When charged, prisoner said some of the money belonged to him. The cash bag and the whole of the articles missing from Mr. Ford's, were found on the prisoner, so he was caught with the results of the plunder in his possession. He (Mr. Talbot) might say that had the man intended to do any harm with the revolver he had ample opportunity to do so. Perhaps a good impulse prevailed at the proper moment, and he threw the weapon away. In a conver- sation prisoner told him (Mr. Talbot) that he meant to fire the revolver to frighten his pursuers, but not to do them any harm. Evidence was then called.

Mr. William Ford explained that the back window i)y, which the house was entered was screwed in the centre. The burglar had broken a small pane and then extracted the screw. One of the windows at the stores office had been broken, and the door and several windows had been tampered with. The stolen keys fttted the safe and all the cash receptacles in the office, and there was also the key to one of the outer doors.

Walter John Ford, grocer and provision dealer, 77, Buttermarket-street, bore out his father's evidence. Frederick Barnes, baker, 13, Fletcher-street, spoke to finding the prisoner in the yard. T'ne man scaled a wall seven feet high and dropped into an entry. Witness searched the office to see if, prisoner had any accom- plice, and the other bakersjtook up the chase. On the sill, °lithe broken window were a board and a rope. Aftei breaking the window prisoner had carried the glass some distance away, in order that it would not make a noise or impede him.

Charles Eaton, another baker, gave evidence of the chase. Prisoner, after rushing down Cairo-street, doubled back along St. Austin's-lane into Bold-streetl but he was followed. The bakers saw him enter a garden near Emmannel Church, and they had practically sur- rounded it when the officers arrived.

P.C. Stuart said he caught the -Prisoner as he w s trying to open the yard gate. After a short struggle Hudson said "I'll give in. I'm collared." Prisoner dropped his soft shoes in the chase, and they were found near the place of the arrest. Dora Caldwell, servant in the employ of Mr. H. B. White, said she found the revolver lying in a flower bed in the garden, and handed it to the police. Mr. Daintith, gunsmith, Bridge-street, said the cart- ridges found in prisoner's possession were exactly the same size as those with which the revolver was loaded. It was only necessary to touch the trigger in order to discharge the weapon. He was surprised 'it had not gone off in the meantime. The Chief Constable asked at what distance the revolver could kill a man.
Mr. Daintith: I would not like to stop it at 200 yards. (Laughter). •

- The Citief 'Constable: It would kill a man at 50 yards? Mr. Daintith replied in the affirmative. This concluded the evidence and prisoner, who had nothing to say, was committed for trial at the Liver- pool Assizes.

div.head: School Managers Sued.
div.p: School Managers Sued.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, Mary Flanaghan: Martinscroft, sued Thomas Hankin- son, Edwa72, Caldwell, and the Rev. J. Lowe, managers of St. Peter's (R.C.) school, Woolston, for 10s. for work done.—Plaintiff is the school cleaner, and she informed the Court that she was paid at the rate of 10s. per month. At Christmas she did some extra work, for which Father Lowe paid her 10s. She had not, however, received her ordinary wages for January.—Mr. Browne, who defended, explained that the case arose through the representatives of the Parish Council on the board of managers refusing to allow the account to be paid. If Father Lowe and the other managers sued were held responsible they would have to pay the account out of their own pockets. Father Lowe paid the plaintiff for extra work, but the managers would not pass the bill.—His Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff for 10s. - -lb-

ISPECIAL VISIT TO PRESTON.-Mr. Thomas Ison, Oculist and Aurist (of 'Egon's Eye and Ear Dispensary, 'Leeds, established 1871), will visit the Royal Hotel, Crewe, on Monday, June 13th, hours 11 to 1, Castle Hotel, Preston, Friday, May 27th, hours 11 to 5.30, and may be consulted on all cases of failing sight and hear- ing. New treatment without operation. Sufferers should avail themselves of the present opportunity of consultation. Spectacles adapted for weak or defective sight. Those unable to avail themselves of a personal consultation should write to Leeds for printed form of questions to answer, forwarded free. Letters to be addressed to 71, GREAT GEORGE-STREET, Leeds.—Advt.

div.head: RECHABITES IN CONFERENCE TEMPERANCE WORK AMONG THE JUVENILES.
div.p: RECHABITES IN CONFERENCE TEMPERANCE WORK AMONG THE JUVENILES.
Protest Against the Licensing Bill,

There was a large muster of workers in the juvenile section of the Independent Order of Rechabites at Warrington on Saturday, when the North-West of England Provincial Juvenile Conference was held in the Bold-greet Wesleyan schools. About six hours were occupied in the transaction of the business, and in the evening there was a public me.ting. The conference was presided over, by Bro. D. M. Main, H.S.J.T. (of Glasgow), who was supported by Bros. C. W. Churchill, H.D.R. (Corsham, Wilts ), R. Campbell, H.S. ( Manchester), H.Wells Srnith,P.H.C.R.,(Sheffield)W. A. Platt,M.B.D., (Bury),and R. C. Griffin M.B.D. (Birmingham).Fifty one, delegates attended on behalf of districts in Lancashire, ! Cheshire, North-Wales, and Dublin. The standing I orders having been passed, an address on the progress ' of the movement was delivered by the chairman who II also referred to the Licensing Bill. They were just i now passing, he said, through a grave political crisis, I and as the custodian of the lives of the children—the future men and women of our country—they had a right to take a decided stand upon these matters, and , especially upon this scheme which the Government hai I brought in for the consolidation of licences and the depriving of licensing magistrates of their powers. , (Hear, hear.) The rights of the people were being I neglected and the value of the home life sacrificed for I .P.. s. d. profits and shares. Personally he was very sorry that the Government had brought in such a Bill, and I they could not help thinking and saying that it would be I a set back to the temperance cause. (Hear, hear.) The Government dare not ask the people to sanction the Bill, as they would be bound to lose, and he thought he was stating the feelings of the country in saying that the great majority of the people were against it. The Government were defying the wishes of the people in consolidating the trade which was wrecking the life of this country. (Applause.) Their order was making great strides, and especially the juvenile branch, and he hoped they would continue to prosper. (Applause.)

div.head: ALTERATION TO RULE 3.
div.p: ALTERATION TO RULE 3.
ra3 clarer3no3 thei discls33l sugg3st9:l alt2ration and additioas to rules.

In regard to general rule 102 it was proposed "That the juvenile sick fund contribution table in this rule be reduced by one half for the two same benefits." The proposition was not approved. The conference approved the follow3ng alterations : general rule 104. Add to this rule "That the postal ex- penses for transmission of sick pay be borne by the tent"; general rule 109, That the second clause of this rule be altered by adding after, or in the first line the words "guilty of." It was proposed that a new clause 3 be added to general rule 111 as follows :—" On a juvenile member being transferred to an adult tent in the same district it shall be at the option of the adult tent to admit him without a medipal certificate 'provided he has been a juvenile member not less than lour years."—This pro- position was lost, but an amendment was carried that Ajnvenile be admitted to an adult tent without a medical certificate for funeral benefits only." THE NATIONAL CEIALLENGE SHIELD.

The conference considered a re3o n:nandation "That we recommend the Juvenile Committee of the Board of Directors to classify the competition for the Juvenile National Challenge Shield into four divisions similar to the Gaya and Block competitions, the shield to be secured as before but the remaining three highest to be rewarded in some other suitable way." An amendment was submitted that there be four Challenge Shields. This was lost and the recommendation was approved.

div.head: FUNERAL BENEFITS.
div.p: FUNERAL BENEFITS.

A recommendation was submitted "That this Juvenile Provincial Conference desires to draw the attention of all districts in this division to general rule 81, clause 3, which reads ' It shall be imperative that every dis- trict shall make provision for the insurance of funeral benefits to juveniles, in a district juvenile funeral fund, and all tents shall be connected with such fund."
In the course of the discussion Bro. W. Wright (War- rington) said he did not see how any district, after care- fully considering the position, could remain without a funeral fund.
The recommendation was approved. A DISCUSSION ON JUVENILE SMOKING. "EXAMPLE BETTER THAN PRECEPT."

Brother Tyldesley, of Bolton, brought forward the following recommendation: "Thait is desirable for superintendents Sand other workers in our juvenile movement to do all they can to press upon our juvenile members the acceptance of the pledge against smok- ing as well as that against drinking." The question, he said, was not so much one of juvenile smoking, as of the example set by adult members. They should begin at home by setting a good example to the young. Bro. Tyldesley remarked, amid much laughter, that he was sitting between a superintendent and an assistant superintendent who were both smokers. (" Shame.") He had been a, Rechabite nearly sixty years and it wag very alarm- ing to him to see the number of chilaren, many belong- ing to their bands of hope, who walked about with cigarettes in their mouths. He appealed to all the adult brethren to make the matter a personal one. They could not talk to children about the evil effects of smoking if they themselves were not consistent by denying themselves tobacco. Bro. H. WELLS SMITH hoped the members would keep the office of High Superintendent unsullied by never appointing a smoker. Anyone who aspired to the honour and was a smoker had better take heed to his ways. Bro. WIDBERLEY, of Southport, seconded the resolu- tion. So long as they had juvenile work in hand, he said, the best thing they could to would be to free themselves from" this dirty, filthy habit." Bro. JA.KEMAN, of Southport, did not approve of the proposal to " press upon " the children the signing of the non-smoking pledge.. He moved an amendment "That it is desirable for superintendents and other workers in our juvenile movement to do all they can to educate the members on the evils arising from juvenile smoking with the object of inducing them to sign the pledge against smoking." On the matter being put to the vote the members de- cid2d not to discuss it on the lines of the amendment. The CHAIRMA.N pointed out that adults who were smokers might be convinced that the habit was injuri- ous to children. He believed the resolution was a good one. He did not object to a man smoking if he was convinced that it was right and good for him, but he contended that juvenile smoking was an evil. Brother C.V. CHURCHILL Said that if smoking wits bad in itself—and he contended it was—it was not only bad for children but for "children of a larger growth." He hoped the members of the confer- ence who were really zealous for the work of Juvenile Rechabitism would feel that if they wanted to inculcate teaching against smoking into the minds of children, they themselves ought to give up the habit. If a superintendent who smoked asked a child to sign the pledge on the ground that smoking was had for him, thechild would no doubt say "What is good for you is good for me." They might just as well have some superintendents who were not teetotallers. He appealed to those who had not clean hands on the question to go in for "clean hands and clean mouths." Bro. T. CUNLIFFE, of Preston, said they were not dis- cussing the question of superintendents smoking. It was quite possible for a superintendentlto be a heavy smoker and yet be able to place the evils of the habit before the juveniles—possibly in a stronger way than a non-smoker. Bro. JAIIENIAN said they must educate the children if they were going to make non-smokers of them. He ventured to assert that their juvenile tents were not sufficiently used as educational mediums. (Hear, hear.)l Many meetings were wholly taken up with frivolity. I He would not for a moment banish everything in the I shape of amusement from the meetings, but he would see that the amusement was in the form of a sugar coat- ing to the pill. It was quite possible for, a man who enjoyed his pipe to be able to teach the members of the evils of juvenile smoking. Visiting as he did, more than 300 schools every year, he (the speaker) was brought face to face almost daily with the evil effects of juvenile smoking with regard to educational work. A cigarette smoker could not keep pace with the non- smoker in his class. In educating the children the adults would be educating themselves, and there was just the possibility that a superintendent who studied Cie evils of juvenile smoking migttt discover titat the habit was injurious to adults. The recommendation was unanimously approved. ADVERTISING THE ORDER.

On the recommendation of th) Bolton district it was decided "That it is desirable that we should do more to advertise the Order in the vnrious districts by pushing the Juvenile Magazine,' Juvenile .Motto CArds and Calendars.

div.head: PLACE OF MEETING.
div.p: THE PLACE OF MEETING.

The Bolton district recommended "That each pro- vincial conference be allowed to suggest the next place for meeting in case provincial conferences are held." After discussion the resolution was withdrawn. TRANSFER TO ADULT TENTS.

The following recommendation appeared on the agenda" In the case of a member arriving at the age of 21 years and being unable to obtain a satisfactory certificate to permit him to join an adult tent,and being prevented by rule from remaining a member of the juveniles, that some provision be made to recompense him—having due regard to the amount of sick benefit the member may have received." The proposal was withdrawn as it was considered the matter was satisfactorily dealt with by the alteration to rule 3. TWENTY YEARS' 'WORK OF THE JUVENILE MOVE NIENT. INTERESTING PAPER.
HI-other H. WELLS Sul-Tx read an interesting piper on "The Juvenile movement-1881 to 1901," explaining

that that was the period of his official connection with the Order. Twentyyears ago, he continued, the parent body was aged 49. It was estimated that there were I then 24,000 juveniles in about 600 branches. It was not clear what else there was, excepting that down thd ages from 1837 or 1838 the sum of £14,000 had accumulated and remained as funds belonging to this imperfectly organized Section or Order as it was then styled. Those of them who delighted in remini- scence rejoiced in the fact that much that could not be tabulated took practical shape in those days and that good, earnest devoted men and a few women were con- trolling and shaping the lives and characters of many rough diamonds with less of the financial in their curri- culum than was contained in present day charts or courses. It was quite certain, however, that from the time of the disruption in the fif- ties to the eventful period beginning with 1881 there was a desire of the movement to emerge from its chrysalistic state to one of greater beauty or perfection. Indeed the Douglas Conference in August 1883 and the anticipation of the Jubilee H.M.C. to be held in August 188:5 seemed to have set many people thinking and working. The general rules of the Order were brought into continuous readable condition and, he believed, a Chief Superintendent of Juveniles was first so styled in those days. The difficulties of the times were largely as to methods. Mr. Wells Smith pro- ceeded to review the decisions as to organization at vari- ous conferences.ln 1893 the newly elected board entrusted the re-arranging of general rules and the incorpora- tion of rules governing the juveniles to the respected Bro. J. Lee, H.C.R. (since deceased) and him- self, and ultimately they satisfied the registrar of Friendly Societies,and secured beyond doubt the Juvenile Section as an equal legal part of their constitution. In 1897 the EI.M.C. approved a recommendation from the Board of Directors that the registration of the Juvenile Section rules as formerly existing be cancelled. The cancellation followed, fourteen years being the time covered by the transition stages of a reform far-reaching in its character, calculated, he believed, to bind the membership more firmly together than any other matter dealt. with Curing his official , connection with the Order. He might be pardoned for passing lightly over his four years services as H.S.J.T. 1895-9 but he wished to say that from the moment that he felt the juvenile movement to be properly placed, he , aimed at securing the rights and privileges for its Sectional Chief with such powers of decentralisation as 1 a growing high-class educational body should be possessed of. Time required him to draw the I contrast. They had very little but the teaching in 1881. Now what had they not secured? They were the most perfect of Juvenile Benefit Societies and the best I organised of Juvenile Temperance Organizations. They had 130,000 juveniles contributing for benefits, an 1 increase of 106,000 in 20 years, and they had purified the stream of entrants into the adult tents during that period by passing on more than 46,000 juveniles, most of whom had been abstainers from birth. They had organized their districts, tents and funds until the benefits and ideas were practically one and the same throughout the Order with the provision adopted at Swansea in 1903 that all juvenile tents should be connected with a District Juvenile Funeral Fund. General rule 33 provided that a juvenile district should be a branch of an adult district, and rule 81 gave two methods of Juvenile Dis- trict management to select from. The levy on the juvenile membership of one farthing per quarter was merely nominal. " What is our mission for the next 20 years ?" continued the speaker. "Surely still to train the young, to guide their footsteps, to educate them in the moral beauties of self-restraint and dignified endeavour, to make men of them in the real sense and to supply the ever-increasing need and demand. To be less of a Benefit Society (par- ticularly to the sickness benefit side) and to be more of a teetotal society. To change our methods with the times, to be as witty and as clever as the jester at the pot-house, to be broader in our views and less violent towards the victims of the enemy, and above all to teach ourselves to live the lives that we would have others follow. We must do more to shock the Church at the use of intoxicants at the Lord's Table and be prepared to bear contumely and to crucify the hatred that is in our hearts, and to be faith- ful to Him whose allegiance we own. Ours is essenti- ally a working class organization, and can only be strengthened by a considerable section of the middle classes when we get nearer superannuation benefits as decided at the last H.M.C. We may, however remember our duty in our station of life by making our homes our empire, and by, remembering that in that great Union of States across the Atlantic two men like unto ourselves (Lincoln and Garfield) did so much for their fellow men as to continually excite our admiration." (Applause). Supplementing his paper with q. brief speech, Bro, Wells Smith strongly criticised the present system of flaying sick benefits in the juvenile section. So long as they made sick pay a sort of high-class•out-door relief self-respecting members would not allow their children to join them. They must make the section a high-class total abstinence society where there was temperance teach- ing. Healso contended that Rechabites should be in the van as far as superannuation benefits were con- cerned.
On the proposition of Brother Churchill, a hearty vote, of thanks was accorded to Bro. Wells Smith for his paper.
THE COLLECTION OF JUVENILE MEMBERS'
CONTRIBUTIONS.

A short discussion took place on this subject. Several members expressed the opinion that lapses Would be greatly reduced if there was a system of collection of contributions, instead of the juveniles having to bring the money to the tent meetings. Bro. Johnson, of Hey- wood, gave details of the success which had attended the adoption of this method in connection with the adult tents at Heywood. Bro. W. WRIGHT, of Warrington, said they would have to be cautious in the matter. He believed in educational meetings for the young, and his opinion was that if the contributions were collected from the houses the main object of their juvenile work would not be fulfilled. He agreed that members who could not possibly attend the meetings should be called upon by collectors. By relieving all the juveniles of the obliga- tion of payinr, their contributions at the tent meetings they would be running the risk of increasing the num- ber of lapses. BrO. CAMPBELL (high secretary) pointed out that in 1900 the Order lost 12,882 adults and 16,552 juveniles by lapses; in 1901, 12,723 adults and 18,737 juveniles; 1902, 12,865 adults and 17,836 juveniles. With those figures before them they must conclude that there was some- thing wrong or the lapsing rate would not be so large. If it were possible to reduce the number, even one half, by collection, it was an argument in favour of the system. They could collect from members who were in arrears or did not attend regularly. PROTEST AGAINST THE LICENSING BILL.

Bro. C. W. CHCRCTIILL moved "That this provincia, conference of the Independent Order of Rechabite3 in the North-West of England is strongly opposed to the Licensing Bill before Parliament on the ground that it gives a vested interest in a licence which has always been granted as a privilege. It therefore calls upon the members of Parliament favourable to temperance reform to strongly oppose the passing of the Bill in its present form." He said that Rechabites had been charged with belonging to that extreme wing of the temperance party which opposed every and any temperance reform simply because it was not based on the lines which they desired. They were surprised that men holding high offices in the Government should be so ignorant as to say such things about their Order. Rechabites held some stronty, principles and they ob- jectei to making a vested interest in licences which would certainly mean handing over a sum estimated at between 200 and 250 million pounds as a freehold to the brewers. Whatever specious arguments were advanced as to the publican benefttting under the Bill, he did not believe anyone who had given the matter five minutes consideration would for a moment imagine that one out of every 100 of the so-called licence-holders was going to receive a single penny. Whatever might be said to the contrary or to the effect that compensation would come out of the trade, the Bill was evidently intended to strengthen the position of the great drink traffic in their mist. What was to prevent the Government, with their auto- matic majority, bringing in another Bill and shifting the burden of pros iding compensation from the shoulders of the trade on to the shoulders of the taxpayers? The Government had done things just as outrageous already. The motion was unanimously agreed to. The conference expressed its entire confidence in the action taken by the High Officers in issuing petitions against the Bill. An excellent Luncheon and tea were served to the delegates at the Winmarleigh Cafe and the members of the Warrington District were heartily thanked for their admirable arrangement.

div.head: PUBLIC MEETING.
div.p: PUBLIC MEETING.
REV. G. H. CARNSON AND COUNTER-ATFRAC.
TIONS TO THE PUBLIC-HOUSE.

In the evening a procession of representatives, adult and juvenile members was formed In Bold-street, and headed by the new district banner and the Brick street and Friars' Greens chools brass band, paraded the principal streets. A meeting was afterwards held in Bold-street school;presided over by the Rev. G. H. Carnson. The CIIAIRMAN said he believed total abstinence was the wisest and best oourse to take. They were in the midst of a great fight just now—indeed he did not know when they had not been. Even yet they had got hardly any nearer, and it seemed as if they had been ' spending their shot against granite walls. He had been wonderinc, whether they ought not to begin at the other end, and try and offer the Workingman something in lieu of the public-house. If the publicans and brewer& were determined to get rich out of the workingmen, temperance workers would have to put something within the reach of workingmen that would empty the public-house. Until they accomplished that, he did not think they would be doing very much. He hacl'a great deal of confidence in the workingmen. Hp did not believe that as a rule they went to the public-house simply for the drink. They went for the company, the music, and the talk. He thought that if as art experiment some place could be provided as a counter-attraction to the public-house, the temperance party would be doing a very good thing. He knew it would not pay, and that

would be the serious difficulty. Subscriptions would have to be obtained for some time; but really he did not think teetotalers were spending a tremendous SUM of money on their teetotal work. They did not spend as much upon it as the churches did on theirs, and certainly not as much as the public authorities spent on ' other things.in coll3luslon he urged the children to take advantage of the benefits of the Order by being thrifty - and providing for a rainy day. Bro. D. M. MAIN spoke at some length upon the evils of intemperance and em- phasised the responsibility which rested upon temperance workers. What, he asked his hearers, were they doing to uplift those who had been dragged down to the slums? Had they made their influence felt on behalf of the safety of mankind? Were the churches doing what they ought to do in regard to this, great question? Hal they clean hands? Had they net participated in the benefits that came through some of the chann3ls of the drink trade, and had not some of their ministerial friends shares in the breweries? If they were despondent they should take heart again, and go forward with the great hope that they would one day triumph in the battle they were carrying on. (Applause). Bro. C. W. CHURCHILL said the losses in the South African war were nothing to be comfared with the numbers killed at home during the same time' by drink. Rechabites were determined that they would not allow the traffic to be more firmly rooted in the land if they could avoid it. However they might seem to be defeated by stronger forces they had the great Gocrof righteousness and justice on their side,and in th e end they would prevail. (Applause.) Songs were rendered by Miss Elsie Spruce, Messrs. Gough and Boys.

div.head: PRESENTATION OF CERTIFICATES,
div.p: PRESENTATION OF CERTIFICATES,
Meetin4 in Brick-street Mission.

On Monday evening a public meeting was held in Brick-street Mission, and several juvenilE members were the recipients of legion of honour certificates. Bro. W. Wright, D.S.J.T. presided and was supported by Bro. R. Campbell, H.S., and Bro. W. A. Platt, M.B.D. An interesting programme of songs and recitations wit& submitted by Elizabeth H. Bibby, Phyllis Ingham,Elsie Wright, E. Gallop, Florrie Noble, A. Wood, and Master S. Jones.

An address was delivered by Brother CAMPBELL whcr gave a brief history of the ()icier which was instituted for adult members in 1835. Two years later twenty - juvenile branches were op3ned. They had now' 130,000 juvenile members, and one of the most remark- able things was the smallness of the death rate whiclz only reached about 2 per 1,000 each year. No tent had been allowed to break up for want of funds. Every branch, irtespective of its membership or liabilities, hail a claim upon the central funds for relief purposes in case of ,the branch funds being exhausted. There were 203,000 adult members of the Order,l and the total amount claimed from the central relief funi last year was not more than £lOO. At tho pit:sent time they- were completing a valuation of the Order. In regard to the insurance and funeral funds,• they had £1 4s. 81. to meet every ,C 1 liability. During the year the Order had been ex- tended to several new localities. New tents had been' opened in Germany, the Transvaal, Gibraltar,and Malta. There were representatives of the Order in 160 ships in the navy, and also one in the royal yacht. Branches of the Order were to be found in nearly every part of the' world. Twenty Rechabite magazines were published, and the Gloucester district had recently purchased n house and estate for the purpose of founding a conva- lescent home. He thought Lancashire and Cheshire would have to follow that example at an early date. The income to the Order was about £350,000 a year,and they spent about £230,000 in benefits to the members. It would thus be seen that a considerable amount was being saved to pay old age pensions. During the past eighteen years their income had been three and a half millions and they had spent only two and a half millions. Such a large Order had an undoubted claim to recognition.- When they found measures like the Licensing Bill intro- duced toi retard the temperance movement, it was time for them to look round and see what could be done to prevent, if possible, the passing of a Bill that would be - detrimental to the people. (Applause.) Bro. W. A. PLATT Presented legion of honour certifi- cates to the following girls :—Lettice Warburton, Elizabeth H. Bibby, Elsie Wright, and Marian Betties. He also made each recipient a present of a brooch and- a bound volume of the "Juvenile Magazine."

div.head: FIRES AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: FIRES AT WARRINGTON.
Mr. E. Connor's Stables Gutted.

In the early hours of Sunday morning a fire which did considerable damage broke out on the King-street premises of Mr. Edward Connor, cab proprietor. A lamplighter named Hadlan saw flames issuing from the building and at once informed Constable Metcalfe was in the neighbourhood. The two proceeded to the- fire station and gave the alarm, and afterwards returued to King-street and rendered valuable help in reill°°'l,-g vehicles and other property. The fire brigade pronlPl' responded to the call under the direction of Super iii tendent Turner, and the engines "Captain' " Major " were got to work. The buildihg,. which comprisea stables, granary, and saddlery' department, was well alight and it was at once seen that the brigade would have a difficult task. A large number of horses had been released from the stables in the cellar and on the ground floor by an employee named.E. Cartwright. The firemen workedhard to save adjoining property which was endangered, And fortunately their efforts were successful. Although there was no wind the' inflammable nature of the contents caused Mr' Connor's premises to blaze fiercely, and it was three hours before the flames were got tinder control. It Was' then reported that a horse was missing and the firemen' commenced to search for it. Ultimately they found a black mare in a corner of the ground floor stable alive' but evidently suffering from fright. Tons of water must have fallen on the animal. One of the stableulen' then descended into the flooded cellar stable, having removed a portion of his garments and found another horse alive. It was brought safely out amid much e"-- citernent. It had been in the he-at and hot water for, over three hours. The brigade were kept hard at 'icor!' until 10 a.m., when the engines were withdrawn. Th. tour-storeyed building, with its valuable contents, was- totally destroyed. A ward of praise is due to a detach- ment of police in chirge of Inspector Taylor, who rell"- dered acceptable assistince. The brigade were again summoned to the smouldering debris on Monday morn- ing, and remained several hours. The origin of the fire. is a mystery, but it is believed, it broke out in tye- , hayloft. The damage, which is estimated at £2,000 not quite covered by insurance. Fortunately the flame!' did not spread to the carriage building departmenl' which is also in King-street, and the fire brigade are to be complimented upon their smart work. About 1 o'clock on Sunday afternoon a boy named J. Darbyshire, of Brick-street, was passing Mr. It..t Naylor's timber works at Howley, in company "7:il. several friends. Noticing smoke issuing from the boiler, house, Darhyshire climbed over the works wall, an found that the structure was well alight. He went to• the Fire Station and gave the alarm, but when the: brigade, with the two steamers, arrived at the works 11' was found that the flames had been extinguished hY the watchman who resides on the premises, assisted bY- a number of workmen who live in the immediate neigh- bourhood. The roof of the boiler house was barn?" damaged. The superinterdent congratulated the work(i men upon their efficiency in putting out the fire, great praise is due to them as a serious• conflagratiop was prevented.

successor, Dr. R. Spence Watson. The Rev. Dr. Horton has also become a Vice-president. The Society's lecturers and agents have given 600 addresses on Peace and International Arbitration. The observance of Peace Sunday was even more successful than on previous occasions, about 6,000 sermons having been delivered, and $26,000 papers and pamphlets dis- tributed in connection with it. The Society's invitation was also addressed to 1,426 Protestant Pastors in France. A large amount of other literature has been published ;by the Society. The Children's paper, "The Olive I Leaf," now in the second year of its publication,l continues to be appreciated. The autumnal meet— ing - I ' was held this year in London, the Queen's Hall being taken for the purpose. The Secretary, in addition to meetings in this country, attended the rPeace Congress in Rouen and Havre, and the meetings of the International Law Association in Antwerp. Addresses were presented to President Loubet on the occasion of his visit, and more recently in appreciation of the Anglo-French Agreement, and td the King of Italy when he visited this country, and received a depu- tation at Windsor. A special appeal was made to all the Clergy and Ministers of the land, at the beginning of the present war, urging them to use their influence to promote a peaceable spirit and to prevent the spread of hostilities A second appeal was circulated through the Press. The report acknowledges the assistance of the Press on this and other occasions,and after references to the "Herald of Peace," the organ of the society,and th 3 lantern lectures which have been added to within the year, and which t are placed gratuitously at the disposal of members,con- eludes with a reminder that the character of the times demands still greater activity. "The signal successes which have been gAined on behalf of peace ought to furnish a mighty stimulus to increased effort."

A 30 Million Candle Power Beacon. The oil lamp in the lighthouse is gradually being re- placed by the electric light. According to "The Elec- trical Magazine." opinions have differed as to the pene- trating power of the light,in foggy weather for instance in the streets of London on a November day, the small gas lamps often appear to show to greater advantage that in clearer weather, and this is generally put down to their greater carrying power. There is one solid fact, which does not admit of dispute, and that is that in the most advanced lighthouses, and those occupying the most important positions on the coast, the electric light is being gradually introduced. At the lighthouse at Heligoland, occupy- ing one of the most important points on the German coast at the entrance to the Elbe and the port of Ham- burg, the height of the light above high water mark is 270 ft., and it can be seen by an observer,standing 12ft. above the level of the water, at a distance of about 25 miles in clear weather. The installation is one of tile largest in the world, the total light emitted being not less than 30 million candle power, and the duration of the flash about one-tenth of a second. The flashes follow one another at intervals of 5 seconds and in this way the light can be identified by the observer. These results are obtained by erecting three reflectors, placed at angles of 120 degrees, on a rotating platform, the reflectors being 30 inches in diameter, and of paraboloidal form, with a focal length of rather less than 10 inches. This lighthouse may be taken as repre- senting the latest development of the art and science of the specialist in this direction. It is alleged to be second to none in the world, and having regard to the volume of ocean going traffic which passes beneath its light, it may well be called upon to be up to the latest requirements of an exacting public. •
